World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Disaster diplomacy and a persistent peso
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the weekend before this week began in Puebla, kicking off the 2026 National Reforestation Day from the mountain pass between the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes. There, marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, she declared that the Paso de Cortés — named for the conquistador who marched through it in 1519 — would be a great candidate for a new name.

On Monday morning, the president’s attention had shifted south: a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing hundreds. Sheinbaum immediately pledged Mexico would send Colombia everything it needed, but the country’s military rescue brigade quickly ran into a diplomatic hurdle, part of a tangle of certification disputes and friction that unfolded even as quietly extraordinary Mexican solidarity continued — not just with Colombia, but with wildfire-stricken Canada as well. Colombia’s quake also revived an old question for Mexico, one we explore in more depth here: with Venezuela and now Colombia both rattled by major temblors this year, does Mexico’s own position on the Pacific Ring of Fire mean its odds just went up?

Otherwise, the week of Aug. 10-14 in Mexico brought big economic headlines, athletic glory and advances in the Ayotzinapa criminal case.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico extends a hand abroad

Mexico’s instinct to help its neighbors was on full display this week. More than 300 Mexican firefighters traveled to British Columbia to help battle over 100 active wildfires that have forced tens of thousands to evacuate, drawing an outpouring of gratitude on Canadian social media. Farther south, a 45-member team of Mexico’s famed “Topos” rescue brigade reached Cali, Colombia, on Wednesday to dig through earthquake rubble — but only after Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella initially rejected their help, citing sovereignty concerns.

On Thursday, Sheinbaum confirmed that an official Mexican Army rescue brigade had not been authorized to enter Colombia and therefore remained at home. According to the president, Colombia’s new government demanded a type of certification the Mexican team does not have. Mexico kept sending humanitarian aid regardless — more than 58 tonnes of food, water and medicine by week’s end.

Ex-governor bound over in Ayotzinapa case

In one of the week’s most significant justice developments, former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre was ordered to stand trial over his alleged role in the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students. Prosecutors allege Aguirre ordered the destruction of security footage from Iguala’s Palace of Justice on the night the students vanished, partly to protect a nephew with ties to a local criminal gang. Aguirre, who resigned as governor weeks after the disappearances, remains jailed at the Altiplano maximum-security prison as the case — one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved human rights tragedies — grinds toward trial nearly 12 years later.

The super peso returns

Mexico’s currency briefly broke back below 17 to the US dollar on Friday morning for the first time since 2024, in what analysts are calling the return of the “super peso.”

The peso has now strengthened for four consecutive days and appreciated more than 5% this year, a move Citibanamex attributes largely to global dollar weakness rather than Mexican fundamentals. Still, by the MND Peso Index™, which compares a basket of goods in Mexico and Dallas, the currency looks overvalued by 2.4% — a smaller gap than June’s 2.9%, suggesting the exchange rate isn’t too far removed from what prices on the ground would imply.

Homicides fall, but Sinaloa gets reinforcements

Security officials reported on Wednesday that the daily homicide average has fallen 51% since Sheinbaum took office, with July recording the lowest monthly tally of her administration so far. Even so, nearly half of the country’s murders remain concentrated in just seven states, Sinaloa among them. That reality was underscored by the Navy’s deployment of over 1,700 personnel to Mazatlán after the port city logged its bloodiest month of the year in July, as fighting between rival Sinaloa Cartel factions Los Chapitos and Los Mayos continues to spill beyond Culiacán into the tourist-heavy coastal city.

Visa fights spill into the mañanera

Washington’s campaign against Mexican political figures widened this week.

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador and a former Morena party organization secretary, said the United States had revoked his visa, accusing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his deputy of a politically motivated move. At Friday’s mañanera, Sheinbaum called the decision “essentially political in nature,” urging Washington to produce evidence against anyone it targets while insisting the dispute won’t spiral into a broader conflict with the United States.

Business indicators to know

Peso: Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued.

Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued. Inflation: July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.”

July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.” Jobs: Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high.

Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high. Industry: Industrial activity grew 0.2% month-on-month in June, lifted by mining and construction, while manufacturing logged its 12th straight month of annual decline.

Cyclospora cleared in the Riviera Maya

After British health authorities flagged a spike in cyclosporiasis cases among travelers returning from Mexico, Cofepris tested food and water samples from 16 Riviera Maya hotels — and found no trace of the parasite. All 43 samples, drawn from Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Isla Mujeres, tested negative, and no contamination indicators turned up elsewhere. Mexico’s Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cyclosporiasis cases nationwide this year, a tiny fraction of the population, though the source of the UK cases remains unidentified.

Tourism notes

June brought 4.11 million international tourists to Mexico, up just 1.1% year-on-year — a muted bump given that Mexico hosted 12 of its 13 World Cup matches that month.

Tulum’s airport will regain five international routes this winter to cities in Canada and the United States, part of a state push to reverse a steep decline in international traffic.

Sargassum accumulation, though still tracking toward the second-heaviest year on record, has begun easing across most monitored stretches of the Quintana Roo coast as collection efforts and shifting currents bring relative relief to hard-hit beaches like Tulum and Playa del Carmen.

Mexican athletes seize the moment

It was a banner week for Mexican sport. The under-20 men’s soccer team defended its Concacaf title, beating the United States 2-0 at Mexico City’s Estadio Banorte for a record 15th championship, with defender Cristóbal Alfaro scoring twice.

Meanwhile, Mexico delivered its best-ever medal haul at the Central American and Caribbean Games, where the delegation topped the table with a record 407 medals in Santo Domingo. The government announced every medal — not just an athlete’s best result — will now earn a cash prize, a change Conade chief Rommel Pacheco said was Sheinbaum’s own idea.

World.title: How fragile is Chacahua’s lagoon ecosystem? A conversation with locals on the Oaxaca coast
World.content:
A bus from Puerto Escondido. A minibus, aka colectivo, from Rio Grande. Then a lancha, or small boat, across the water to Zapotalito. One more open-air truck and you’ve made it.

Laguna de Chacahua sits along the western coast of Oaxaca, part of the state’s more than 300 milePacific coastline – a lagoon ecosystem padded with jungle flora, where the network of mangroves roots the island in its gurgling brackish tides.

It is part of the municipality of Villa de Tututepec de Melchor Ocampo and around 100 miles down the coast from the popular beach city of Puerto Escondido. In the daytime, the high sun smelts the soft sand and rocks while hammocks loll idly in the low breeze. After sunset, bioluminescent plankton set the water aglow in a neon blue glacé.

Technically, Chacahua is a barrier island, meaning it is not entirely separate from the mainland but is only accessible by boat. The community is predominantly Black and Afro-Indigenous, partially linking back to the Spanish enslavement of Africans and their forced labor in Mexico in the 16th and 17th centuries. But many residents make their way over from the mainland to surf, fish and enjoy the more relaxed pulse of daily life.

“Here, you can be whatever you want to be,” Augusto, an architect living in Chacahua, tells me. “And nobody is going to look down on you; you’re living in a free place.”

‘The sea is starting to reclaim the land’

But it isn’t all peace in paradise. Coastal environments and their communities are facing increased exposure to natural hazards.

The rainy season from June to September brings storms and natural climate variations, but Oaxaca state’s geography, situated along Mexico’s southwest Pacific coast, leaves it particularly vulnerable to climate change. Pacific hurricanes and Atlantic basin tropical systems pose a dual threat, alongside the increasing reality of heavy rains, droughts, and rising temperatures and sea levels.

While it is difficult to find more localised data for the island, average yearly temperature in Oaxaca City rose by 1.1 degrees Celsius (2 degrees Fahrenheit) between 1994 and 2024. While this figure may seem small, it represents a rapid change over three decades, even at the local level.

Global sea level rise has been affecting the coast of Oaxaca, and Chacahua is no exception. Drawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) 6th Assessment Report, NASA’s Sea Level Projection projects extreme sea level rise along Oaxaca’s Pacific coast, and the lagoon’s low relief offers little defense.

Sitting in a cabana just 100 meters inland, Augusto points towards Playa Chacahua. “The sea is starting to reclaim (the) land. That’s why the houses over there are collapsing.”

It was Hurricane Pauline in 1997 that dramatically shifted the landscape of Chacahua, the lagoon rising to such a level that a new inlet was created and swathes of the beach were eaten away. Today, the beach faces an ever-greater risk due to the damaging erosion.

‘Everyone fishes sooner or later’

Fishing is integral to life in Chacahua, and the catch is diverse – shrimp, puffer fish, oysters, blue crabs, and red snapper by the Bajo Este. “There are all kinds of fish,” Antonio says. “There’s a bit of everything here.”

Antonio started fishing at the age of 8 with his grandfather. At 17, he began fishing for sharks; tiburoneros (shark fishermen) use a simbra, a 14-kilometre-long (9-mile) fishing line with around 300 hooks every 18 meters.

“We’d head out along the Guerrero coast, going out toward the horizon where the sun sets … to where you can’t see a thing anymore,” Antonio tells me. “Transatlantic ships pass through there. We’d stay one night and head back the next day.”

The population is no more than 800 and, according to Antonio, more than half of its residents are fishermen.

“Everyone fishes sooner or later,” he says. But security isn’t promised. “Later, some move onto other jobs because fishing is just a matter of luck.”

Santiago was born on the island and has been a fisherman for 20 years.

“Because of the rains and the storms that come, it’s more dangerous now. It’s more dangerous than compared to before. It used to be a good life.”

The ecocide of the Chacahua-Pastoría Lagoons is a key culprit, with toxic chemical influx from local oil-crop industries, as well as chemical waste from a lime-oil factory beyond Zapatalito. Shrimp and fish populations are declining. Locals have faced the consequences of diminishing catch and have even demanded government action.

In 2013, local fishermen’s collective, supported by the Human Rights Ombudsman of the People of Oaxaca (DDHPO), produced a report regarding violations against the inhabitants of Zapotalito, Chacahua, La Pastoría and El Corral details the public health risks, loss of livelihood and environmental degradation that communities have faced due to federal infrastructure projects, such as Irrigation District 110 and breakwaters in the Boca de Chacahua.

The resilience of mangroves

Part of a roughly 51-square-mile national park designated in 1937, Chacahua Lagoon is surrounded by a network of mangrove corridors, anchoring the island in verdant, woody tresses. Mangroves are trees or bushes that thrive in brackish tidal waters, often where a river meets the sea, offering nesting grounds for a diversity of wildlife.

The red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), black mangrove (Avicennia germinans), white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa), and buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) are also essential to maintaining the health of the local ecosystem.

Their long, complex root systems are adapted to survive in low-lying waters, optimising oxygen absorption and filtering out saline contamination. They endure conditions that are virtually impossible for other plants, and their resilience is recognized by the locals.

Angél runs a grocery shop in the central square. His family has been living on the island for generations. The salinity of the sea is getting worse, he concedes, but “the mangroves are strong. We don’t have to cut them that much.”

“The mangroves are doing well,” Antonio agrees. “They’re tough. When they fall, they land upright,” due to their roots.

The resilience of locals

Perhaps Antonio and Angél aren’t giving themselves enough credit. In reality, mangroves are vulnerable to climate change, specifically increasing salinity, hurricane events, and worsening El Niño patterns. But it’s the locals who demonstrate climate resilience every day, in working as a community to restore the things that Angél says the government is neglecting financially and administratively.

“The effort is made every day; it’s part of life here on the island,” Augusto says. “People engage in what’s called tequio, voluntary community work to help the environment.”

In the same way, the fishermen are taking it upon themselves to try and mitigate the marine pollution, but there is a limit to what can be done without wider support.

Tequio “takes place because people love their land,” Augusto explains, but as Angél marks, the climate is getting hotter, the sea saltier, and the water warmer.

On top of this, the briny waves of gentrification are lapping at the island’s shores. Lavish cabanas with their polished wood walls and hiked-up rent are beginning to rear their haute heads.

Tourism has also been shown to worsen pollution. In Mexico’s Caribbean coast, the tourism sector accounts for one-third of the region’s total waste, and light pollution has been proven to pose threats to turtle populations, of which species such as the Leatherback are populous in Chacahua.

What’s in store for Chacahua?

Oaxaca has been strongly affected by hurricanes Otis, John, Erick, and Boris in the last four years.

While federal budgeting continues to be an issue for Natural Protected Areas across Mexico, local cooperatives, in tandem with the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (CONANP), are taking measures to respond to growing tourism in the state of Oaxaca and have made major steps in wildlife protection and sustainable infrastructure, but the direct effects on Chacahua are yet to be comprehensively reported.

Looking into its climate future, Chacahua is standing at a delta. It goes without saying that the community has demonstrated its climate resilience through supporting mangroves, keeping the waters around the island clean, and reconstructing and relocating seafront buildings.

However, without sufficient government support, the effects of environmental jeopardy and injustice may ultimately uproot the mangrove system and local way of life to an irremediable degree.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: Latin American Markets: The Week Ahead, August 17–21, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio Times Markets · The Week Ahead

Key Facts —FOMC Minutes Wednesday’s release of the July meeting account is the week’s pivotal external event, with traders parsing the committee’s reasoning for the pace of rate cuts. —Banxico Minutes Thursday brings the account of Mexico’s latest policy meeting, the clearest read yet on how far the central bank intends to ease. —Colombia GDP Tuesday’s second-quarter print follows 2.2 percent annual growth in the first quarter, a test of momentum as inflation drifts higher. —Chile GDP Tuesday’s second-quarter reading starts from a 0.5 percent annual contraction, the region’s sharpest rebound question. —Peru GDP Monday’s June activity data begins from a 1.80 percent annual pace, alongside a 4.9 percent unemployment rate. —Global PMIs Friday’s flash surveys for the United States, euro area, Germany, and the United Kingdom give the week’s cleanest read on growth momentum.

The week turns on central-bank minutes rather than fresh decisions, with the Federal Reserve’s July account on Wednesday the release most likely to steer the dollar and, with it, Latin American currencies and equities.

Latin American markets enter the week with the dollar and global rate expectations as the dominant external forces, capable of overriding decent local fundamentals. The regional calendar this week leans toward growth rather than inflation: Peru, Colombia, Chile, and Argentina all publish activity data, and the picture is one of divergence rather than a single trend.

The domestic calendar is headlined by second-quarter GDP from Colombia and Chile, Peru’s June activity, and the minutes of Mexico’s latest Banxico meeting. But the pivotal release for regional assets is the Federal Reserve’s July meeting minutes on Wednesday.

Three Themes for the Week

This is a week of central-bank minutes, not fresh decisions. The Federal Reserve publishes the account of its July meeting on Wednesday, Banxico follows on Thursday, and India’s Reserve Bank releases its own minutes on Wednesday. Markets will be reading tone and the balance of risks rather than a headline rate move, which makes the reaction harder to anticipate than a straight data surprise.

The regional calendar shifts from inflation to growth. Peru’s June activity opens the week from a 1.80 percent annual pace, Colombia and Chile publish second-quarter GDP on Tuesday, and Argentina’s June activity closes it. Chile enters from a 0.5 percent contraction and Colombia from 2.2 percent growth—two very different starting points that will shape how much room each central bank has.

Developed-market inflation and the flash PMIs frame the external backdrop. Canada’s CPI lands Monday, the United Kingdom’s on Wednesday with the annual rate seen easing to 2.5 percent, and Japan’s core rate is forecast to firm to 1.8 percent on Thursday. Chile enters its second-quarter reading from a 0.5 percent contraction, Colombia from 2.2 percent growth, and Peru from a steady 1.80 percent pace with unemployment at 4.9 percent. World.title: Ecuador Mining Exports to China Face New Controls
World.content:
Ecuador · Mining

Key Facts New rule: A prior control on the sale and export of processed minerals bound for China.

A prior control on the sale and export of processed minerals bound for China. Products: Gold and copper lead the list, with sampling and verification required before shipment.

Gold and copper lead the list, with sampling and verification required before shipment. Enforcement: ARCOM must certify each cargo, and customs cannot clear it without that certificate.

ARCOM must certify each cargo, and customs cannot clear it without that certificate. Price gap: Ecuador exported gold near US$3,060 an ounce while the world price averaged US$4,876.

Ecuador exported gold near US$3,060 an ounce while the world price averaged US$4,876. China ties: Mining exports to China rose 76.8% in the first quarter of 2026.

Mining exports to China rose 76.8% in the first quarter of 2026. Next step: ARCOM must publish detailed sampling rules within 30 days of the agreement.

ARCOM must publish detailed sampling rules within 30 days of the agreement. BYD launch: BYD sold two new hybrids in August; its fast-charger network is a 2027 plan.

The move aims to close a price gap that costs Ecuador millions each quarter. For you as an investor, it reshapes how mining deals get valued.

If you follow Ecuador’s mining sector, a new rule just changed how gold and copper reach China. The government now checks each shipment’s grade and purity before it leaves, aiming to lift revenue from Ecuador mining exports to China.

Ecuador is tightening checks on gold and copper shipments bound for China. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the New Export Controls Do

Ecuador’s Ministry of Environment and Energy signed a ministerial agreement on 13 August 2026. The Vice Minister of Mines, Galo Garcia Medina, put his name to it.

The order is reportedly docketed as MAE-VM-2026-0001-AM. It applies to processed minerals headed for China.

The rule took effect right away. Any processed mineral shipment bound for China now needs mandatory sampling and technical checks first.

The measure covers processed mineral material under any customs regime. That broad wording is meant to stop shippers from routing metal around the checks.

ARCOM, the country’s mining regulator, must certify the grade and purity of each load. Those results come from accredited labs, and they set the official value of the deal.

Here is the key part. Customs cannot clear the cargo without that ARCOM certificate.

SENAE, the national customs service, cannot authorize loading without it. Shipments can be held at the port until the checks are done.

Why Ecuador Sells Gold Too Cheap

The reason is simple. Ecuador has been selling its gold well below the world price.

In the first quarter of 2026, the global average was US$4,876 per troy ounce. Ecuador’s own export price averaged just US$3,060 an ounce.

That is a gap of more than US$1,800 an ounce. During a record gold boom, the country left real money on the table.

Remember, Ecuador uses the US dollar as its currency. So every figure here is already in US dollars, with no exchange rate to convert.

China is the main buyer of Ecuador’s gold and copper. Exports to China jumped 76.8% from a year earlier in the first quarter of 2026.

Copper concentrate has driven much of that surge to China. It is now the single largest piece of Ecuador’s mineral sales there.

One caveat matters here. Ecuador ships gold mainly as dore and concentrate, not refined pure metal.

So part of that price gap reflects product form and processing costs. It is not all pure undervaluation.

What Triggers a Deeper Review

The agreement sets two red flags for extra scrutiny. The first is when the seller and the buyer are corporate relatives.

The second is when the buyer’s ultimate owner is a foreign state. Officials treat that as a bigger risk to fair pricing.

When a flag appears, ARCOM must sample and verify the mineral before it ships. The goal is to confirm the declared value matches the real market.

If the ministry spots unfair competition, it refers the case onward. It goes to the Superintendency of Economic Competition, Ecuador’s antitrust body.

Tax and pricing disputes go to the SRI, the national tax authority. ARCOM must also publish detailed sampling rules within 30 days.

Exports Are Up, but Revenue Lags

Do not assume exports fell. They did not.

In the first half of 2026, total exports hit a record US$19,571 million. Mining products added US$2,634 million to that total.

Mining is now Ecuador’s third-largest export earner. In the first quarter alone, mining exports reached US$1,381.4 million, up 65.3% from a year before.

Copper concentrate led the way at US$622 million in that quarter. Gold products added more than US$755 million on top.

So the volumes and the dollars are both rising. The worry is that low pricing still costs the state taxes and royalties it should collect.

BYD Launches Hybrids and Plans Fast Charging

In separate news, the Chinese carmaker BYD had a busy August in Ecuador. It launched two plug-in hybrid SUVs and unveiled a charging plan.

The Yuan Pro DM-i arrived on 7 August at a price of US$26,990. DM-i is BYD’s plug-in hybrid system that leans on the electric motor first.

It offers 100 km on electric power alone and up to 1,100 km combined. The first 100 buyers get a US$1,000 bonus.

The larger Ti7 hybrid debuted at Autoshow 2026 in Guayaquil on 11 August. It costs US$54,990 and makes around 483 horsepower.

BYD also announced an ultra-fast flash charger network. But that rollout is a 2027 plan, not something you can use today.

The company aims to install 20 flash chargers in the first half of 2027. Another 40 to 60 units would follow at gas stations and malls.

For now, BYD relies on its existing network of about 150 charging points. Only 21 of those are the faster direct-current type.

BYD says the flash chargers will suit its newer Blade Battery 2.0 cars. El Universo reported a headline charging power near 500 kilowatts.

The plan spans cities like Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca, Ambato, Manta and Loja. The Amazon region would join in a later phase.

Why This Matters to You

If you invest in mining, expect more paperwork and possible delays on China-bound cargo. The upside is a state that wants full value for its minerals.

Better pricing could lift tax revenue and steady Ecuador’s public finances. It may also reward clean, well-documented mining deals over murky ones.

If you drive, the new hybrids widen your low-emission choices at real dollar prices. Just plan around today’s charging map, since the fastest network is still a year away.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did Ecuador change about mineral exports to China? Ecuador issued Ministerial Agreement MAE-VM-2026-0001-AM on 13 August 2026. It requires mandatory sampling and technical verification of grade and purity before any processed mineral cargo can ship to China. The mining regulator ARCOM certifies the value, and customs cannot clear the load without that certificate. Is this a confirmed policy or just a proposal? It is a confirmed, in-force policy, not a proposal. The agreement was signed and took effect immediately. ARCOM still has to publish detailed sampling rules within 30 days, but the control itself already applies. Did Ecuador’s mining revenue actually fall in 2026? No. Both volumes and dollar values rose in early 2026. The real issue is that Ecuador sold gold near US$3,060 an ounce while the world price averaged US$4,876. The new rule targets that undervaluation gap. What did BYD launch in Ecuador, and is the fast charging live? BYD launched two plug-in hybrid SUVs in August 2026, the Yuan Pro DM-i at US$26,990 and the Ti7 at US$54,990. Its ultra-fast flash charger network is a 2027 plan, not live yet. For now, drivers use BYD’s existing 150 charging points.

World.title: Uruguay’s Solar Decade: UTE’s Big Plan and EV Boom Explained
World.content:
Uruguay · Energy

Key Facts Solar push: UTE targets 500–600 MW new solar this quinquenio (by 2030).

UTE targets 500–600 MW new solar this quinquenio (by 2030). Private tender: ~150–200 MW solar call to private developers, first since 2014.

~150–200 MW solar call to private developers, first since 2014. Grid shift: Move from wind and hydro toward solar; installed solar is now ~300-350 MW.

Move from wind and hydro toward solar; installed solar is now ~300-350 MW. EV sales: More than 40% of new 0km vehicle sales were fully electric in July 2026.

More than 40% of new 0km vehicle sales were fully electric in July 2026. Fleet reality: EVs are still only ~1-2% of a ~2.5-million-vehicle fleet.

EVs are still only ~1-2% of a ~2.5-million-vehicle fleet. Regional leader: Highest EV share in Latin America, vs 10.7% regional average.

Highest EV share in Latin America, vs 10.7% regional average. World Cup 2030: Government to support works; possible FIFA tax exemptions ahead.

State power utility UTE plans 500–600 MW of new solar and opens private tenders for the first time in over a decade. New EV sales top 40% of the market, but fleet penetration stays under 2%. Here’s the full picture.

Uruguay is about to open a new decade of solar investment, according to El Observador. The state-owned power utility UTE plans to add between 500 and 600 MW of new solar generation over the current five-year government period, which runs through February 2030.

Uruguay’s utility UTE is planning a new wave of solar capacity. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The Solar Decade: UTE’s Big Plan

UTE plans to add between 500 and 600 megawatts of new solar capacity during the current quinquenio, which ends in February 2030. This is part of a strategy set by the Ministry of Industry, Energy and Mining (MIEM), and it’s the first major solar push in a decade.

A public tender is planned before the end of 2026 for roughly 150-200 MW of new solar, opening the door to private developers for the first time since 2014. Industry Minister Fernanda Cardona said new solar plants would be developed by private firms but ultimately owned by UTE.

The plan is detailed in a 10-year “master plan” covering both generation and transmission, with historic investment concentrated in the next 4-5 years. El Observador’s headline sums it up: “Uruguay opens the door to a decade of solar investment.”

This strategic shift toward solar comes after years of focusing on wind and hydro. UTE’s president, Andrea Cabrera, has framed it as part of a longer-term push that also builds out wind and gas-cycle capacity over the coming decade.

Cabrera has set a first milestone of reaching 500 MW of solar within five years, framing it as part of the largest investment cycle in years. For a small country of roughly 3.4 million people, that is an ambitious bet on cheap, home-grown power.

How the Grid Is Shifting

Uruguay’s electricity mix is changing. In the first half of 2025-2026, most electricity came from water and wind, but the future is solar.

Installed solar capacity is currently around 300-350 MW, and UTE expects to add up to 600 MW during this quinquenio—which would more than double what is in place today. This is a deliberate diversification away from hydro, which is vulnerable to droughts, and wind, which can be intermittent.

The broader master plan also layers in more wind and gas-cycle capacity to keep the grid balanced and resilient. The government hasn’t disclosed specific investment amounts for the solar plans, but the scale is clear.

With Uruguay already at ~90% renewables, this solar push is about reliability and meeting future demand rather than greening a dirty grid. The shift also reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels, which is a key strategic goal for the country.

The EV Boom: What the 40% Really Means

Uruguay has become Latin America’s electric vehicle leader. In July 2026, more than 40% of new (0km) vehicle sales were fully electric, outselling gasoline cars.

The shift is sharper in some segments—among new SUVs and passenger cars, 52% of sales were electric, rising to 57% for passenger cars alone, per the auto trade association ACAU. Ambito reports Uruguay surpassed 40% EV share in the second quarter of 2026, versus a regional average of 10.7%.

But here’s the precision you need: the 40%-plus figure is the share of NEW vehicle sales, not the total fleet. EVs are still only about 1-2% of Uruguay’s roughly 2.5-million-vehicle fleet.

So while the transition is accelerating rapidly—in 2025 about one-fifth of new cars were electric—overall adoption is still early. In 2025, Uruguay sold around 71,000 vehicles, with about 14,400 fully electric, a 20% share.

In H1 2026, EV sales hit 12,426 units. Monthly BEV share was 41.2% in May 2026—so the trend is consistent and shows no signs of slowing down.

The gap with the rest of the region is striking, and it keeps widening. Cheap renewable electricity and government incentives have made switching to electric an easy call for many buyers.

World Cup 2030: Government Support and FIFA Exemptions

President Yamandu Orsi confirmed the state will “accompany” the 2030 World Cup works, and anticipated possible tax exemptions for FIFA. Uruguay hosts at least one match in the centenary tournament, with opening matches split among Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay.

Orsi said FIFA will ask for “some kind of exemption… these things always happen,” but gave no specifics. No specific Uruguayan law exists yet, but FIFA’s standard “Government Guarantee No. 3” typically requires broad tax exemptions for FIFA and its subsidiaries in host countries.

The government is working with the Uruguayan Football Association (AUF), the National Sports Secretariat, and the Montevideo city government. This support could mean significant infrastructure investment and potential fiscal impact—worth watching.

Why This Matters for Investors and Expats

For Latin American investors, Uruguay is proving to be a stable, forward-looking market. The solar tender represents the first private renewable opportunity since 2014—a clear signal that the government is opening up to private capital.

With a 10-year master plan, you have visibility into energy policy, which lowers regulatory risk. For expats, the EV boom translates into better charging infrastructure and more EV options as you settle in.

And the World Cup 2030 will bring a wave of development and tourism, potentially boosting property values and business opportunities. Uruguay’s renewable leadership and early EV adoption put it ahead of the regional curve.

Whether you’re looking at energy, autos, or infrastructure, this is a market worth your attention—and the solar decade is just beginning.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is UTE planning for solar energy? UTE plans to add 500–600 MW of new solar capacity by 2030, with a public tender for 150–200 MW to private developers before end-2026. This is part of a 10-year master plan that also includes wind and gas capacity. Why is Uruguay’s EV share over 40% but the fleet is under 2%? The 40% refers to new vehicle sales in mid-2026, not the total fleet. Across Uruguay’s roughly 2.5 million cars, EVs are still only about 1-2% of what’s on the road. What does the World Cup 2030 mean for taxes in Uruguay? President Orsi confirmed government support for the World Cup works and anticipated tax exemptions for FIFA. FIFA typically requires broad tax exemptions via ’Government Guarantee No. 3’, but no specific law has been passed yet. How does this solar plan affect my electricity bills as an expat? More solar capacity should help stabilize the grid and potentially lower wholesale costs over time. Since UTE is state-owned, any benefits may eventually pass to consumers, but there’s no guarantee of immediate rate cuts.

World.title: Minsur’s Santo Domingo Tin Project: US$250M Peru Plan
World.content:
Peru · Mining

Key Facts Santo Domingo: The Santo Domingo tin project is Minsur’s estaño prospect in Puno, Peru.

The Santo Domingo tin project is Minsur’s estaño prospect in Puno, Peru. Investment: ~US$250 million reported; Senace lists US$265 million.

~US$250 million reported; Senace lists US$265 million. Status: Exploration/planning; Minsur filed groundwork for a future EIA-d.

Exploration/planning; Minsur filed groundwork for a future EIA-d. Link to San Rafael: Ore may be trucked to Minsur’s San Rafael mine.

Ore may be trucked to Minsur’s San Rafael mine. Exploration spend: US$42 million planned for greenfield exploration in 2026.

US$42 million planned for greenfield exploration in 2026. Minsur global: Second-largest refined tin producer; San Rafael is one of the world’s largest tin mines.

Minsur moves forward with the Santo Domingo tin project in Puno, a ~US$250 million plan still in early exploration stage.

Peruvian miner Minsur is taking early steps to develop its Santo Domingo tin project in the Puno region, with plans that could see around US$250 million poured into the site. The company has filed a request with Peru’s environmental regulator Senace to prepare the groundwork for a future detailed Environmental Impact Study, but this is still just planning—not a green light for construction.

Underground mining underpins Peru’s tin output. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Santo Domingo: Early Planning, Not a Done Deal

Minsur, part of Grupo Breca, has asked Senace to adopt the ‘Common Terms of Reference’ (TdRC) for the Santo Domingo project, which sits in the districts of Nuñoa and Macusani in Puno. This is the first administrative step to define how a detailed Environmental Impact Study (EIA-d) would be prepared—it does not mean the mine is approved.

According to local outlet Energiminas, the project carries a price tag of roughly US$250 million, though Senace’s own documentation lists US$265 million. You should expect that figure to evolve as the study process moves forward.

The company itself emphasizes that this is advance planning, not a commitment to build. Any construction would only start after the EIA-d is approved and a final investment decision is made—so don’t book your flights to Puno just yet.

The site straddles the provinces of Melgar and Carabaya in Puno, a high-altitude mining region in southern Peru. Minsur belongs to Grupo Breca, one of Peru’s largest family-owned business groups, which gives the project deep financial backing if it does go ahead.

What Santo Domingo Would Look Like

Santo Domingo is a tin project, and Minsur’s plan includes the option to truck the ore to its existing San Rafael mining unit, which is also in Puno. The preliminary transport route would use internal roads plus the PU-100 and PE-34B highways, though details are still sketchy.

Beyond that, the company is keeping its options open—it could also sell the ore to third parties. The infrastructure and logistics decisions will be refined if and when the project moves past the planning stage.

For now, there is no published production target, mine life, or construction start date for Santo Domingo. That level of detail typically arrives only once the detailed Environmental Impact Study is drafted and put out for public consultation.

The Bigger Picture at San Rafael

San Rafael is Minsur’s flagship tin mine and is described as one of the world’s largest tin mines. It’s separate from Santo Domingo, but the two are linked: Santo Domingo’s ore could feed San Rafael’s concentrator.

Minsur is also investing heavily in San Rafael’s future. A life-extension project, which would push the mine’s life to 2041 and boost its concentrator capacity by 44% (from 3,480 tonnes per day to 5,000), carries an investment exceeding US$1.7 billion.

In the second quarter of 2026, Minsur’s capital spending rose 49% year-on-year. That money went mainly to a new tailings dam at San Rafael and to extending the mine’s life, showing the company is committed to keeping its tin production strong.

Minsur’s Global Tin Role

Minsur is the world’s second-largest refined tin producer, and Peru is one of the top tin-producing countries. That makes Santo Domingo a potentially significant addition to global tin supply.

The company produced 7,000 tonnes of refined tin in Q2 2026, down just 0.5% from a year earlier, despite a 15.4% dip from the previous quarter due to maintenance. Cash costs rose to US$10,500 per tonne in the quarter.

To keep future projects moving, Minsur plans to spend US$42 million on greenfield exploration in 2026, with Santo Domingo among the targets for drilling. That’s a sign the company is serious—but again, exploration is just the first step.

Tin prices have been firm, which helps explain why Minsur keeps spending on both existing mines and new prospects. A steady, low-cost supplier like Minsur benefits when the metal stays scarce and demand holds up.

Why This Matters for Investors

Tin is a critical metal for the global electronics industry—it’s the primary component of solder, the alloy that joins components on circuit boards in everything from smartphones to solar panels. With demand for electronics and renewable energy rising, the world needs reliable tin supply.

Santo Domingo could help fill that gap, but it’s years away. For investors, the real story is Minsur’s long-term strategy: backing up its world-class San Rafael mine with new projects like Santo Domingo to secure its position as a top-tier tin producer.

Watch for the EIA-d submission and any drilling results from Santo Domingo in 2026—those will be the key milestones to gauge whether this project moves from paper to reality.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Santo Domingo project? Santo Domingo is a tin project owned by Minsur in the Puno region of Peru. It’s still in the exploration and planning stage, with a potential investment of ~US$250 million. What stage is Santo Domingo at? Minsur has filed a request with Peru’s environmental regulator Senace to adopt common terms of reference for a future detailed Environmental Impact Study. This is groundwork for planning, not a construction decision. How does Santo Domingo relate to San Rafael? Santo Domingo’s ore could be trucked to Minsur’s San Rafael mine for processing, using roads like PU-100 and PE-34B. San Rafael is the company’s flagship tin mine, separate from Santo Domingo. What is Minsur’s global role in tin? Minsur is the world’s second-largest refined tin producer, and San Rafael is one of the largest tin mines globally. Peru is a top tin-producing country.

World.title: NICA Act Extension to 2035: New Bill Targets Nicaragua’s Gold Sector
World.content:
Nicaragua · Sanctions

Key Facts Two words: Bill S. 5369, introduced 7 Aug 2026, still in committee.

Bill S. 5369, introduced 7 Aug 2026, still in committee. Gold trigger: Operating in Nicaragua’s gold sector becomes a sanctions trigger.

Operating in Nicaragua’s gold sector becomes a sanctions trigger. Extension: Would extend NICA Act authority to 31 Dec 2035.

Would extend NICA Act authority to 31 Dec 2035. Early exit: Sanctions lapse if US President certifies democratic progress.

Sanctions lapse if US President certifies democratic progress. IPSM added: Officials of Nicaragua’s military pension fund join priority review list.

Officials of Nicaragua’s military pension fund join priority review list. Broad targets: New triggers for religious freedom abuses, political prosecutions, Russia/Iran aid.

New triggers for religious freedom abuses, political prosecutions, Russia/Iran aid. Trade measures: Bill would suspend CAFTA-DR benefits and ban new US investment.

A bipartisan bill in the US Senate would extend Nicaragua sanctions to 2035 and add gold as a specific trigger—here’s what it means for investors.

A new bipartisan bill in the US Senate could significantly expand sanctions on Nicaragua, with a particular focus on the country’s booming gold sector. The proposal—formally the Restoring Electoral Fairness and Opposition Rights through Mandates for Accountability Act, or REFORMAR Act—would extend and broaden the existing Nicaragua Investment Conditionality Act (NICA Act) through 2035, but it’s still just a bill, not yet a law.

Gold is Nicaragua’s top export – and now a US sanctions target. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Bill Does

The REFORMAR Act, introduced on 7 August 2026, would reauthorize the NICA Act and extend its sanctions authority until 31 December 2035. That’s a big deal because the current law would otherwise expire sooner—and this bill gives it a longer leash.

Senators Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican, and Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat, introduced it together and sent it straight to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. That bipartisan pairing matters—it means the push to keep pressure on Managua isn’t coming from just one side of the aisle.

To avoid the 2035 end date, sanctions would lapse earlier only if the US President certifies to Congress that Nicaragua has held free and fair elections, stopped violence against civilians, and investigated protester killings. That’s a high bar, given the current political climate.

The bill also adds new sanction triggers: religious freedom abuses, politically motivated prosecutions, and providing goods or services that aid Russia or Iran. If enacted, it would also suspend Nicaragua’s CAFTA-DR trade benefits and prohibit new US investment in the country.

Gold Becomes a Prime Target

Perhaps the most striking change is making Nicaragua’s gold sector a specific sanctions trigger. The bill says that operating—or having operated—in gold mining or related activities could land you on a US sanctions list.

Gold is Nicaragua’s top export by value, bringing in nearly US$2 billion in 2025—about 22% of total exports that year, or roughly 37% if you count only merchandise goods outside the free-trade zones. The United States is the main buyer, taking about 44% of Nicaragua’s exports in the first five months of 2026.

Big miners such as Calibre Mining, Mako Mining, and Colombia-based Mineros operate in Nicaragua today—yet nothing in the text implies any of them is currently sanctioned. The bill simply hands the US government a new tool to target the sector if it chooses to use it.

In the first five months of 2026 alone, gold shipments were worth roughly US$1.35 billion. That pace shows just how central the metal has become to Nicaragua’s foreign earnings—and why Washington sees it as leverage.

Why the Military Pension Fund (IPSM) Matters

The bill also amends the RENACER Act to add officials of Nicaragua’s military pension fund, known as IPSM, to a priority list of people US authorities must review for sanctions. The IPSM is the military’s pension and holding body—basically a social-security fund for soldiers, but also a major economic player.

We don’t have exact asset figures for IPSM, and you shouldn’t invent them. But including its officials signals that US lawmakers see the military as a key pillar of the Ortega-Murillo regime’s financial structure.

By naming IPSM, the bill aims to pressure the military directly, not just the government. That could have ripple effects for anyone doing business with Nicaragua’s defense-linked entities.

How the NICA Act Mechanism Works

The NICA Act framework is all about using the US’s voting power in international financial institutions—like the IMF, World Bank, and Inter-American Development Bank—to oppose or condition loans that benefit the Nicaraguan government. This bill would keep that pressure on and add a coordinated diplomatic strategy to restrict international investment and lending.

In plain terms, the US would work to block or limit multilateral lending to Nicaragua, making it harder for the government to access cheap money. The bill also requires annual reports for three years, with the first one due within 90 days of enactment.

If you’re an investor, this means Nicaragua could face increasing financial isolation, which raises the risk for anyone with exposure to the country’s economy.

For a small, dollar-dependent economy, that kind of squeeze bites over time. Cheaper multilateral loans often underwrite roads, power, and public payrolls—so cutting them off narrows the government’s room to maneuver.

Why This Matters for Investors and Latin America

For anyone watching Latin America, this bill is a clear signal that the US is doubling down on Nicaragua—and gold is now in the crosshairs. If you hold assets in Nicaraguan mining or rely on exports to the US, the legislative risk just went up.

Gold is Nicaragua’s lifeline, and the US is its biggest buyer. A sanctions trigger on gold could disrupt supply chains, affect commodity prices regionally, and make other Latin American countries wary of similar measures.

The regional message is also important: when the US targets a sector like gold, it sends a signal to other governments in the region that certain industries could face similar scrutiny. That’s why this bill is worth watching, even if you don’t have direct ties to Nicaragua.

Also note the broader context—US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned in July 2026 that Nicaragua should not expect relations to continue as normal after Ortega’s election-related move. This bill is part of that hardening stance.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the NICA Act extension? The NICA Act extension is a bill (S. 5369) that would extend and expand the Nicaragua Investment Conditionality Act of 2018, adding new sanctions triggers, including on gold, and extending the authority to 2035. It is not yet law. Is the REFORMAR Act a law? No. The REFORMAR Act is a bill introduced in the US Senate on 7 August 2026 and referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. It has not passed either chamber or been signed by the President. How would the bill affect gold companies in Nicaragua? If enacted, the bill would make operating in Nicaragua’s gold sector a specific sanctions trigger, meaning US authorities could impose sanctions on entities involved in gold mining. Companies like Calibre Mining, Mako Mining, and Mineros S.A. could be at higher risk, though none are currently sanctioned. What are the early exit conditions for the sanctions? Sanctions would lapse before 2035 only if the US President certifies that Nicaragua has met democratic conditions, including free and fair elections, halting violence against civilians, and investigating protester killings. As of now, that seems unlikely.

World.title: Panama Canal Draft Limits Cut Again in 2026 – What It Means for You
World.content:
Panama · Shipping

Key Facts Canal birthday: The Panama Canal turned 112 on 15 August 2026, having opened in 1914.

The Panama Canal turned 112 on 15 August 2026, having opened in 1914. Draft cuts: Max draft drops to 48.0 feet on 26 August and 47.5 feet on 3 September 2026.

Max draft drops to 48.0 feet on 26 August and 47.5 feet on 3 September 2026. Phased steps: Limits fell from 50 ft to 49.5, 49.0, 48.5, 48.0, and now 47.5 ft since July.

Limits fell from 50 ft to 49.5, 49.0, 48.5, 48.0, and now 47.5 ft since July. Traffic rising: Transits hit 10,726 in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, up 5.2% year on year.

Transits hit 10,726 in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, up 5.2% year on year. Profit up 19%: Cargo tonnage climbed about 7%, and profit rose roughly 19% over the same period.

Cargo tonnage climbed about 7%, and profit rose roughly 19% over the same period. Lake level healthy: Gatun Lake sat at about 84 feet in late July 2026, roughly five feet higher than in 2023.

Gatun Lake sat at about 84 feet in late July 2026, roughly five feet higher than in 2023. El Nino driver: The 5 August advisory cites current and projected Gatun Lake levels; a forecast El Nino is the wider driver behind the ACP’s water-saving stance.

The Panama Canal is cutting its draft limits again in August and September 2026 as a precaution against a forecast El Nino. Here’s what the new numbers mean for shipping costs and why Latin American exporters should watch closely.

The Panama Canal draft limits tightened again on 15 August 2026—the waterway’s 112th birthday—as the maximum depth for big ships stepped down to 48.5 feet under a phased plan. The newest cuts—to 48.0 feet on 26 August and 47.5 feet on 3 September—were announced on 5 August, even as canal traffic and profits boom.

The Panama Canal is trimming vessel draft again as lake levels fall. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The Canal’s Busy, Profitable Year

In the first nine months of fiscal 2026 (October 2025 to June 2026), the canal handled 10,726 transits—about 35 ships per day. That’s up 5.2% from 10,191 in the same period a year earlier.

Canal profit rose about 19%, and cargo tonnage climbed about 7% year on year. Normal healthy operation is roughly 36-38 ships per day, so you can see the canal is running close to full capacity.

This boom has been driven by strong demand for moving goods between Asia and the US East Coast, as well as growing exports from Latin American countries like Brazil, Chile, and Peru. The canal’s strategic importance in global trade is undeniable, especially for the region’s agricultural and energy exports.

The New Draft Cuts, Step by Step

Here’s a quick refresher: draft is the maximum depth a loaded ship can sit in the water. A lower draft limit means ships must carry less cargo to float higher, which raises shipping costs per ton.

The canal authority (ACP) announced on 5 August 2026 that it will cut the maximum draft in the big Neopanamax locks further. Effective 26 August, the limit drops to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters), and on 3 September it drops again to 47.5 feet (14.48 meters), until further notice.

These are the newest steps in a phased 2026 sequence: 50 feet (the normal design max) down to 49.5 on 3 July, then 49.0 on 24 July, 48.5 on 15 August (the anniversary), 48.0 on 26 August, and 47.5 on 3 September. The July step came via ACP Advisory, and the August steps are confirmed by an official notice and Reuters.

It’s worth noting that the step on 15 August was not a new announcement but a pre-planned reduction. The ACP set this schedule well in advance, giving shippers time to adjust their loads and schedules accordingly.

Why the Tightening? It’s About Water

The canal’s locks run on fresh water from Gatun Lake, a rain-fed reservoir. The 5 August advisory itself points to current and projected Gatun Lake levels—while the ACP’s wider caution reflects a forecast El Nino that could bring below-average rainfall to the watershed.

So the canal is conserving water now, even though Gatun Lake measured about 84 feet above sea level in late July 2026—roughly five feet higher than the same date in 2023. The canal also trimmed daily crossing slots from 36 to 34 in late July and suspended some short-notice slot auctions.

The idea is to bank water now, so if the El Nino hits hard, the canal can still operate without more severe restrictions. This proactive approach contrasts with the reactive measures seen during the 2023-24 drought.

Also, the ACP has been investing in water-saving measures, such as water recycling basins in the new locks, but these don’t eliminate the need for fresh water entirely. The reservoir is still the backbone of the system.

Not a Repeat of the 2023-24 Crisis

You might remember the 2023-24 El Nino drought, when Gatun Lake fell to about 79.6 feet in August 2023, its lowest in decades. Back then, the canal slashed daily transits from the normal ~36 down to 24 per day, and reports had lows near 18 per day by February 2024—a one-third cut.

Draft was also cut far more severely, toward the mid-40s in feet. So the 2026 tightening is a milder, precautionary step: a couple of feet of draft and a small slot trim, not the deep rationing of 2023-24.

That previous crisis caused massive shipping delays, with queues of vessels waiting for days or weeks. This time, the canal is acting early, and the milder measures reflect both a healthier starting lake level and a more cautious but less drastic approach.

The 2023-24 event also saw record auction prices for passage slots, with one slot going for nearly $4 million. So far, no such extreme measures are in place for 2026, indicating a much more controlled situation.

Why You Should Care

If you’re investing in or trading with Latin America, the Panama Canal is a lifeline. Brazil, Chile, and Peru exporters use it for goods heading to Asia and the US East Coast—grains, copper, fruit, LNG and LPG.

Lower draft means ships load lighter, which raises shipping costs per ton and can lead to surcharges. But the milder 2026 restriction means far less disruption than 2023-24, when one slot once auctioned for a record ~$4 million.

For investors, watch for potential increases in shipping freight rates, which could affect commodity prices and company margins. For exporters, it’s wise to plan for slightly higher logistics costs in the coming weeks, but the impact should be manageable given the modest nature of the cuts.

Also, keep an eye on ACP advisories for any further changes, as the situation could evolve depending on rainfall and El Nino intensity. Being informed is your best defense in these uncertain times.

What Happens Next

After 3 September, the draft limit will hold at 47.5 feet until further notice, unless the ACP sees a need to tighten further. The decision will depend on daily lake levels and the El Nino forecast.

The ACP will likely continue to monitor Gatun Lake closely and could issue additional advisories if the drought intensifies. Shippers and traders should stay alert and flexible, as the situation can change with little warning.

For now, the new limits are a precaution, not a crisis. But the coming months will reveal just how strong this El Nino becomes, and whether the canal’s proactive steps will be enough to avoid a repeat of history.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a draft limit mean for shipping? Draft is how deep a ship sits in the water. A lower limit forces ships to carry less cargo, so they float higher. That increases the cost per ton of cargo and can lead to higher shipping rates. When are the new draft limits effective? The maximum draft drops to 48.0 feet on 26 August 2026, and then to 47.5 feet on 3 September 2026, until further notice. Why is the Panama Canal cutting draft limits if the lake is higher than in 2023? The canal is being cautious because forecasters expect a potentially record-strength El Nino that could bring below-average rain. They’d rather conserve water now than risk a crisis later. How does this compare to the 2023-24 drought? It’s much milder. In 2023-24, daily transits were cut to as low as 18-24 per day, and draft limits went down to the mid-40s. Now, slots only dropped from 36 to 34, and draft limits are around 47-48 feet.

Argentina’s Travel Sale runs 24-30 August 2026. Here is how to navigate it as a foreign resident, including discounts, instalment options, and currency rules that can catch you out.

Argentina’s Travel Sale 2026 runs from 24 to 30 August, and it hasn’t started yet. This guide for foreign residents walks you through what is known so far, how financing works.

The Ezeiza international terminal in Buenos Aires. Argentina’s Travel Sale runs 24 to 30 August 2026, with more than 100 agencies taking part. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Travel Sale 2026 Is and Who Organizes It

Travel Sale is a week-long online campaign designed to boost tourism across Argentina. Trade press coverage says it is organized by FAEVYT, the federation that represents travel agencies in the country.

The event is presented as an online campaign where agencies and airlines publish their promotions on the official Travel Sale website. This makes it your best starting point for comparing deals.

The 12th edition runs from 24 to 30 August 2026. With more than 100 travel agencies participating.

Institutional support comes from provincial tourism boards in Neuquén, Salta, and Jujuy, among others. The government note does not list every co-organizer by name, but it verifies the dates and the sector campaign.

Articles say the event brings together the main agencies and airlines. However, no formal list of participating carriers is published yet.

This means you will need to check each agency’s site for their airline partnerships. Treat any article that names specific airlines as speculative.

The 2026 edition focuses on financing and online sales, according to trade press coverage.

Which Companies Actually Take Part

The government says more than 100 travel agencies from all over Argentina will participate. That is the verified figure, and trade press repeats this number.

No official source provides an exact count, so treat this figure as the precise, confirmed number for 2026. Airlines will also publish promotions through the official sale website.

There is no formal, public list of which carriers have signed up for 2026 yet. You must check individual agency sites for their airline partnerships.

Do not trust articles that name specific airlines for this year’s event, because that information has not been officially released. The government note mentions provincial tourism bodies as institutional supporters, not private airlines.

This includes Neuquén, Salta, Jujuy, Catamarca, La Rioja, and the Buenos Aires City Tourism Board. When you read about airline participation, the only verified fact is that airlines will offer promotions through the official site.

The names of specific airlines are not yet public. Identify the agencies you trust before the sale starts.

Visit their websites and check their terms for the sale. This will save you time during the week, and it will help you spot which airlines they work with.

What Discounts Were Achieved in 2025

Last year’s Travel Sale generated more than 5,100 tourism products, according to trade press. It also reached more than 13 million impressions across participating agencies.

These figures are activity metrics, showing strong consumer interest and a wide array of offers. They are not discount percentages or sales revenue.

No official source has published the average discount percentage that buyers actually got, nor total sales volume in pesos or dollars. Claims of up to 50% off are marketing caps, not measured averages.

They represent promotional ceilings used by agencies to attract attention, not audited statistics from the campaign. For 2025, the verified data are limited to the 5,100 products and 13 million impressions.

There is no public breakdown by national or international destination. There is also no official report on conversion rates or ticket volumes per airline.

Any more detailed assessment would require proprietary analytics from individual booking sites, which are not published. You should view the 2025 numbers as evidence of participation, not proof of deep discounts.

How Instalment Plans and Financing Work

Financing is a central hook for the 2026 Travel Sale. You will see offers with up to 18 monthly instalments for some travel products.

As reported by consumer and trade media covering the event. For domestic trips, some promotions advertise up to 12 interest-free instalments.

The coverage says the sale prioritizes zero-interest payments, especially for local destinations. You do not need to register to see the deals, though you can 

Each agency sets its own payment terms, so check their conditions directly before you commit to any booking. Registration is optional and used mainly for email notifications, not as a requirement to access discounts.

Banks and card networks are not yet listed for 2026. You will need to visit each agency’s site to find which cards qualify for the interest-free plans.

As no consolidated list has been published so far. Previous editions used a pattern where each agency published its own bank-card promos, and the same is expected for 2026.

Because there is no official list of banks, do not rely on assumptions about which cards will work. Check with your bank and the agency during the sale.

Card and Currency Rules for Foreign Residents

The tax rules for international travel purchases are still in force in August 2026. A 30% Impuesto PAIS applies to the peso value of foreign-currency transactions, according to an explainer article on the dollar card rate.

On top of this, a 30% income tax perception is charged in most cases. Calculated on the base that includes the PAIS amount.

For monthly card spending above US$300, there may also be a 25% perception for personal property tax, depending on your taxpayer status. This article underlines that airline tickets and international tourist packages are explicitly within the operations that maintain the full tax burden.

So if you pay a foreign-currency card statement in pesos, you face the dollar card rate. This was about ARS 1,963 per US dollar on 14 August 2026.

A rate that includes the 30% tax component, according to La Nación market data. There is a way to reduce this cost for international purchases.

If you pay the dollar balance directly from a local dollar account. The 30% perception does not apply, according to August 2026 guidance on card payments.

This is a key strategy for expats with local dollar savings.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Travel Sale 2026 run? The Travel Sale runs from Monday 24 August to Sunday 30 August 2026. It has not started yet, so you have time to compare prices beforehand and plan your purchases. Who organizes Argentina’s Travel Sale? The event is driven by FAEVYT, the federation of Argentine travel agencies. Argentina’s national government also presents and supports the campaign, as confirmed on Argentina.gob.ar. Can I get interest-free instalments as a foreign resident? Yes, many agencies advertise zero-interest instalments for domestic travel, up to 12 months. However, specific banks and card networks are not confirmed until each agency publishes its offers during the sale week. How do I avoid the 30% tax on international purchases? For international travel, you can pay the dollar balance directly from a local dollar account. This avoids the 30% perception that applies when your card is charged in pesos, according to August 2026 card guidance.

The Expresso do Rock Experience and What It Includes

Once on board, all passengers enjoy a live rock band playing classics during the outbound journey from Estação da Luz. This sets a festive tone for the day as the train winds through the landscape for about two hours toward Paranapiacaba.

Adults also get a complimentary wine tasting as a special treat during the ride, according to the operator’s promotional post. The experience combines the romance of rail travel with a cultural destination in a unique way.

Every ticket tier includes a kit ferroviario. It is a snack box with biscuits and a water or soft drink.

You also get some railway-themed gifts to remember the trip. The return journey departs Paranapiacaba at 16:30 from the same station area.

You should be back at Estação da Luz around 18:30, giving you a solid block of time to explore the village. Remember that drinks at lunch are not included in any package, as flagged by the Estação da Luz article.

Budget for that separately if you want a beverage with your meal in a restaurant.

Ticket Tiers, Prices, and What Each Package Offers

Expresso Du Mauá offers three clear ticket tiers for this trip, with all prices listed in Brazilian reais by the sources. The basic package costs R$ 190 and covers your round-trip train ride, the snack kit, and the themed gifts.

Using the Banco Central PTAX close of R$ 5.2236 per US$ 1.00 on August 14, 2026, that equals roughly US$ 36.37. The intermediate tier is R$ 250, which is about US$ 47.86 under the same rate.

The intermediate tier includes everything from the basic package, as stated in the Instagram post and Estação da Luz article. It also gives you your choice of either an all-you-can-eat lunch or a guided walking tour.

The complete package is the top tier at R$ 300, approximately US$ 57.43. It bundles in both the lunch and the guided tour, offering the full experience for one price, without the either-or choice.

The guided tour in the top tier also includes admission tickets to three key attractions, confirmed by the Estação da Luz article. You will visit the Museu Castelinho, Casa Fox, and the Sistema Funicular, all with entry fees covered.

How to Book Your Seats on This Special Departure

Booking is handled directly through Expresso Du Mauá for this specific event. The most direct method is via WhatsApp at +55 (11) 91364-2170, which is listed in all promotional materials.

You can also reach out through their official Instagram profile, @expressodumaua, to inquire about reservations and availability. The operator uses an official online sales platform, but the specific website URL is not published in the sources we reviewed.

As of August 16, 2026, the trip is still being promoted with a 10% discount on remaining tickets, per the Instagram post. This suggests availability is likely limited, so acting quickly is wise for potential travelers.

The exact quota of discounted seats and the cutoff date for the promotion are not published in the provided articles. Contact them soon if you are interested, as these details remain unconfirmed and time-sensitive.

Since this is a single departure, seats could sell out before the August 22 date. There is no published deadline for when sales close, so early booking is strongly advised to avoid disappointment or missing the chance.

A Step Back in Time: Exploring Paranapiacaba Village

Paranapiacaba is a preserved railway village in Santo André, noted in travel coverage. It is known for its English-inspired architecture and cobbled streets that feel frozen in time, offering a unique visual experience.

The complete ticket package gives you access to the Museu Castelinho, a museum housed in a former railway officials’ residence. It tells the story of local rail history in a unique setting, with admission covered.

Casa Fox is worth a stop too. The interpretive space sets out the village’s railway heritage.

The Sistema Funicular, the remains of the old inclined railway system, is another stop. Beyond the packaged tour, the village has a lively cultural scene year-round.

The Festival de Inverno brings over 80 cultural attractions and about 400 artists. Entry to most events is free.

The village also has numerous restaurants, cafés, and craft beer stands open to visitors. You can easily spend your free hours exploring the local gastronomy and soaking in the atmosphere during your stay.

Those CPTM departures have their own calendar and pricing structure, which is different from what Expresso Du Mauá offers. For this themed trip, your only option is the August 22 departure from Luz.
