World.title: Woman abused by man in Budapest in broad daylight, authorities do nothing
World.content:
A woman was allegedly pinned against a wall and strangled by her former partner in broad daylight near Budapest’s Lehel Square, according to a social media account shared by actor and women’s rights activist Áron Molnár. Two women reportedly intervened to help the victim, who was allegedly being forcibly kissed and threatened.

Woman strangled in broad daylight in Budapest as witnesses intervene

The incident is said to have happened on 14 August at the Bulcsú Street exit of the Lehel Square metro station. According to the account published by Eszter Spira and subsequently shared by Molnár, the alleged attacker grabbed the woman by the neck, pressed her against a wall and attempted to kiss her against her will.

Most passers-by reportedly continued walking, but Spira and another woman stepped in after seeing what was happening.

Two bystanders reportedly helped the woman escape

According to Spira’s account, the two women approached the victim, took hold of her hands and urged her to come with them. The man allegedly shouted that the incident was a “family matter”. After the woman managed to get away from him, he reportedly threatened to kill the two women who had intervened.

The women then shouted for help. The alleged attacker reportedly backed off, allowing them and the victim to flee towards the entrance of Lehel Market, where they contacted Budapest police. Spira said the victim told her that the man was her former partner and that she had experienced months of abuse at his hands. A 60-day restraining order was reportedly already in force against him.

The victim also allegedly said that the man had continued to harass and threaten her after their relationship ended. According to the account, he attacked her outside her workplace on the day of the incident and then forcibly took her towards the metro station.

Alleged attacker was released by Budapest police

Spira said officers arrested the man at the scene and took both the victim and witnesses to Budapest’s 13th District Police Headquarters. However, she claims that after around four hours of waiting, they were told that neither the victim nor the witnesses would be questioned that day and that the man would be released.

The account also alleges that attempts were made to obtain urgent assistance from organisations supporting women who have experienced violence, including emergency accommodation, protection and legal help, but that no immediate solution was found. These claims have been made in social media posts; the information provided for this article does not include a police statement or an independent account of the investigation.

Activist calls for tougher protection for women

Molnár, who shared Spira’s account on Facebook, described the events as “unfathomable” and questioned why authorities were unable to provide stronger protection in such a case. He argued that women and children should be protected by the strictest possible laws and called for tougher action against relationship and domestic violence.

Molnár also cited figures in his post claiming that a woman dies every day as a result of relationship violence and that only a fraction of cases are reported and lead to proceedings.

“I’m angry at the helplessness,” Molnár wrote, arguing that the current political moment should be used to introduce stronger measures to protect women, especially because the incident in Budapest has shown again how victims of domestic violence are protected when a restraining order is already in place, and about what safeguards are available immediately after a reported attack.

If you or someone you know might be in danger, you can reach out for the Women For Women Together Against Violence Association (NANE) Association’s helpline for abused women and children toll-free at +36-80-505-101 (Mon., Wed., Fri.: 6:00 PM–10:00 PM, Tues.: 10:00 AM–10:00 PM, Wed.: 12:00 PM–4:00 PM). You can find further information about the association’s support services on their website. From abroad, the association’s helpline can be reached at +36-1-267-4900.

Read also: Budapest in deep trouble as more threatening individuals on streets, cheap drugs becoming increasingly widespread

World.title: Romanian swimmer David Popovici claims third European 200m freestyle title after 100m triumph
World.content:
Romanian swimming star David Popovici has won the 200m freestyle race at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris, his third consecutive European title in the event.

The win on August 14, following the August 12 gold in the 100m freestyle race, makes him the only athlete to have won both races at three consecutive editions of the European championships.

The 21-year-old Romanian swimmer finished the race with a time of 1:44.15, 0.40 seconds ahead of runner-up Tomas Navikonis of Lithuania, and 0.72 seconds ahead of Britain's James Guy.

In the 200m freestyle event, Popovici also won the Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, as well as two world titles, in Budapest in 2022 and in Singapore in 2025.

His personal best in the 200m freestyle came at the 2022 European Championships, when he clocked 1:42.97, the third-fastest time in history.

World.title: Romanian executive to submit fifth payment request under Recovery and Resilience Facility
World.content:
The Romanian government is set to submit the fifth payment request under the EU-backed Recovery and Resilience Facility, or PNRR, according to an announcement from European Investments and Projects minister Dragoș Pîslaru.

Payment no. 5 is worth EUR 2.84 billion, and is the penultimate request that Romania will submit within the PNRR. Once approved, the fifth payment will bring Romania’s absorption rate of PNRR-related grants to 78%, from 66% currently.

“One final request remains, request no. 6, worth EUR 2.58 billion in grants and EUR 1.76 billion in loans. From a total of EUR 13.57 billion allocated at the time the PNRR was signed, we will reach EUR 10.56 billion after request no. 5,” Pîslaru said during a press conference.

Initially, the European Commission planned for a single final payment request, reuniting the now separated requests no. 5 and 6, the minister noted.

The final payment request will be submitted at the end of September, and with it “we could reach 97.2% of the PNRR,” he said, referring to the grants component.

“47% was the percentage of the PNRR when I came to the ministry, after four years since the program was launched. The annual average was about 10.4% of the PNRR. In one year and two months, under the Bolojan government, we added 31% of the PNRR,” the minister also said.

Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan is financed through EUR 21.41 billion under the EU mechanism, including EUR 13.57 billion in grants and EUR 7.84 billion in loans. The fourth payment request, worth EUR 2.62 billion, was approved by the European Commission in May of this year.

World.title: Drone crashes in Romania’s Tulcea County
World.content:
A drone crashed on Friday, August 14, in the area of Luncaviţa, a locality in eastern Romania’s Tulcea County, about five kilometers from the border with Ukraine, the Defense Ministry (MApN) announced.

The drone crashed in a wooded area and caused no casualties, according to preliminary information provided by MApN.

The drone was not detected by MApN’s radar surveillance systems as it was flying at a very low altitude, the ministry said.

The crash resulted in an explosion followed by a fire, which has been extinguished, the Emergency Situations Inspectorate of Tulcea announced.

A MApN team, using an IAR 330 PUMA SOCAT helicopter, will investigate the area.

A day earlier, drone remains were discovered in the sea, close to Romania’s Costinești beach, on the Black Sea shore. Five drones were tracked nearing Romanian territory on the night of Wednesday, August 12, to Thursday, August 13, around 1 AM. One drone briefly entered Romanian airspace in Tulcea County but then exited and headed to Ukraine. Another drone was detected in Romanian airspace around 9 AM. Earlier this week, two Gerbera-type drones were destroyed by divers of the Romanian Army in the exclusive economic zone, approximately 165 kilometers from Constanța, in the Neptun Deep exploitation area.

At the end of the August 14 government meeting, prime minister Ilie Bolojan said the country’s military was doing “everything in their power to combat the drones.”

“We have a reality that we cannot deny, namely that the war resulting from Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is having an impact, including along our borders, and we can expect drone debris, drones reaching the river areas along Romania’s border, in the vicinity of ports, to stray into Romania,” the PM said.

“It is regrettable that we are facing such situations, but given what has happened in recent months, we are beginning to see that this is becoming something of a constant; it is not just in Romania, we have seen what has happened in other areas as well. It is becoming clear that equipping our Armed Forces as quickly as possible with counter-drone systems is a necessity,” he added.

World.title: Romanian telco Digi reports 10% higher revenues in Q2 2026
World.content:
Romanian telecommunications company Digi (BVB: DIGI) reported consolidated revenues of EUR 608 million in the second quarter of 2026, representing an 11% YoY increase.

Adjusted EBITDA (ex. operating leases) for Q2 2026 increased by 23% compared to the result from Q2 2025, reaching EUR 169 million. Consequently, in the first semester of 2026, the group recorded consolidated revenues of EUR 1.2 billion, a 10% increase versus 6M 2025, and adjusted EBITDA of EUR 398 million, up 17% YoY.

“Spain continues to be our primary growth engine, maintaining strong commercial momentum and progressing in line with our long-term plans, while Romania continued to perform well,” said Serghei Bulgac, CEO of Digi Communications.

Last month, Digi successfully completed an initial public offering for its Spanish subsidiary. The Spanish IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, showing investor appetite for the company’s shares.

In Q2 2026, Digi reached 33.9 million revenue-generating user agreements (RGUs) across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy, a 14% increase compared to Q2 2025.

The mobile segment stands out for generating the most RGUs within the group’s array of services, accounting for 51% of the overall clients across the four markets. In Q2 2026, the mobile segment saw its RGUs climb to 17.3 million, a 19% YoY increase, covering mobile telephony clients across Romania, Spain, Portugal and Italy.

In Romania, the mobile service segment remained the largest, reaching 8.4 million RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026, a positive evolution of 20% compared to Q2 2025. Broadband services registered an increase of 4% in Q2 2026, compared to Q2 2025, up to 5.2 million RGUs, while the segment of Pay-TV services (cable and satellite) increased by 2% YoY, up to 6.1 million RGUs. Together with fixed-line telephony, the total number of RGUs in the Romanian market amounted to 20.5 million customers as of Q2 2026, a 9% increase versus Q2 2025.

Spanish operations continued the strong performance in Q2 2026, with the number of users of fixed services, internet, and mobile telephony increasing by 23% compared to Q2 2025, to 11.9 million RGUs. Mobile users increased by 19% to 7.8 million RGUs, while broadband users increased by 28% to 2.9 million.

In Portugal, the number of RGUs amounted to 960k, up 22% YoY, of which 545k were mobile, and 186k were broadband users.

In Italy, mobile users increased by 4,5% YoY, reaching 535k RGUs as of the end of Q2 2026.

In the United Kingdom, Digi launched its fiber broadband services and continued expanding its network footprint during the second quarter of 2026, while onboarding its first customers.

World.title: Romania’s Presidential Administration to host summit on animal welfare
World.content:
The Presidential Administration will host the second edition of Animal Summit Romania on September 29 - 30, Diana Pungă, a state adviser for relations with civil society at the institution, announced on Friday, August 14.

The event, organized by the non-profit Sache Vet Association and Bucharest’s Animal Protection Administration ASPA, will take place at Cotroceni Palace.

Over two days, it will gather public administration representatives, veterinarians, legal and education specialists, non-governmental organizations and other experts to discuss animal protection and welfare and solutions to challenges in the field.

“Romania continues to face major challenges in the field of animal protection. Beyond the issue of abandonment and the lack of education about responsible pet ownership, civil society frequently raises concerns about the non-transparent operation of some private shelters, suspected abusive euthanasia practices and difficulties in uniformly enforcing existing legislation. In many communities, volunteers, NGOs and active citizens end up compensating for the lack of coherent institutional mechanisms by becoming directly involved in animal rescue, shelter monitoring and the promotion of responsible sterilization and adoption,” an announcement from the organizers reads.

All of these aspects point to an urgent need for clear standards and consistently implemented public policies protecting both the communities and the animals, the organizers said.

World.title: Central Romania: EBRD extends EUR 120 mln loan for PV plant, battery system near Brașov
World.content:
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Friday, August 14, that it has extended a financing package of up to EUR 120 million for the development, construction, and operation of Econergy’s Părău 2 project in Romania.

The project includes a 342 MW solar photovoltaic plant and a 150 MW/300 MWh battery storage system in Brașov, according to a statement by the lender.

The financing consists of an EBRD A loan of up to EUR 57 million and an EBRD B loan of up to EUR 63 million, which includes a EUR 3.6 million debt service guarantee provided by commercial banks Privredna banka Zagreb and NLB.

According to the EBRD, the Părău 2 project will increase renewable energy production, help improve grid flexibility, and strengthen Romania’s energy security.

The project is co-financed by BSTDB (the Black Sea Trade and Development Bank), OTP Bank, and Exim Banca Românească, as part of a debt financing package of up to EUR 229 million.

“By financing one of the country’s pioneering solar and battery storage investments, the EBRD is helping to increase the generation of renewable energy, strengthen energy security and support a more resilient and flexible electricity system. The support of the European Union through InvestEU demonstrates how public and private partners can work together to mobilize financing for the green transition,” said Georgios Gkiaouris, the EBRD’s Head of Energy Europe.

The project is backed by Romania’s Contract for Difference scheme, which was developed with EBRD technical assistance and aims to unlock 5 GW of solar and onshore wind capacity. The solar plant has secured a 125 MWac allocation in the first auction at a strike price of EUR 49.4/MWh for 15 years, while the remaining capacity will operate on a merchant basis.

The European Union supported the EBRD A/B loan through a first-loss portfolio guarantee provided by the InvestEU programme, which covers up to EUR 115 million and helps mitigate the risks associated with the project’s substantial exposure to merchant revenue.

World.title: Romanian consumer goods distributor AQUILA reports slightly higher revenues amid challenging context
World.content:
AQUILA, one of the largest players in the fast-moving consumer goods distribution sector from Romania and the region, reported revenues of RON 1.6 billion in the first half of 2026, amid an economic environment marked by declining consumption, according to a report submitted to the local stock exchange.

The figure represents a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year.

Revenue from the distribution segment increased by 6% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, driven by the organic growth of this business line. The main contributor to this performance was the traditional retail channel, which grew by 22%, followed by the HoReCa channel with 7% growth, and the gas station channel with 1%, evolutions that offset the 19% decline recorded in the organized retail channel.

Revenue from the logistics segment increased by 6%, driven by higher operating volumes and the expansion of logistics activities across multiple temperature categories, particularly in the frozen products segment. Revenue from the transport segment increased by 13%.

The company's own brands continued to strengthen their contribution to the group’s performance, with revenues of RON 78.5 million in the first half of 2026, up 23% compared to the same period in 2025.

The results for the first half of the year were affected by a more challenging operating environment, marked by weaker consumer spending in Romania, an approximately 30% increase in fuel costs, and unfavorable foreign exchange movements, as well as by the temporary impact of the group’s market share expansion strategy and continued investments in the development of our operating platform.

In this context, EBITDA amounted to approximately RON 61 million, down 33% compared to the same period in 2025, while the net result was negative, at approximately RON 21 million.

During the first six months of the year, the group invested EUR 3 million in the development of its logistics infrastructure, process digitalization, operations automation, and equipment modernization, in line with its growth strategy and commitment to improving operational efficiency.

“Our distribution segment continued to deliver growth, supported by the expansion of the traditional retail and HoReCa channels, the consolidated contribution of our own brands, and the commercial synergies generated through the integration of the acquired companies. At the same time, we chose to prioritize strengthening commercial relationships and increasing market share, which play an essential role in supporting long-term growth and value creation,” said Cătălin Vasile, CEO of AQUILA.

The company head noted that the strategy had a temporary impact on commercial margins and profitability but created “a foundation for capitalizing on the investments made and supporting sustainable performance in the period ahead.”

World.title: Raiffeisen Bank Romania issues a new series of bonds denominated in RON
World.content:
Raiffeisen Bank, one of the largest banks in Romania, issued on August 13, 2026, a senior preferred eligible bond issue maturing in 2033, with a total value of RON 750 million.

The tranche represents the bank’s 0th series of eligible bonds, the financial institution informs through a statement sent to Economica.net.

The bond issue was addressed to institutional investors and was placed at a fixed coupon of 7.538% for the first five years, respectively 0.85% above the yield of the benchmark Romanian government bonds denominated in lei.

World.title: Albania Ruling Party Documents Highlight Country’s Ageing Demographic
World.content:
Documents produced by governing Socialist Party experts for a reform of the country’s municipal set-up, seen by BIRN, reveal an ageing population that could have adverse economic consequences for Albania.

The “Administrative-Territorial Reform 2.0” documents, prepared by experts on a special parliamentary committee, also show how emigration and internal migration have emptied out small towns and rural areas while concentrating the population in a few urban centres.

At one end are several urban centres where both population and economic activity are increasingly concentrated. At the other end are peripheral areas, particularly in the northeast, southeast and mountainous regions, which are caught in a vicious cycle of population decline and subsistence economies, with few formal jobs.

In these areas, municipal budgets survive largely on central government transfers, with funds often used mainly to cover the salaries of local administration staff.

The Urban Mass Index, UMI, one of three analytical documents underpinning the proposed new map of 46 municipalities – which would merge 15 local government units with larger municipalities – documents the territorial transformation of Albania since the 1990s, with a few centres continuing to grow as an increasing number of municipalities lose residents.

The “dependency ratio” in the index, which measures the burden that children and elderly people place on the working-age population, shows that in 51 municipalities out of 61 in total, this burden is higher than the national average. In many of them, the number of elderly residents exceeds the number of children.

The data highlights an Albania divided into three distinct realities: a small group of municipalities that continue to attract population and economic activity; a group of municipalities with intermediate potential; and a majority of the country’s territory, which is losing the critical mass of population needed to sustain local economies and public services.

The analysis is based on data from the 2023 census and, as part of the technical report accompanying the reform proposal, suggests that Albania is experiencing a growing concentration of its population in an ever-smaller number of urban centres, while the rest of the country is losing residents, functions and development capacity.

The index results show that only 13 municipalities are classified as having a high level of urban mass and are home to 62.5 per cent of the population.

By contrast, 30 municipalities – covering almost half of the country’s administrative map – are classified as having a low level of urban mass and account for just 14.2 per cent of the population.

Another 18 municipalities fall into the intermediate or medium category.

According to the data, the country’s population is concentrated in the capital, which is home to more than half a million people, followed at a considerable

distance by the municipalities of Durres, Vlora, Elbasan, Shkoder, Fieri, Kamza and Berat.

At the other end of the scale, municipalities such as Pustec, Libohova, Himara, Kelcyra, Memaliaj, Selenica, Dropull, Finiq, Delvina and Kolonja have the smallest populations.

The ruling-party experts did not build the index solely on population size. It also combines other indicators, including population density, the spatial distribution of residents, the demographic dependency ratio and the level of urbanisation.

This means that a municipality may cover a large area, but if its population is concentrated in a small town while the rest of its territory is largely empty, it is considered structurally weak.

One of the most significant findings is that, on average, 57 per cent of Albania’s territory is uninhabited.

The analytical document notes that the country no longer has the same population distribution it had in 2014, when the current administrative-territorial division was introduced with the aim of creating larger and more efficient municipalities.

“Some areas have grown, while others have lost a significant share of their population,” the report says, arguing that some municipalities are struggling to secure sustainable finances, qualified staff and adequate administrative capacity.

The Socialists have submitted a bill to parliament proposing a new administrative-territorial map that would merge several smaller municipalities with larger neighbouring ones – without explaining how the proposed map would address these underlying problems.

The proposal has faced opposition from residents in the affected areas. Some fear mergers will leave them with even more limited access to public services.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Man Suspected of Spying for Serbian Intelligence
World.content:
Fehim Sali, second left, at a court hearing in Pristina on August 14, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court on Friday ordered 30 days of detention for a dual Kosovo and Serbia citizen, Fehim Sali, who is suspected of spying for Serbia’s intelligence agency, the BIA.

It is alleged that he passed the BIA information about Kosovo officials, politicians and Islamist radicals, including potential recruitment targets, and received money in return.

Sali, a resident of Kosovo’s southern Dragash/Dragas municipality, was arrested on Thursday at the Merdare border crossing point while entering from Serbia. He appeared before the Basic Court in Pristina on Friday.

“The court’s assessment took into account the circumstances relating to the risk of absconding, the risk of influencing witnesses and evidence, and the risk of repetition or continuation of the criminal offence,” the court said in a statement.

According to the prosecution file, Sali is suspected of “maintaining contact with BIA officers using four different mobile phones”, which were found during raids at his house on Thursday, alongside around 40,000 euros in cash.

The prosecution file alleges that Sali “worked as a recruited agent for Serbia’s Security Information Agency, BIA, in exchange for material benefits”. The file alleges that he acted on the instructions of a senior BIA officer identified as Zelimir Matovic, nicknamed Zeljko.

It alleges that Sali provided the BIA with information about Kosovo’s political situation and helped it identify officials of Kosovo’s own intelligence agency, the AKI. According to the case file, he photographed some of its officials to facilitate their identification.

Sali is also accused of providing information about members of the radical Islamist Wahhabi movement as well as other people whom he allegedly proposed to the BIA officer as potential targets for contact and recruitment.

According to prosecutors, Sali also “mediated matters and documents connected to Serbian state institutions and maintained contacts with people with political and social influence in Serbia and Kosovo, particularly members of non-majority communities”.

The prosecution stated that he provided some of these people with “guidance on political activity, with the aim of gathering and transmitting information of interest to the BIA”.

Prosecutors argue that these activities were carried out against the state interests of Kosovo and endangered its constitutional order and national security.

The prosecution also alleges that the 40,000 euros found and seized during a search of Sali’s home came from his alleged activities on behalf of the BIA.

According to the case file, the evidence against Sali includes his own statement.

Prosecutors claim he described in detail his alleged activities, including how and where he communicated with BIA officials, exchanged information and provided assistance to the Serbian intelligence service.

Prosecutor Bekim Kodraliu told media that Sali admitted having been recruited and maintained regular contact with BIA officials.

“The suspect himself stated that he had been recruited and had ongoing contacts with BIA officials,” Kodraliu said.

The case comes two months after another Kosovo espionage conviction involving Serbia’s intelligence service.

In June, the Pristina Basic Court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage.

Prosecutors said Selimi had provided the BIA with information about religious radicalisation in Kosovo, former members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and people who had joined Islamic State.

World.title: Week in Review: Between the Absurd and the Unexpected
World.content:
Kosovo’s governance drama is beginning to border on the absurd. Weeks after the June election results were certified, two months after the elections were held, MPs have yet to elect a parliamentary speaker and deputies and, in doing so, constitute the new parliament.

The winning party, Vetevendosje, has the votes to elect a new speaker, and indeed a new government. But it has conditioned the election of a speaker on reaching a wider agreement with the opposition on the election of a new president. With deadlines imposed by the Constitutional Court passing, is Kosovo heading to a fourth parliamentary election in two years?

World.title: Thousands Flee, 14 Hospitalised as Wildfire Menaces Croatian Coastal Town
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said on Friday that 14 people have been hospitalised, with ten in intensive care, after a wildfire that reportedly forced some 2,000 people to evacuate homes around the Dalmatian coastal town of Omis overnight.

“The government and all relevant services are coordinating to protect people and rectify the consequences of the large fire in Omis,” Plenkovic wrote on X.

The fire swept through forested areas to destroy property and vehicles. Chief national fire officer Slavko Tucakovic told media that he had “never experienced anything like this in my career”.

“Unfortunately, many houses were damaged or burned down. A large number of vehicles were also burned up,” he said.

The Croatian coast has seen record high temperatures this summer. The heatwave left dry vegetation as fuel for the fire, and the flames were spread by high winds, Tucakovic explained.

World.title: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN .

The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June.

Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls.

“From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group.

“The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added.

“We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election.

Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency.

“We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said.

“We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added.

Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties.

So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

World.title: Democracy Digest: US Charges Mexican Cartel Members over Czech Weapons Deal
World.content:
Russia on the radar; Slovakia picks a fight with Brussels over same-sex marriage

Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has been forced into an embarrassing retreat over speed cameras with suspected Russian links, a week after dismissing opposition warnings about their origin. The National Security Authority (NBU) confirmed on Tuesday that the two devices in question contain Russian components. The finding vindicates concerns raised by Progressive Slovakia (PS), the country’s strongest opposition party, which had warned that the cameras could pose a security risk. There were red flags from the start. Journalists found that the cameras closely resembled equipment made by the St Petersburg-based company Simicon. More strikingly, the measurement software listed in the Slovak certification had the same digital fingerprint as software used in a Russian CORDON speed camera. The ministry’s story has shifted ever since. It first insisted the cameras were not Russian, then conceded it could not prove their origin, before ordering IT supplier Soitron to remove the test devices. It now says two ministry employees will lose their jobs and cooperation with Soitron will end. Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok, of the governing Hlas party, has resisted calls to take political responsibility. “We were lied to,” he said on Thursday, blaming the Slovak Institute of Metrology, which certified the cameras. The institute says checking cybersecurity risks, supply chains or the origin of components is not its job. Soitron also denies misleading the state. Soitron obtained the devices from a Slovak distributor whose CEO had worked in Russia for many years and had previously imported similar equipment to Slovakia through another company. The ministry will not publish the NBU analysis, and it is unclear why the country’s security services failed to spot the potential problem before opposition politicians and journalists did. The General Prosecutor’s Office has now said it will examine the case.

There was another controversy this week involving the Interior Ministry, and Interior Minister Sutaj Estok in particular. His ministry has refused to register same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad. Several Slovak same-sex couples applied in December to have their foreign marriage certificates entered into Slovakia’s special registry. After waiting eight months, they received an answer not from the registry, but directly from Sutaj Estok. He argued that registering the unions as marriages would conflict with Slovak law and the constitution, which has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 2014. Among those affected are former diplomats Ivan Novotny and his husband Metod Spacek. They argue that the minister intervened in a procedure that should have been handled by the registry and are now preparing an administrative lawsuit. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union involving a Polish-German same-sex couple. The court ruled that an EU country cannot refuse to recognise a same-sex marriage legally concluded in another member state if doing so interferes with rights guaranteed under EU law, particularly freedom of movement and residence. The ruling does not require member states to introduce same-sex marriage into their domestic law. The European Commission has reminded Slovakia that EU law, as interpreted by the EU’s top court, takes precedence over national law and that member states are required to implement its judgments. It told the SME daily that it would continue to monitor the situation and could use the tools at its disposal if needed. The ministry argues that EU law may require Slovakia to recognise same-sex marriages for specific purposes, but does not oblige the country to enter them in its registry as marriages with the same legal status as marriages recognised under Slovak law. Novotny, Spacek and other couples dispute that interpretation. Their planned legal challenge could now put that question before the Slovak courts.

World.title: Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law Won’t Succeed Without More Gynaecologists
World.content:
Imagine a woman called Milica. She is 29, on a fixed-term contract, and every month menstrual pain keeps her from working for several days.

Milica has not seen a gynaecologist in two years. There aren’t enough appointments where she lives and she cannot travel to the capital, Podgorica, because of work.

When she finally gets a diagnosis, she learns a law offering paid leave exists, and she must renew her medical diagnosis certificate every year.

But she wonders whether her employer will extend her contract if he learns why she has been absent.

World.title: BIRN Reality Check: What Has Albania’s AI ‘Minister’ Achieved So Far?
World.content:
According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process.

But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear.

At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage.

“There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement.

According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system.

The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules.

The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties.

Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption.

According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement.

“Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said.

He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.”

Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place.

Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes.

“Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”.

For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems.

“Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said.

World.title: The Croatian River With the Remains of an Ancient City Below the Surface
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – There’s a Croatian river which is home to the remains of an ancient city and a 1,800 year old Roman barge. Over 9,000 fascinating artefacts have been discovered at this single location.

The Kupa River in Sisak is home to the remains of ancient Siscia, a Roman bridge and a cargo barge about 1,800 years old, while underwater research continues to uncover new traces of the past. The course of the Kupa River through Sisak today seems peaceful, a familiar part of the city’s everyday life. Putni kofer writes that along the banks there is a promenade and fishermen, kayaks can occasionally be seen on the river, and a few kilometres downstream it flows into the Sava. However, beneath that calm surface lies a completely different Sisak. Over the past hundred years or so, thousands of archaeological objects have been recovered from the riverbed, while underwater, parts of ancient buildings, traces of a Roman bridge and a large river barge that sailed the Kupa approximately 1,800 years ago have been preserved.

One of the most extensive archaeological collections found in European rivers

The scale of these finds is exceptional even far beyond Croatian borders. In a scholarly paper dedicated to the Roman river barge from Sisak, the collection of objects recovered from the Kupa is described as one of the most extensive collections of archaeological material found in European rivers. The objects span a long period of time, from the Copper Age to the Middle Ages, but the Roman layer is particularly rich, created in the centuries when Siscia was one of the important cities in this part of the Empire.

A large part of this collection was not found during classic archaeological excavations. It was brought to the surface by major dredging of the Kupa at the beginning of the 20th century, especially the works carried out in 1912. The monograph Urbanism of Roman Siscia states that the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb holds around nine thousand ancient artefacts dredged from the riverbed, while the Sisak City Museum mentions around ten thousand recovered objects and more than nine thousand archaeological finds in connection with these interventions. Items that at first glance have little in common were recovered from the Kupa at that time: military equipment and weapons, jewellery, coins, pottery, tools and everyday objects. Together, however, they give an unusually broad picture of the people who lived along this river for centuries and used it as a transport route, a source of food, a place of work and a connection with the rest of the world.

Segestica, then Siscia left behind enormous wealth…

The explanation for this wealth lies primarily in the location of the city. Segestica, and later Roman Siscia, developed right next to the river and an important navigable route that led via the Sava towards the Danube. Because of this, the Kupa was much more than the natural border of the city. People travelled and traded on it, a port and other facilities related to river traffic developed along it, and over the centuries objects ended up in the water in various ways. At the same time, the riverbed itself changed. Erosion of the left bank affected part of the area of the ancient city, so structures that once stood beside the Kupa are today partly located within it.

It is precisely this shifted edge of the ancient city that has become the focus of new research in recent years. Since 2021, systematic international underwater investigations have been carried out in the Kupa that no longer depend only on what the river happens to throw up or what dredging pulls out of it. Sonar, diving research and other methods have enabled archaeologists to document what still stands or lies on the bottom. The masonry remains of Siscia’s fortifications that collapsed into the water, large wooden piles connected with the Roman bridge, and parts of lead water pipes that crossed the river have been located. In 2025 the City of Sisak reported that remains of ramparts, bridges and other structures are being documented in the riverbed, so the relationship of ancient Siscia to the Kupa can now be reconstructed much more precisely.

a 1,800 year old roman barge lies in the depths…

Among all these traces, one vessel stands out whose story began long before the current research. At the Kovnica site a Roman river cargo barge was discovered as early as 1985, but the conditions at the time allowed only part of the structure to be investigated. The ship then remained underwater for decades until archaeologists returned to it in the 2025 campaign. A significantly larger part of the wreck, now known as Sisak 1, was then uncovered. The French Ministry of Culture states that the ship has so far been revealed to a length of at least twelve metres, with a preserved width of 3.34 metres, while one of its ends is probably still under bank sediment. It has been dated to the 3rd century, a time when river navigation was an important part of the transport system of Roman Siscia.

The construction of the ship itself is particularly interesting. Archaeologist Anton Divić explains that elements of local river shipbuilding can be recognised on it, as well as techniques known from the Roman maritime tradition. Sisak 1 is therefore important not only as a rarely preserved cargo ship, but also as evidence that different shipbuilding knowledge met and mixed in Siscia.

the home of discoveries from the 2nd century bc

Interestingly, the large cargo vessel is not the only old craft that the Kupa has preserved. More recent research has also revealed a series of logboats – simple boats hollowed out from a single tree trunk. Five of them have been investigated and dated so far, and the results obtained stretch from the 2nd century BC to the end of antiquity. Because of such a wide time span, not all the vessels can be linked to the same period or the same community.

Perhaps the most interesting thing today is that the story of Roman Siscia is not taking place only in museum display cases. Part of the city lies beneath modern Sisak, part of its former edges ended up in the Kupa, and part still remains to be investigated. Over the past century the Kupa has yielded thousands of objects, but its bed has clearly not yet told the whole story.

World.title: Rimac: Top Croatian Export Products are Luxury Cars and Battery Systems
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – Entrepreneur Mate Rimac has stated that some of the top Croatian export products are now luxury cars and battery systems.

Mate Rimac published on Facebook a table of the 50 largest Croatian goods exporters in 2025, compiled by the portal Lider. Index reports that among the top ten are two companies from Rimac’s business system. Bugatti Rimac took fourth place, and Rimac Technology seventh.

“Croatia’s top export products in 2025 are oil and derivatives, medicines, transformers, luxury cars and their components, dietary supplements, battery and propulsion systems for cars, aluminium foil, food, HVAC systems and pharmaceutical products,” Rimac wrote. This is Rimac’s summary compiled on the basis of the activities of the companies at the top of Lider’s ranking. The table itself ranks companies according to the value of their exports.

Who is actually on the table?

In first place is INA, which achieved 1.23 billion euros in exports in 2025. It is followed by Pliva Hrvatska with 474.4 million euros and Končar – Distribution and Special Transformers with 409.8 million euros.

Bugatti Rimac took fourth place with exports worth 369.1 million euros, which accounts for 94.33 percent of the company’s total revenues. In fifth place is Končar – Power Transformers with 313.5 million euros in exports, and sixth is dietary supplement manufacturer EMPWR with 227.4 million euros. Rimac Technology is in seventh place with exports worth 214 million euros, or an export share of 79.86 percent of total revenues. Also among the top ten are Aluflexpack Novi, Podravka and Klimaoprema.

According to Lider’s data, the 50 largest Croatian goods exporters in 2025 achieved a total of 7.4 billion euros in exports. At the same time, Croatian goods exports exceeded 25 billion euros, of which 21.7 billion was generated by the manufacturing industry.

World.title: The Night Omiš Will Never Forget – Everything Went Up in Flames in a Second
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – The night that Omiš will never forget was one marked by apocalyptic scenes and dramatic rescues from the sea.

An enormous fire that initially broke out in Lokva Rogoznica, driven by strong winds, spread rapidly towards Omiš. The fire threatened houses, reached the Adriatic Highway and forced residents and guests to flee into the sea to escape the flames. The testimonies of the people who found themselves facing the blaze show just how quickly the situation turned into a fight for survival.

“it all happened in a few seconds”

Dražen Ravlić was among the first to warn about the approaching fire. He said he noticed cars starting to turn back from the direction in which the fire was spreading. He immediately warned people at a nearby car park and called the firefighters.

“Everything happened very fast. I went ahead to the parking area and told people to move their cars,” he told Index. Together with a motorcyclist who happened to be there, he tried to help, but without equipment they could not do much. What remained in Ravlić’s memory were the sparks flying, carried by the wind. Afterwards he said he regretted that he could not do more.

Goran Lović, the owner of a cafe near the area where the fire first broke out, described how suddenly the blaze actually spread. “Everything went up in flames in a second,” he said. Lović believes the fire was started deliberately and handed surveillance camera footage over to the police. The cause of the fire has not yet been officially determined and this remains unconfirmed.

cars went up in flames and people fled into the sea for safety

When the fire reached the main road, the road was no longer a safe way out. Some people left their cars and headed towards the coast. Among them was Karla from Zagreb. At the moment of evacuation she was in a car, but the fire reached the road. “Cars started burning and then we went down towards the sea,” Karla said.

During the escape she fell and injured herself. With others she took shelter in a small cave by the sea, where they waited around two hours for rescuers. “Above us, the terrifying fire was blazing viciously,” she described. She managed to save only her documents, but says she is grateful to be alive. People fled into the sea or climbed onto boats they found along the shore. 194 people were rescued from the sea, mainly in the area from Nemira to Ruskamen. Intensive rescue operations lasted from after midnight until almost 03:00.

seasonal workers from mostar fled their apartment with barely anything

Two seasonal workers from Mostar said they fled their apartment with almost nothing. They spent the night in the car, waiting for the danger to pass and trying to find out what had happened to the place where they worked.

The café Mala Luka, where they worked, burned down completely. “We saw it approaching. I told her: “We’re not going to mess around.” We got into the car and left towards Omiš,” they said. Similar testimonies could be heard throughout the burned area. People described how in the dark they watered their yards, extinguished sparks carried by the wind and waited until the last moment before leaving their houses.

“when i saw there was no hope, i had to leave”

Marin Ozretić tried to defend his house as the fire came closer and closer. As the flames descended from the hill, he watered the pines and the area around the house, trying to stop the fire from spreading.

“I spent my entire life building this… When I saw there was no hope left for me, I just had to go,” he told Index. He described flames several metres high coming down from the hill. At the last moment he got into his car and left the area. He saved himself and the vehicle, but was unable to save his house.

Also at the fire site was Anđelko Kovačić, whose house in the old village, workshop and boats he was repairing all burned. Czech tourists who were staying in his apartment were left without a car and did not know how they would get home.

the morning light revealed the true scale of the unimaginable damage

Only when daylight came did the full extent of the fire become visible. Burned cars, destroyed buildings, blackened pines and large areas covered in ash remained. According to the latest information, 43 people sought medical help. Fourteen of them were kept in hospital, and eight were in life-threatening condition. During a search of the burned area, police also found the body of one person whose identity has not yet been released.

World.title: Omiš Resident Describes the Fire: It Was Like Being in Hell
World.content:
August the 16th, 2026 – An Omiš resident described the horrendous fire that swept through the area leaving a trail of unimaginable destruction behind it as like “being in hell”.

Index reports that a resident of Čelina near Omiš, Karlo, spent the night defending his house from the fire that devastated his village. One house burned down completely, and at one point the residents were left without water, so they tried to fight the flames with shovels. Children were evacuated to Omiš, while help is arriving in the affected area from all over Croatia.

“it was like we were in hell”

“It cannot be described in words. We were surrounded by smoke and fire. We used water for as long as we could, but our water supply depends on electricity. When the power went out, the water was gone too. Even the firefighters ran out of water, and we continued with shovels. By some miracle we managed to save some of the houses,” Karlo told N1. He said that it was primarily ruins which were entirely burned down in the village. “A house burned here too, that is the worst image of the fire I have in my mind. I don’t even want to mention the body that was found, it’s just beyond a horror.”

“the fire arrived in just 45 minutes”

Karlo said he didn’t expect the fire to spread so quickly. “We watched the light approaching. The fire reached our village in 45 minutes. We poured water all over the houses and that saved us. The night was endless, we couldn’t sleep or eat,” he described. They moved the children to safety in Omiš, while the men stayed to defend the property. “My mother stayed – she isn’t afraid of anything – and she was also watering the house. A neighbour’s car burned in a covered garage.” He admits he was not afraid, but he was fully aware of the danger.

help from across croatia

In the meantime, volunteers from all over Croatia are arriving at the fire site. Among them is Mario from Petrinja, who came with his father and son bringing a donation. “I was sleeping when my wife called and asked if I would drive a donation. I agreed, and I didn’t even know why. Within a few hours we gathered, people were calling, I didn’t even know where I was going. I came with my father and son,” he said.

World.title: Man Tried to Defend Home in Omiš Fire, But Lost Everything
World.content:
August the 15th, 2026 – A man attempted to defend his home and all he had been building up since the 1990s in the Omiš fire, but tragically lost absolutely everything to the flames.

The horrendous fire that swept through the Omiš area has left catastrophic consequences in its wake. The blaze swallowed houses, cars and hospitality facilities, causing enormous material damage and creating chaos on the ground. One person tragically died in the fire, while more than 40 people sought medical help. Index/Lukrecija Zderic reports that the scale of the tragedy and the scenes of burned buildings testify to the destructive power of a fire that in a short time endangered the lives, property and livelihoods of numerous residents.

A stroll through the burned area, which according to initial estimates has scorched more than 1,000 hectares, is staggering. Many spent hours defending their homes from the flames, but when the fire became too great a threat they were forced to abandon their houses and flee, some into the sea directly, in order to save their own lives. Complete devastation now lies where houses and trees once stood, and the testimonies of residents best illustrate the scale of the tragedy and the fear they experienced as the fire approached their homes.

“I’ve lost everything i spent my life building”

A resident of Mala Luka near Omiš, Marin Ozretić, lost the home he built in the 1990s. When the fire broke out he tried to defend the house he lived in, but when the flames approached the building itself he was forced to flee so that his car would not burn and so that he would not remain trapped in the fire.

“How can I tell you… I’d been building this my whole life. We had to run. When it started, when it came from above, the flames were more than two or three metres high. I evacuated myself. There wasn’t even a moment of fear, because we were pouring water so it wouldn’t pass. I was watering these pines here, I watered these as far as the hose could reach. And then, after that, when I saw there was no hope left for me, I just had to go. Then I got into the car and at the last moment I saved the car, and myself,” he revealed.

Tourists from the Czech Republic also lost their car to the fire, leaving them still unsure how they will return to their homeland. The owner of the apartment where they were staying, Anđelko Kovačić, lost his house in the old village, as well as the workshop and the boats they were repairing, since he is engaged in servicing and repairing vessels.

Kovačić stated that he doesn’t expect much help from the state, emphasising that a possible compensation of 500 euros cannot restore what he’d been creating his whole life. An investigation into the causes of the fire is still ongoing, and it is not known how one of the largest fires to hit this area in recent years started and claimed one human life. While firefighters continue to extinguish the fire on the hill, residents in disbelief walk around their homes and what remains of them, confronting scenes that the blaze turned into ashes in just a few minutes.

World.title: Woman from Zagreb Found Safety from Omiš Fire in a Cave
World.content:
August the 15th, 2026 – A woman named Karla from Zagreb ended up finding safety from the devastating Omiš fire in a cave. “I am so happy to be alive” she stated.

Among the hundreds of people evacuated from the fire-ravaged area around Omiš is Karla from Zagreb, who is now staying at the reception centre at Gripe in Split. Index reports that while fleeing the advancing flames she was injured and lost almost everything she owned, managing to save only her personal documents, reports Dalmatinski portal.

The major wildfire that broke out near Lokva Rogoznica and quickly threatened several settlements around Omiš forced many residents and visitors to abandon their homes in a matter of minutes. Strong winds drove the fire towards houses, cars and the main coastal road, creating chaotic scenes as people scrambled to escape.

Karla described the terrifying moments when the fire closed in on her group. “We were on the road, in the car. At that moment the fire reached the main road. Cars started burning and then we went down towards the sea,” she said. In the desperate rush towards the coast she fell and suffered injuries. With the flames closing in and no clear escape route left on land, she and others took refuge in a small cave by the sea.

“We waited for about two hours in a little cave by the sea until the rescue service arrived. Above us the fire was blazing,” Karla recounted. The group sat in the darkness of the cave, listening to the roar of the fire and the sound of burning vegetation, unsure whether help would reach them in time. Eventually, emergency services located them and brought them to safety.

Although she was left with nothing but her documents and the clothes she was wearing, Karla stressed that material losses pale in comparison to survival. “I’m just happy to be alive,” she said. Her story is one of many emerging from the Omiš fire, which according to the Croatian Firefighting Association burned around 900 hectares of grass, scrub and pine forest before being brought under control. Hundreds of residents were evacuated, several people required medical attention, and numerous homes and vehicles were damaged or destroyed.

World.title: Miro Bulj: Sinj Providing 20,000 to Omiš
World.content:
August the 15th, 2026 – Mayor Miro Bulj says that Sinj will gladly provide funding in the amount of 20,000 to Omiš following the devastating fire which broke out last night.

Mayor Miro Bulj has made a decision allocating 20,000 euros in aid from Sinj to Omiš following the major fire that has devastated that area. Index reports that in a statement, he emphasised that the assistance is an expression of solidarity with the citizens of Omiš in these difficult moments.

“It’s extremely hard to watch Omiš go up in smoke and flames, people evacuating their homes, parents rescuing their children, and families fearing for everything that generations before them have built. In a short time, the fire destroyed houses, cars, olive groves, memories and years of hard work,” Bulj said.

He added that the fire has not, however, destroyed the most valuable thing – the courage and strength of the people of Omiš to defend their homes. “Dear people of Omiš, your pain today is also ours. When one town suffers, the whole of Croatia feels it. When one person is threatened, we are all called to help. Sinj and Omiš are not just neighbours. We are connected by a love of stone, the Cetina river, the sea, faith, tradition and homeland. We are connected by the pride of people who throughout history have defended what is theirs and have always helped others in need.”

“The amount of 20,000 euros is a modest contribution given the scale of the damage, but it represents the sincere solidarity and friendship of all the women and men of Sinj. It is a message to every resident of Omiš: we stand with you, we feel with you, and we will help you rebuild your homes and restore normal life in the town,” the mayor’s statement reads.

He told the Mayor of Omiš, Zvonko Močić, and the President of the City Council, Karlo Lukasović, that the City of Sinj is at their disposal for all necessary assistance. “I wish a swift and full recovery to all the injured. To the families who have lost their homes or suffered damage, I say: hold on and know that you are not alone.”

Bulj also called on others to join in. “I expect all institutions and everyone who can to get involved in the aid effort. Now is the time for concrete help to everyone whose home and future are under threat.” He particularly thanked the emergency services.

“I thank our firefighters, members of the emergency services and all those who helped. In the hardest moments they stood between the fire and human lives and defended every home and every person. Their courage, strength and self-sacrifice inspire pride and restore faith in people.”

On the eve of the Feast of the Assumption (Velika Gospa), Bulj also offered a prayer. “I pray for the intercession of Our Lady of Sinj the Miracle-Worker to protect Omiš, all its residents, their families and our firefighters. May she bring healing to the injured, peace to the frightened, and strength and hope for a new beginning to those who have lost their homes.”

“Dear people of Omiš, take care of your town and of one another. Your streets will once again be filled with life, homes will be rebuilt, and your pride and love for Omiš will be stronger than the fire. Sinj will always stand with you,” Mayor Bulj said.
