World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

World.title: Man killed in hit-and-run near Ballarat
World.content:
Victorian detectives are investigating a fatal hit-and-run in the Ballarat suburb of Canadian overnight.

Police say a green Ford Fiesta struck a man on Butt Street just after midnight.

CPR was administered but he died at the scene.

The car did not have numberplates and was found on nearby Elsworth Street.

Police are appealing for anyone in the area to check their CCTV and dash cam and any witnesses are urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Concerns for emergency response during rolling Telstra upgrades
World.content:
Telstra customers in regional Western Australia say the telco's decision to conduct week-long upgrades without providing backup services could hamper emergency responders in one of the state's most prolific rescue zones.

The town of Gnowangerup, 350 kilometres south-east of Perth, sits at the base of the Stirling Range in the state's Great Southern.

Gnowangerup, home to about 1,200 people, is one of WA's most profitable grain-producing regions, and popular year-round with tourists visiting Bluff Knoll and the Stirling Range National Park.

The town of Gnowangerup sits at the base of the Stirling Range, a popular spot for hiking and tourists. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Last week, Telstra told customers to expect service outages from Friday, August 14, lasting up to eight days, with outages of up to eight hours a day as it upgrades its 4G and 5G networks.

The timing and duration of the upgrades have "frustrated" customers and come at a time when the telco's regional service was facing increased scrutiny.

It has also raised concerns in Gnowangerup that first responders may be unable to muster volunteer crews effectively in an emergency.

Mandy Hanna, who is with the SES, is concerned the length of the outage could disrupt rescue operations. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Emergency concerns

Gnowangerup State Emergency Service (SES) manager Mandy Hanna said its volunteers were often the first to respond to a road crash or distress call on Bluff Knoll.

"We're quite busy in the Stirling [Range] so if we can't be contacted at all we're not going to know if anything's happening," she said.

"My main concern is because we have that road crash capability, this is affecting people's lives."

Mandy Hanna says first responders and volunteers rely on mobile phones to coordinate their movements in an emergency. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Ms Hanna said she had a personal Starlink satellite but stressed most SES members relied heavily on mobile phones to coordinate their movements in an emergency.

"Worst case, we can't be contacted for a road crash, and someone loses their life because we just don't know," she said.

"It's the same with St John's Ambulance [volunteers]; if we can't be contacted, we don't know."

Telstra is working to upgrade 4G and 5G services in the region. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

A Telstra spokesperson apologised for the inconvenience and confirmed the planned upgrades would not impact NBN, Satellite internet services, landline services, or mobile coverage from other providers.

They said calls to Triple Zero (000) would connect to another mobile network, if available.

"We're sorry for the disruption, but unfortunately this work is what's required to upgrade mobile connectivity in the area," they said.

"The team have planned this to minimise disruption as much as possible."

Darren Robertson says eftpos has been largely unusable since the service disruption. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Business taking IOUs

The impact is being felt by some businesses in the town, including Darren Robertson, who owns the town's only cafe.

He said the outages of up to eight hours coincided with his opening hours, making his eftpos system unusable.

And with the ATM next door out of money, he said the cafe had been taking IOUs and hoping customers would return to pay.

Darren Robertson is taking IOUs from locals, but cannot serve tourists from out of town. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

"Yesterday it never worked at all … This morning it was on until about eight o'clock, and then it went off," he said.

" The locals are fine, but it's impacting my business because we've got people coming through that are from out of town, and a lot of people don't carry cash these days. "

Mr Robertson, who also uses a Starlink satellite at home, said he was considering replacing his Telstra service at the shop with another satellite to avoid future blackouts.

He also asked why Telstra could not use similar technology to maintain services for customers while the network was down.

"It goes to show how much we rely on Telstra, but I don't know why they couldn't set up a little portable tower or something while they do work on this big one," he said.

David Nicholson says Telstra's planning of the upgrades has been frustrating for customers. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Shire chief executive David Nicholson has strongly criticised Telstra's communication and planning, suggesting shorter outages would reduce the impact on the town.

"I think it's quite atrocious and really poor customer service," he said.

"There should be some plan where perhaps the outage wasn't so long during the day.

"I get they've got work to do, but eight hours, I mean, my goodness, it's just basically down tools if you rely heavily on Telstra."

Telstra says customers can continue to make calls and send texts during the upgrades by switching on wi-fi calling, which requires access to a wi-fi source.

World.title: Broken zips, sleeve sewn shut: Union raises SA firefighter safety concerns
World.content:
Adelaide fire trucks have been grounded and some firefighting training temporarily cancelled, a union claims, amid concerns about the supply and maintenance of protective gear.

The United Firefighters Union has lodged a dispute in the SA Employment Tribunal, claiming the SA Metropolitan Fire Service (MFS) has failed to provide enough personal protective equipment (PPE) to its firefighters.

In documents lodged to the tribunal, the union argued the MFS had also failed to ensure its protective gear was "maintained, repaired, or replaced such that it continues to minimise risk to the worker who uses it".

"We seem to be faced with a massive failure of the PPE system in the MFS," Union acting secretary Peter Russell told the ABC.

"We've had items sewn on incorrectly, we've had things facing the wrong way, I think we had a sleeve sewn shut at one point in time.

" If that PPE is not working properly a firefighter could be exposed to severe injury or they could be killed. "

Photos provided by the union to the ABC show MFS gear with broken zippers and repairs.

A Metropolitan Fire Service firefighter wearing a coat with a faulty zipper. (Supplied)

Mr Russell said it was "impossible" to quantify how much MFS gear the union considered unsafe, as the service was unable to provide records.

"Even the newest gear… we have a very severe concern that the zips on those ensembles are faulty and [are] capable of coming apart during firefighting activities, exposing firefighters to risks of severe burns or death," he said.

The MFS said all of its "current operational structural firefighting" PPE met relevant industry standards and there was enough supply to ensure firefighters could safely respond to calls for help.

It said since 2023, the MFS had also been introducing new PPE.

"The safety of firefighters and the community is paramount," a spokesperson for the service said.

A faulty zipper on Metropolitan Fire Service personal protective equipment. (Supplied)

Concerns over laundering delay

Mr Russell said firefighters had told him "on many occasions" about their concern for how long PPE was taking to return from laundering.

He said delays of six weeks or longer had been reported to him and it had led to shortages.

"Firefighters are reluctant to put their firefighting gear in for laundering when it needs it, and risking using contaminated gear, because they do not trust that the system will return their gear to them," he said.

A lack of sufficient PPE is also to blame for fire trucks at the Elizabeth MFS station not being usable across the June long weekend, according to Mr Russell.

He said the union's own investigation had uncovered this was not an isolated incident.

"It became apparent to us that it wasn't an issue isolated to that station,"Mr Russell said.

" In effect, 30-year-old, 25-year-old sets of PPE had been reintroduced into circulation that never should have been. "

A MFS spokesperson did not comment on the Elizabeth example but said it was "not unusual" for a truck to be taken "offline" after it had responded to an incident.

"During this period firefighters and appliances are decontaminated, and equipment and PPE are restored and/or replaced as necessary," they said.

"Established processes are in place to ensure coverage is maintained and response times met during these periods."

The union claims that some MFS fire trucks have been grounded due to issues with PPE availability. (ABC News)

The spokesperson said in addition to individually-issued PPE, the MFS had reserves in several storage spaces "strategically located" across Adelaide.

"These caches are used to replenish PPE sent for decontamination and ensure firefighters continue to have access to fit-for-purpose protective equipment when responding to multiple incidents," they said.

"Older PPE sets identified in some caches have been removed."

'Temporary pause' on structural firefighter training

In a memo released earlier this month, and seen by the ABC, MFS chief officer Jeff Swann wrote that its Angle Park training centre "must not be used for training unless approval has been granted by the chief officer due to extenuating circumstances".

"This temporary pause will remain in place while the MFS considers the matters raised and determines any further steps that may be required," he wrote.

"Staff are reminded that recent MFS safety alerts have been issued regarding structural firefighting personal protective equipment, including alerts relating to the operation of LHD Sabre structural coat zippers and potential zipper separation."



Mr Russell said the shortage of PPE was partly to blame and he did not known when training would resume at the site.

"The situation has gotten so bad that they've had to close part of their training centre because they cannot operate it anymore safely," he said.

" If we're not running training, how are firefighters being equipped? "

A MFS spokesperson said a review was underway to ensure the training centre remained "safe and effective".

"Other training can continue to take place on site and this pause does not impact frontline emergency response," they said.

Emergency Services Minister Rhiannon Pearce said the state government continued to invest in firefighter equipment, training and resources.

"The Malinauskas Government has increased funding for emergency services including an extra $3.7 million for the MFS in 2024-25, compared to the previous financial year, and a further $589,000 to support the agency's large scale event response," she said.

World.title: Stroke rates buck trends in young people amid missed signs and misdiagnosis
World.content:
Ben Murphy's first stroke took more than three days to be identified as he was shuffled between hospitals.

Aged 27 at the time, he puts the delayed diagnosis down to his age.

Calls for greater stroke awareness in the NT When then-38-year-old Alison Reidy woke up with a migraine, she never thought it would be a stroke. Now she's tyring to improve stroke awareness in the Northern Territory.

"It happened during COVID, so they were trying to get people in and out," he said, adding he was deemed fit for discharge after just 10 days.

Scans had also found a "hole" in Mr Murphy's heart, but doctors did not recommend he get it treated then.

Five years later, he had another stroke. This time far more severe and lead to a three-month stay in south-east Queensland hospitals.

"I completely lost my speech … and then I couldn't walk either because my right limbs, my hand, my leg, were just non-functional," the 33-year-old said.

" My life isn't really the same again, because this time, I'm still recovering. "

The severity of the second stroke prompted a procedure to close the heart opening.

Two years on, life back on his family farm in the Scenic Rim near the Gold Coast and a gradual return to activities like driving are helping him make strides towards independence.

Young stroke rates bucking the trend

Data from the Stroke Foundation shows more than 440,000 Australians were living with stroke as of 2023, with one in four strokes occurring in people of working age.

According to a review published by the World Stroke Organization (WSO) in January, the incidence of strokes amongst people aged under 55 has increased globally since the early 2000s, despite decreasing at older ages.

Stroke Foundation chief executive Lisa Murphy said it was a similar picture in Australia because prevention efforts still only targeted an older demographic.

"We've known for a long time that risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes and a thing called atrial fibrillation, which is an irregular heartbeat, all contribute to a risk factor of stroke," she said.

Lisa Murphy says stroke symptoms are regularly being missed in emergency departments, by paramedics and other health professionals. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

"And we know what to do about those … [however] that hasn't translated into young people yet, and I think one of the reasons why is a lot of those risk factors are actually silent."

Neurology professor Vincent Thijs from the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health said the increased incidence in young people was limited to ischemic strokes, but the reasons as to why were not fully understood.

Ischemic strokes occur when a blood clot blocks an artery supplying blood to the brain and account for 80 per cent of all stroke events in Australia.

Many cases have no known cause

Professor Thijs said there had also been an increase in young stroke cases with no identifiable cause, known as cryptogenic strokes, with links to increased drug use, air pollution, longer hours at work, and delayed pregnancies.

Signs of stroke — use the FAST test Face: Has the mouth drooped?

Arms: Can they lift both arms?

Speech: Is their speech slurred?

Time: If you notice these signs, call Triple Zero (000) immediately. The Stroke Foundation also says regular health checks, exercise and a well-balanced diet go a long way to reducing the risk of strokes.

A Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO), a type of opening in the heart as with Mr Murphy, is another factor that has been associated with cryptogenic strokes.

Australian clinical trials suggest they are present in up to 50 per cent of cases in young people.

However, Professor Thijs said PFOs were common in healthy young people too and there was often no need to get them closed until a first-time stroke.

"More and better screening should occur after a stroke in the 18- to 60-year-olds as closure prevents a second stroke from happening if a PFO [with certain features] is identified," he said.

Gold Coast woman Ash De Cotta was "totally fit and healthy" before she suffered a brain stem stroke at the age of 35 and, two years on, still does not know why.

Ash De Cotta wants others to know stroke does not discriminate and to listen to their bodies. (ABC Gold Coast: Glenn Mullane)

"I had severe neck pain leading up to it, just out of the blue … and I had migraine with aura, which is where your vision sort of goes fuzzy, and that was about a month leading up to my stroke," she said.

" I did go to the doctors a few times, but I was just given painkillers and sent on my way. "

She ended up spending six months in hospital after suffering locked-in syndrome, a full-body paralysis caused by ischemic strokes.

Ms De Cotta said it was crucial people listened to their body and questioned unusual symptoms.

Different needs of young survivors

The Florey's Young Stroke Service is the sole dedicated service for young people, aged 18 to 55, recovering from a stroke but is only available in Victoria and South Australia.

Professor Thijs said there was a huge need for tailored support and funding to deliver such services Australia-wide.

"Younger people have different goals. They want to get back to work, they want to return to driving," he said.

Vincent Thijs says strokes in young people are still not the norm but having it on the radar is important. (Supplied)

"Our health system isn't particularly catered towards the needs of these younger stroke survivors, so that's why the impact is different and bigger in many respects."

Ms De Cotta agreed.

"Typically, people think older people have strokes, and that's not the case, and services do need to catch up with that," she said.

World.title: Data centres to be fast-tracked in NSW, despite community group pushback
World.content:
A new government initiative incentivises data centre builders to comply with freshly set guidelines if they want to fast-track their developments.

Builders will have to meet environmental and efficiency standards, impose no net cost to consumers and fund additional supply of water and energy.

They will also have to enhance local community infrastructure, invest in "future industries" and commit to skills training and support jobs.

In return the state government promises to assess their applications within 75 days.

19 more data centres are currently on the way in NSW. (ABC News)

'We have to replace a lot of old energy sources'

With more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction in NSW and 19 more in the planning and approval pipeline, the government said it was time to set regulations.

Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the government had been working on the framework for more than a year.

"We are launching a nation-leading policy to make sure that rising data centre investment is matched with increased investment in renewable energy and water infrastructure," he said.

Mr Mookhey said under the new framework data centre builders would foot the bill for new clean energy, sparing Australian taxpayers.

Daniel Mookhey announced the new scheme on Monday. (ABC News)

"There's no doubt we have to replace a lot of old energy sources like coal fire power. We do and should replace that with clean, green, renewable power," he said.

" We want data centre builders to help pay their fair share, so it doesn't just fall to households to pick up the cost. "

The framework trades compliance for speedy government assessments, but it does not set out penalties for builders that refuse the government's offer.

Mr Mookhey said builders that did not meet the standards could have their proposals rejected.

"Those data centre builders that choose not to comply with these guidelines will have to take the risk that their projects are going to get refused," he said.

"We're pretty clear that these are our expectations … any data centre builder that chooses not to comply with these standards will find themselves almost alone."

Data centres face backlash

A group of students and community organisers protested the increase of data centres around Western Sydney on Sunday.

Gokulan Gopal questions where the water is going to come from for new data centres. (ABC News)

Gokulan Gopal is a local community organiser who spoke at the protest calling for a moratorium on new AI data centre builds until the community is consulted and has a better understanding of the impacts of living next to these data centres.

"Where is the water going to come from? Where is the power going to come from? How are we going to manage the waste? When the outage happens, what kind of backups are they going to use?" he said.

" If they're going to consume that much power, what will happen to our power price? What will happen to our water price? So there is really some serious unanswered questions. "

Sophie Shanaaz represents a campaign called 'Stop the Slop' which opposes the expansion of data centres in Western Sydney.

"We're really focused on getting all these AI data centres out of our suburbs … eating our resources. We're not happy about it and we want to do something about it," she said.

"I live in very close proximity to one being developed and I feel that there is not enough regulation at the moment."

Mr Mookhey said he was aware of community concerns and believed the new regulations would address them.

"This technology is only going to have social license if people can see that there is a strong dividend for them and their children, as well as our state and our nation's future," he said.

"The principle that we're setting for today is really straightforward. Data centres that want to build in New South Wales need to bring power, not take it."

Builders who do not meet the fresh guidelines could have their proposals rejected. (ABC News)

Water usage addressed in guidelines, Mookhey says

Under the new framework, data centre builders would need to show they were entering into power purchasing agreements with renewable energy providers.

"That means that if these data centre builders sign those contracts, it results in less bills for households," Mr Mookhey said.

Similar to energy consumption, data centres are also resource intensive when it comes to water usage.

Mr Mookhey said the guidelines addressed this by setting certain water usage efficiency standards and by incentivising data centre builders to invest in water infrastructure.

The Sydney suburb at risk of becoming a 'data centre wasteland' Sydney is in the middle of a data centre boom fuelled by the global AI race. In Lane Cove West and Ryde, residents and councils say they are the ones paying the price.

The framework will come with a water pricing review to be conducted by the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART), which would aim to "ensure water users on the network are protected and the impacts of drought and water scarcity are appropriately managed".

A new Office of AI will also be established to coordinate government investment in digital and AI assets to "ensure AI supports workers, strengthens capacity and is implemented responsibly across the public sector".

The new framework comes into effect on Monday, while the IPART review and Office of AI might take longer.

World.title: After constant chopping and changing, Green goes 'back to what worked'
World.content:
Cameron Green has delivered for a shell-shocked Australian side to give himself breathing space at number five, leading captain Pat Cummins to predict a long stint in one position in the batting line-up.

Green's 104 in the second innings of the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin was his first in Australia and also broke an 11-innings run without passing the half-century mark.

The 27-year-old all-rounder has been heavily criticised in Australian cricket for not turning his undoubted potential into results.

But his knock in the loss means he leaves the Northern Territory as one of the only Aussie batters who can hold their heads high, with Cummins "not too sure" on the best course of action to turn things around before the second Test starts in Mackay on Saturday.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

"We're always quite individual, everyone goes about it slightly differently, so coaches will work with each player individually," he said.

"I don't think there was a huge trend, everyone got out a little bit differently, but I think it's pretty clear it's not quite functioning as well as we'd like as a group.

"If we need to make some changes to our style, we've got a week or so, we better do it pretty quickly."

Cummins said before the Test that Green had been encouraged to "intimidate" and he did it the way he knows best, driving with commanding power and poise while accumulating runs at a steady rate without taking risks.

It is a method that has worked in Sheffield Shield cricket and he showcased why Test selectors have persevered with him despite the outside noise calling for his head.

Green's third Test century did not lead to a win but that was largely due to the failure of the rest of the order to stay with him in good batting conditions on the third and fourth days.

Australia will consider making changes to the underperforming top order for the second Test in Mackay that starts on Saturday, but Green will be one of the first picked.

"I'm sure he will get an extended run somewhere," Cummins said when asked if Green had tied down the number five position.

"I thought he was really impressive and controlled his innings. He looked in total command of his skills out there. He just needed one or two of us to bat alongside him."

Green and Steve Smith were the only Australian batters who could be happy with their output. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green struggled in the last Ashes series, as many batters did, making just 171 runs at an average of 24.42 after being moved around from fifth to eighth in the order.

He earlier did a solid job on the West Indies tour, averaging 30.66 at first drop as the only member of the top three to average more than 20 across the three Tests.

"We obviously think very highly of Cam," Cummins said.

"The last Ashes series probably didn't go as well as he would have liked but before that on the West Indian tour he was probably our best batter in really tough circumstances when he was batting a little higher.

"It was great for him to go out there and show the rest of the world how good he is."

Quick hits as Bangladesh wraps up famous win Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them. Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

Green was fortunate in the final session on the third day when an inside edge off Taskin Ahmed grazed his leg stump on the way to the boundary.

The bails were not dislodged and the all-rounder dug in and made the most of his reprieve.

Green told Fox Cricket after his knock that he had approached his innings against Bangladesh like he used to do "back in the day".

"I think I've just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so it's nice just to go back to what worked," Green said.

"It has been a long couple of months so it is nice to get a few rewards for it."

As for the critics, Green said it just came with the territory.

"I feel like there are always wolves when you are playing Test cricket. When you play for Australia, you always have to perform," he said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: DV advocates call for action as under-18 violence increases
World.content:
Advocates in Alice Springs say people are increasingly experiencing domestic, family and sexual violence from a younger age and it needs to be addressed.

It comes after Northern Territory Police arrested a 16-year-old boy for punching, choking and pushing his 17-year-old partner to the ground in an Alice Springs shopping centre on Tuesday morning.

Chay Brown says domestic violence is an issue across Australia. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

Specialist domestic, family and sexual violence researcher Chay Brown said she was saddened, but not shocked by the incident.

"Domestic violence is a problem right the way across our nation," she said.

"We find it in all socio-economic class groups, we find it amongst all people of all cultures, of all creeds.

" This is an Australian problem and that's why it needs a coordinated national response to address it. "

Violence from a younger age

Dr Brown said people were starting to use and experience violence from a younger age.

"That's partly because people are getting into relationships earlier, but it's also partly … symptomatic of domestic and family violence in the wider society," she said.

"There's a really strong correlation between people who experience violence as children, often through the family, and those who go on to use violence.

"We must intervene much, much, much earlier."

Women's Safety Services of Central Australia chief executive Larissa Ellis said data showed girls under 18 years who experienced domestic, family and sexual violence were an emerging need in the NT, but society could not become complacent.

She said there was no crisis accommodation specifically for girls under 18 in Alice Springs, yet domestic and family violence in the Northern Territory was three times the national average.

"In the Northern Territory, there is very little money spent on prevention or early intervention," she said.

" These girls, these women are members of our community, they are valued members of our community and we do need to respond to them. "

Larissa Ellis says there needs to be more specialist support services for girls under 18 years experiencing violence. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

Not impossible, but hard work

Michael Liddle, an Alyawarre man who runs men's behaviour programs, said young men and boys were angry, which in part explained the increase of violence in younger cohorts.

"The distance between the haves and the have-nots is getting wider," he said.

"In that distance is alcohol, ice, jealousy, all the traits that make people angry, lack of employment, lack of education to understand what's happening to my body, to my mind.

Michael Liddle says young men are angry, which is contributing to increasing violence. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"Now whether they be against a partner or whether they be against a friend, they're getting more violent and people are seeing it more often."

Mr Liddle said he and others continued to adapt their approach to meet the changing face of domestic, family and sexual violence.

"It's not impossible, but it's hard work," he said.

World.title: Director faces investigations following Mundella collapse
World.content:
Creditors say they may not see a cent of the millions owed to them by collapsed West Australian dairy processor Mundella Foods and two other associated companies.

Mundella, Margaret River Dairy Company and The Cheeky Cow were put into liquidation this month.

Director Hayden Russell is facing investigations by liquidators at Mackay Goodwin following administrators' preliminary suggestions of insolvent trading and hundreds of potentially "unreasonable transactions".

Dairy farmer and Mundella Foods milk supplier Phil Hall told the ABC he was owed "enough money to buy a house" and expected to get nothing back from the liquidation.

Phil Hall says he is still owed hundreds of thousands of dollars by Mundella Foods. (Supplied: Facebook/Halls Family Dairy)

"I don't know what happened to Mundella, but I know this year we basically never got paid," he said.

"Myself and another dairy farmer, we both did the same thing, believing in this company.

"We wanted this to work because it was the only way forward for the future."

A trio of well-known dairy companies have collapsed after being put into voluntary administration a year ago. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

The unpaid debt contributed to his family's recent decision to sell their farms at Wokalup in WA's South West and leave the dairy industry after six generations.

"I remember being three and running around this farm," Mr Hall said, choking back tears.

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch via email Daly.Jonathon@abc.net.au

Failed rescue plan

Mundella, Margaret River Dairy Company and The Cheeky Cow were put into liquidation on August 6, following the termination of a Deed of Company Arrangement (DOCA) put forward by Mr Russell in August last year.

Mr Hall is among the unsecured creditors still owed millions.

They were told they could see a potential return of 68 cents to the dollar under a rescue plan to sell the real estate portfolio of the companies under lease-back arrangements.

But administrators told the ABC the DOCA had been terminated as a result of Mr Russell's non-compliance with the terms of the deal.

It is not known what breach triggered the termination of the rescue plan.

Hayden Russell is facing scrutiny following the liquidation of the business and other associated companies. (Supplied: Kira Price)

A financial statement seen by the ABC shows more than $620,000 was paid from the administration account during the DOCA period for expenses, including administrator fees, trading costs and supplier payments.

Just over $12,000 remained when the deed was terminated.

There appears to have been no significant distribution of money to unsecured creditors.

The companies' property and remaining assets have been transferred to the mortgagee, Bowral Capital Pty Ltd.

Mr Hall said he held no ill-will towards Mr Russell, because he had initially paid dairy farmers 90 cents a litre for milk, compared to 76 cents offered by other processors.

"I'm not angry with Hayden because he was trying to do the right thing for the dairy industry," he said.

"None of the other milk companies were offering anything near the price he was offering, and nor are they trying to do anything for the farmers left in the industry."

Former Mundella Foods employee Mairee Wall is less forgiving.

Mairee Wall says the collapse of Mundella Foods "broke" her and other employees, who were once proud of the brand. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

She said she was still owed about $10,000 of unpaid annual leave and superannuation.

Ms Wall worked as a pasteuriser at Mundella Foods' Mundijong manufacturing facility near Perth from 2012, well before the company was purchased by The Cheeky Cow, a company majority-owned by Hayden Russell.

"That's when things very quickly unravelled," she said.

"Things went drastically wrong. There was no protocol. There was just no structure."

Ms Wall said she was once proud of making the Mundella brand of yoghurt, which had previously won national awards.

"We put everything into it, and it really broke a lot of people, me being one of them, when things just fell apart and just so quickly," she said.

Thoroughbred industry reports named Hayden Russell as the buyer of the stallion God Has Spoken in November last year. (Supplied: OzRace)

Thoroughbred purchases

Industry reports and bloodstock sale records indicate Mr Russell expanded his involvement in WA's thoroughbred industry during the past year.

Thoroughbred Breeders WA reported in November last year that "Margaret River Dairy Company owner Hayden Russell" had purchased a stallion named God Has Spoken, and the ABC has confirmed that purchase agreement.

The dairy companies' assets and properties have been transferred to the mortgagee, Bowral Capital Pty Ltd. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Sale results on online horse auction site Magic Millions list a buyer identified as "Hayden Russell, WA" as purchasing five horses.

There is no evidence in the administrators' reports linking Mr Russell's thoroughbred purchases, which had total costs of under $10,000, to the dairy companies' funds or to the transactions flagged for further investigation.

The ABC has contacted Mr Russell for comment.

Liquidators to investigate

In a report lodged with the corporate watchdog, administrators stated that the downfall of the companies was the combined result of "poor financial control/lack of records", "poor strategic management" and trading losses.

The liquidation process will involve further investigations of Mr Russell's duties as director.

Administrators flagged about 235 transactions worth more than $100,000 that may be considered "unreasonable director-related transactions" across the three companies.

The administrators also noted "sufficient evidence to suggest" Mundella had traded while insolvent from July 2024 and Margaret River Dairy Company from December 2023.

They estimated about $3.7 million in debt was incurred during that time, and said Mr Russell "may be personally liable for insolvent trading".

Administrators said preliminary findings had identified potential offences they intended to lodge with the corporate watchdog.

World.title: Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul
World.content:
Breaking WorldAsiaDonald Trump Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul Costas Pitas Updated August 17, 2026 — 8:42am ,first published 8:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump said he had instructed the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea in a social media post that also mentioned Seoul’s refusal to take part in actions against Iran. Trump said in a post on his Truth Social site on Monday morning (AEST) that, although it was too late to cancel the latest round of exercises entirely, he was “not happy” that the US had previously agreed to participate. Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un in 2020. The US president met the North Korean leader three times during his first term. Getty Images The US president also cited his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un. “These exercises are not only costly ... but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” he wrote.



Trump also pointed to South Korea’s stance on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran. “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’” Trump wrote. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military drills are scheduled to run from August 17 to 27. A South Korean army K1A2 tank fires during a drill as part of the annual the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercise in Cheorwon, South Korea, in 2023. AP/South Korea Defence Ministry The exercises involving 18,000 South Korean soldiers are designed to beef up readiness against North Korean threats.



North Korea on Friday threatened unspecified stern steps against the US and South Korea, describing their military drills as a “a rehearsal for an aggressive war” that are triggering greater instability in the region. The warning was typical of the harsh rhetoric that North Korea often deploys ahead of major US-South Korean military exercises. Members of US Special Operations Command Korea and South Korea’s Army Special Warfare Command during Ulchi Freedom Shield in Yangyang in 2023. AP Experts say North Korea has often used its rivals’ drills as a pretext to ramp up testing activities to expand its weapons arsenals and promote public support for leader Kim. US and South Korean forces were expected to practice joint operations in complex scenarios, including a live-fire exercise to test joint precision targeting and manoeuvre, a wet gap crossing, and distribution of prepositioned military equipment, according to the US military.



The US military has said the exercise “reinforces the role of the alliance as the linchpin for regional peace and security” and reaffirms “the ironclad commitment between the United States and the Republic of Korea to defend their homelands”. The joint training comes days after North Korea resumed ballistic missile testing activities that are banned by the UN. Photo: TruthSocial Earlier this month, South Korea, the U.S. and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from North Korea in what was the North’s first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June. The missile landed in the waters off North Korea’s east coast. North Korea has been pushing hard to enlarge its nuclear and missile arsenals since Kim’s high-stakes diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. Experts say Kim likely believes a bigger weapons arsenal would increase his chances for wresting more concessions from the US in future negotiations.



Trump met with the reclusive North Korean leader three times during his first term to discuss the country’s nuclear program, most recently in 2019. Since returning to office, Trump has expressed interest in continuing those discussions. Trump’s announcement came a day after he posted a photo of himself standing next to North Korea’s Kim, writing that the two leaders get along great “despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture”. This is not the first time that Trump has sought to end the exercises. During his first term he also issued a surprise announcement that called the war games “provocative”. “We will be stopping the war games, which will save us a tremendous amount of money, unless and until we see the future negotiation is not going along like it should,” Trump told reporters after his 2018 meeting with Kim in Singapore. Reuters, AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor marked down on migration; Hanson ramps up fight against gun buyback scheme
World.content:
London: The BBC asked a US court for help in getting documents and testimony from members of President Donald Trump’s family in connection with his $US10 billion ($14 billion) defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster, a court document showed.

Lawyers for the BBC argued that Ivanka Trump, her husband Jared Kushner, and Donald Trump Jr have “personal knowledge” and likely have records relevant to elements of Trump’s claims against the broadcaster. The broadcaster has been unable to serve subpoenas because the three have Secret Service protection, the court filing says.

Donald Trump in New York on Friday. AP

The president filed the lawsuit in December, accusing the BBC of defamation and deceptive and unfair trade practices. The allegations centre on the way a 2024 documentary edited a speech Trump gave on January 6, 2021, before protesters attacked the Capitol in Washington.



The lawsuit accuses the BBC of “splicing together two entirely separate parts” of Trump’s speech to “intentionally misrepresent the meaning of what [he] said” and that the editing was “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 election.



The BBC apologised to Trump for the misleading edit, but said it had not defamed him.



The latest court filing said that Trump’s family members had knowledge relevant to Trump’s argument “that it would be materially false to imply that he incited violence”. The BBC asked the court to allow the subpoenas to be served by email and certified mail.



Trump’s legal team said “the BBC is seeking to harass [Donald Trump], his family, and supporters by abusing the deposition process”. A trial has been provisionally set for February.



AP

World.title: Haddara crime family boss shot in Altona North
World.content:
Alleged one-time gangland boss Fadi Haddara has been ambushed and shot in the driveway of his Altona North home. Police believe Haddara, 48, was the victim of a targeted attack when he was shot in a parked car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue, near Millers Road, just before 8pm on Sunday. Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South Neighbours, who did not want to be identified over fears of retaliation, said they heard multiple gunshots around 8pm. Police and paramedics were quickly on scene. The neighbours said they heard yelling inside the home as detectives arrived.



Haddara was ambushed in his driveway on Sunday evening. Penny Stephens Despite his reputation, neighbours said Haddara was friendly, often waving to neighbours as he drove along the street. He is believed to be in a stable condition at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Haddara’s lawyer has been contacted for comment. Police were quickly on scene after the shooting. Nine



The road remained blocked off on Monday morning. Penny Stephens Half of Marigold Avenue remained completely blocked off on Monday morning. Police cars can be seen parked outside the home and along the street. The front lights at Haddara’s home were on, but police tape has blocked the driveway. Alleged gangland boss Fadi Haddara.



Haddara, the alleged patriarch of the Haddara crime family, once held a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne but had been squeezed out by new gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2024. Related Article Exclusive

Crime When the head of a crime family found trackers on his car, he knew the game was up The Age has previously reported that the Haddaras surrendered their stake in the illicit tobacco smuggling and distribution market following a relentless firebombing and shooting campaign waged by Hamad in 2023-2024, including Fadi finding multiple GPS trackers on his car. The attack on Fadi has been met with surprise in the underworld given the clan was largely sidelined following Hamad’s establishment of cartel-like control over the tobacco market. Attempts by some criminal players to take advantage of Hamad’s arrest in Iraq in January have met with acts of serious retribution by Hamad’s gang, known as The Commission or the 313.



Four businesses and a home owned or linked to the crime gang led by Haddara were attacked in March of this year alone, including the torching of the Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown and a drive-by shooting targeting a crowd of men standing outside an Altona North kebab shop in the heart of the gang’s territory.
