World.title: The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw Michael Gleeson Updated August 17, 2026 — 5:56am ,first published 6:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Carlton lost their coach in round nine and surely found their new one in the next 13 rounds.

Magpie Dan McStay continues a resurgence that few could have foreseen

Remember this: Hawks would not have won had they attempted to rush the ball through.

North’s win over the Dogs last week and the loss this week against Geelong shows the movement at Arden Street.

Quirky rule exposed Hawthorn would not have won had they attempted to rush the ball through for a behind after the siren. But they would have won had Collingwood punched it over the goal line. Weird, isn’t it? Collingwood’s Sam Swadling punches the post-siren kick from Dylan Moore into the field of play, ensuring Saturday night’s match at the MCG ended in a draw. @CollingwoodFC



Hawthorn’s Dylan Moore launches his shot at goal. Getty Images Under AFL rules, if Hawthorn – say Lloyd Meek for instance, who wound up to punch the ball and missed – knocked the ball through it would not have registered as a rushed behind to deliver a Hawthorn win. You can’t punch your own ball through for a score after the siren. It’s considered a secondary act of play to assist the score, and given play is technically dead after the siren, there can’t be a secondary play after the siren. Unless you are the other team. Under rule 16.5.2, had Collingwood punched the ball through, or it came off Collingwood hands and crossed the line, then a behind would have been registered and Hawthorn would have won. So, this won’t comfort Dylan Moore any, but he needed to clear the pack and get a score off his own boot. It does seem inconsistent that one team can create a score by touching the ball after the siren and not the other. Logically, any team touching the ball from the kick should mean it is a secondary act.



Incidentally, viewers had no idea what was happening on the goal line watching the lamentable Fox coverage, which managed at the most critical moment to crop out all of the play on the goal line. Draw’s a win for Fraser, his Blues and the AFL’s wildcard In a game with no winner there were two victors and a clear loser. Josh Fraser’s Carlton won. The AFL’s contentious wildcard round won. St Kilda lost. Josh Fraser was typically understated as the Blues locked away a wildcard berth with a draw against the Bulldogs. Getty Images Josh Fraser’s Carlton will play “finals”, or at least a quasi-final round. St Kilda will not.



Carlton lost the biggest name of the off-season to St Kilda as well as the son of a scion of the club, and are now certain to finish ahead of the Saints. Carlton lost their coach in round nine and surely found their new one in the next 13 rounds. View post on X Fraser should not have needed the draw, which affirms the Blues of a place in the pre-elimination final elimination final that is the wildcard round, to convince those who matter of his bona fides as a senior coach, but it can’t have hurt. Appropriately for the wildcard round concept, the final team to qualify is the very definition of a joker in the pack.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 No Joshing: The AFL’s second draw in 24 hours confirms Carlton’s stunning run to finals spot To take a rabble of a team and turn them around in season is a major achievement. For Carlton to have the wherewithal to know in the last minute that a draw was enough for them to make the wildcard round, and then to have the composure to just hold possession, betrayed a maturity not long seen at Princes Park. I’ve been a cynic of the whole wildcard round based on it rewarding the mediocre – 10th in a field of 18 making the finals has shades of ribbons and lollipops for everyone. But it is difficult to argue with the merit of it after this game. Does it mean the ninth and 10th sides are serious chances of going anywhere in September? Maybe not, but in a competition of small margins and a season in which one of those teams under their caretaker coach has been one of the best performed in the league over 13 rounds, anything is possible. It now feels implausible that the person who inherited the team that had won one game in the first nine matches could not then be appointed senior coach for next year. Josh Fraser has now won 10 and a half games from 13 matches.



The Bulldogs’ Matthew Kennedy and Carlton’s Patrick Cripps come to terms with Sunday’s draw. AFL Photos via Getty Images Put differently, consider an alternative world in which Fraser was not appointed senior coach. Firstly, who has the conversation with the players and explains the rationale? Who says, “I know we’ve just won 10 and a half games of 13 (it could be 11 in the unlikely event they beat Fremantle next week) and we made finals, but we’re still not sure he’s the man for us. We’d rather go with someone else, someone who has not coached at this level for three months and turned around an entire team and this club in a short space of time”? Pity also then the coach they do appoint instead of Fraser, especially if they then lose a few games on end next year. Those fans who were chanting “Fraaaser” after recent wins will only get louder. But the niggling memory of David Teague is sitting there for all Carlton fans and board members alike. It is an unsettling memory and completely unfair on Fraser who is plainly a very different person and coach.



Carlton’s victory in securing the top-10 place – as opposed to a win – was St Kilda’s loss. The Saints’ big cash splash recruiting splurge of last off-season results in them finishing no higher than 11th. Last year they finished 12th, the same place they finished in 2024. They look a different team, and they have played a better brand of football. But as their coach is wont to say, football gives you feedback every week, and in this results-based industry the result of this year is no finals. It is not to say their decisions were wrong, but it is a reminder that the storylines of summer are different to those of spring.



Two points each, two different views of a draw Craig McRae had a choice. In the moment of the draw, the Collingwood coach got to instantly choose – much like the English cricket team after losing another Ashes Test – whether to view the result really as a win or a loss. McRae channelled the English and chose to own victory. Hopefully for his sake the comparison ends there. McRae celebrated like the Magpies had won a final because they sort of had, but also because he knew that with the team they had out there they should not really have been able to beat a top-four team. Taking two points with that team against Hawthorn was as good as a win. Craig McRae pumped his fist after the Magpies came away with a draw. Getty Images



Hawks coach Sam Mitchell confessed to not knowing if a draw was good for his team or bad. In truth, ladder position movements were irrelevant to whether the draw was good for them or not. A draw against this Collingwood team was a loss, even putting aside the fact victory was in their hands until even after the siren had sounded. Hawthorn will still make the top four, but they are not playing like a top-four team. And that is the reason Mitchell should be under no illusions that this provided a signal about where his team is at. Loading In the six games since their loss to Melbourne, Hawthorn’s only impressive win came against resurgent Carlton. Outside of that, they have been a “victim” of a soft draw which had them touch up only the lowly Richmond, Essendon and North Melbourne in successive weeks. Their subsequent 67-point loss to Brisbane came off that run, showing their previous weeks flattered to deceive. They needed a corrective performance against Collingwood. They needed to make a statement, but the only comment they offered was, “yeah, nah, not sure”.



They were outplayed for much of what was a finals-like game of high pressure. They were certainly outplayed in the first half when they kicked only three goals. They then played very well in bursts but never with the sort of ruthlessness you would expect of a top-four side. Related Article AFL 2026 Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw That they were playing such a callow, albeit well-coached, opposition only accentuated the point. Hawthorn gave up 60 inside-50s to 47, they lost clearances 41 to 29, and were out-worked with 92 tackles to 55 and, in particular, out-muscled inside the arcs, where Collingwood laid 20 inside-50 tackles to Hawthorn’s three. Tom Barrass was lumbering and a liability when the ball hit the ground. He also gave away a 50m penalty and certain goal for being lippy. James Sicily looked more influential on a wing after being out-marked in defence and looking slow at ground level. As for Mitchell being unsure whether a draw was good or bad for the Hawks, it’s true that two points was better than none, but how his team played will have been little comfort to the coach.



McRae, on the other hand, knew he wanted to appropriate the narrative. This was as good as a win, is what he wanted to say. And given his team lost the ability to control the result with Dylan Moore’s final kick, the fact they did not lose was a victory of sorts. But McRae was speaking to an understanding of his team. He got away with Noah Howes in the back line, and even playing at length on Nick Watson. He had Liam Puncher doing OK on Jack Gunston. Beau McCreery played his best game for the club and Sam Swadling, like Ed Allan, demonstrated that the Pies can pick good players when they don’t trade away their draft picks. But most critically Dan McStay continued a resurgence that few could have foreseen. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was not as certain about how he felt after Saturday night’s draw against Collingwood. Getty Images He looked gone early in the year. He was the player who looked, as Woody Allen would say, like a cellist in a marching band. In the past two months he has played the best football of his career.



That is a turnaround that not only has in-season ramifications, but out-of-season consequences as the Magpies consider their trade options. Roos leaping forward In two weeks North Melbourne, with nothing to play for, have played like they are playing for something. Their win over the Dogs last week and loss this week against the Cats –which should have been a win – shows the movement at Arden Street. The Geelong loss sort of felt like a win, which is also the crappy netherworld of small mercies North still find themselves in to find succour from loss.



Losing Harry Sheezel to a head knock was a blow for North Melbourne in Saturday’s game against Geelong. AFL Photos Related Article AFL 2026 Swans secure two home finals, Gulden picks up 47 touches in Dons demolition At least North have shown something. Is it all a bit hollow once the season is dusted, or does it suggest a spirit that they are playing out the season and showing some pride and commitment to carrying momentum from one season into another? That will only answerable next year, but Nick Larkey was back to kicking straight and looking authoritative, and they found another player in Zac Banch, a crafty little forward. If Harry Sheezel had played out the game, it feels like North probably would have won. Maybe that’s unfair on Geelong, who found a way to win, as the better sides do. The Cats also lost players but none of them were as important as Sheezel, or playing as well as Sheezel was. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Surge in demand for Sydney’s metro trains leaves passengers waiting
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney Metro Surge in demand for Sydney’s metro trains leaves passengers waiting Matt O'Sullivan August 17, 2026 — 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Commuters catching trains on Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro rail line during the morning peak have surged over the past 12 months: two stations in the central city have easily exceeded forecasts made two years ago and some trains have been too packed for passengers to get on. On the eve of the two-year anniversary of the opening of the line’s city section, new government figures show a 14 per cent rise in passengers filing through ticket gates at Martin Place metro station during the morning peak in May and June, compared to the same months a year earlier. A commuter waits for the next train at Crows Nest station because he cannot get on a packed service. Peter Rae Martin Place station’s average patronage of 20,500 passengers on weekday mornings in May was almost a third higher than forecasts released in 2024, shortly before the section between Chatswood and Sydenham opened on August 19 of that year. Gadigal station, near Town Hall, is also easily beating forecasts. About 10,700 commuters passed through its gates in the morning peak between 6.30 and 10 in May, up 8 per cent on the prior period, and 43 per cent higher than predictions made in 2024.



Victoria Cross station in North Sydney had a rise of more than 10 per cent during morning peaks in May and June, while Central Station’s metro platforms were up about 9 per cent, as commuters switched from heavy rail services to metro trains. The number of commuters entering and exiting North Sydney station on a typical weekday has halved since the metro’s city-section opened two years ago and patronage for St Leonards station has fallen by a third. Both heavy rail stations are close to metro stations. The growth in patronage on metro trains comes two months before the M1 line’s final stage between Sydenham and Bankstown is expected to open. Confidential government documents have slated a target date of mid-October, but the start of passenger services will hinge on approval by the national rail regulator. Crows Nest resident Lucy Wang catches metro trains every weekday to travel to Martin Place for work because they are faster than double-decker services on the T1 North Shore heavy rail line.



Wang said it was always a case of squeezing into packed metro carriages or waiting for the next one if she could not get on during the morning peak. “I usually only wait for one, or squish [into a carriage],” she said. “I do wish it was less packed, but there’s really nothing you can do.” Crows Nest resident Lucy Wang, left, on a packed city-bound metro train during the morning peak. Peter Rae After driving to Crows Nest to drop her daughter at day care, Norwest resident Ashley Felsman is used to being unable to get on a city-bound metro train during the morning peak. “I’m always having to wait for the next one because I can’t get on,” she said. Trains run every four minutes in both directions on the M1 line during weekday peaks between about 7am and 10am, and from 3pm to 7pm. They operate every five minutes from 10am to 3pm, and every 10 minutes at other times. Over the coming years, the two options for boosting passenger capacity on the M1 line are to lengthen trains from six to eight carriages, or to increase the frequency to a service every three minutes, which would require the NSW government to buy more trains.



Sydney Metro customer and planning executive director Samantha Phillips said the agency was keeping a close eye on crowding on city-bound trains departing Crows Nest, which was the “pinch point” on the network in the morning peak. Passengers file through Gadigal station during the morning peak. Peter Rae Phillips said the most likely option, if capacity was boosted, would be to increase train frequency to every three minutes. “Frequency matters. That’s what people really value,” she said. “I want to make sure I’ve looked at all the different options before I’m saying to government or to the community we need to spend a lot more money on additional fleet. It is a big investment.” Phillips said increased housing along the rail corridor and commuters’ willingness to give up seats on double-decker trains for a faster journey standing in metro carriages were key drivers of the patronage growth.



Related Article Exclusive

Sydney Metro Secret chart that reveals target date for Sydney metro line’s opening “I was always really a bit sceptical around people preferring to give up their seat to choose the metro, but the evidence is speaking for itself. People are choosing those faster journeys,” she said of commuters switching from heavy rail to metro services at stations such as Chatswood and Epping. University of Technology transport researcher Mathew Hounsell said the metro line’s strong patronage growth demonstrated that modelling had underestimated passenger demand. “It is the same all over the world – when you build an automated metro that is reliable and fast, people use it,” he said. “Buses are great for moving people around a local area but it’s trains that build a city.” Hounsell said the government needed to improve feeder bus links to metro stations along the M1 line, especially in Sydney’s northwest. “Getting people to these stations now is the limiting factor in terms of [patronage] growth,” he said.



While Martin Place and Gadigal are easily beating expectations, Waterloo station continues to lag Sydney Metro’s patronage forecasts and Barangaroo’s figures were nearly flat year-on-year. Phillips said Waterloo and other stations that had had slower patronage growth reflected a lag in proposed development around them. World.title: Record number of fraudsters booted from NDIS as Labor negotiates path for cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDisability Record number of fraudsters booted from NDIS as Labor negotiates path for cuts Nick Newling August 17, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 100 criminals and “dodgy consultants” operating within the National Disability Insurance Scheme have been banned as Labor seeks to crack down on fraudsters amid ongoing negotiations over the future of the $56 billion scheme. In the three months following the Albanese government’s April move to empower the scheme’s policing body, 111 individuals and providers have been issued banning orders, including one supplier who is alleged to have fraudulently claimed around $4 million in NDIS funds. The fraud crackdown comes as the federal government attempts to cut $36.2 billion out of the scheme by removing up to 300,000 participants. Shutterstock A Sydney operator was banned in May after at least 70 NDIS participants told investigators from the scheme’s Quality and Standards Commission they were not aware of the firm and did not authorise claims on their behalf. The record uptick in bans represented 70 per cent of the 158 bans handed down in 2026, and constituted the highest number of bans issued in a single quarter.



“Working in the NDIS is a great privilege, and if you abuse that privilege, you will be kicked out of the scheme,” NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said. Related Article Disability Labor-led committee warns of human rights risks in NDIS reform “The new powers we’ve legislated have given the NDIS Commission the strong powers it needed to really take the fight to the shonks and grifters who thought they could take advantage of one of our society’s most important social programs.” The crackdown comes as the government attempts to cut $36.2 billion out of the system by removing up to 300,000 participants, returning the scheme to its foundational intention of only supporting people with permanent and significant impairment. Appearing on ABC TV’s Insiders on Sunday, McAllister said the government was confident of reaching an agreement on the legislation this week, and that attempts to curb fraud in the scheme were of “very strong” interest to both Labor and the Coalition.



“This scheme has to operate with integrity. When we see fraud, we very frequently see harm to people with disability, and I think there’s a shared view across ourselves and the Coalition,” McAllister said. The NDIS has suffered significant hits in public perception after years of reports of rorts within the scheme, and its ballooning bottom line. Health Minister Mark Butler, who announced changes to both youth participation in the scheme and its overall size in speeches over the past 12 months, is seeking to restrict eligibility to those who can prove permanent impairment from 2028. A Senate inquiry into Labor’s NDIS reforms released its final report green-lighting the laws on Friday despite weeks of testimony from disabled Australians, rights groups and legal services who said the changes could remove hundreds of thousands of people from the scheme within five years. “I remember what it was like when we didn’t have a scheme of this kind. It was really bad,” McAllister said. “We consider that changes to clarify who is eligible for the scheme and clarify what kinds of supports they should receive are absolutely essential if the community is to retain confidence in the scheme.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street slips after weak update on the US economy
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street slips after weak update on the US economy Stan Choe August 17, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market edged back from its all-time high following the latest report on the economy to come in surprisingly weak, this time about how much shoppers are spending at retailers. Such data could keep interest rates low, which is something Wall Street loves, but it also raises the risk of a slowing economy when inflation is still high. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent from its record set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.3 per cent. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 33 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The Australia dollar was trading at US70.79¢ at 5.16am AEST. US stocks gave up modest gains from early in the morning after oil prices swung higher. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1.7 per cent to $US88.52 as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again.



Also raising uncertainty was a report showing shoppers spent less at US retailers last month than the month before. That surprised economists, who were forecasting another month of growth. On the bright side for financial markets, such a pullback in spending could take pressure off inflation. Inflation remains much higher than anyone would like, but reports earlier this week suggested the pace of increases in prices is decelerating. Related Article Opinion

Big four Betting against the bank. ‘Widow-maker’ trades are making a comeback Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor If inflation keeps trending that way, it could encourage the Federal Reserve to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The downside of such data, including last week’s surprisingly weak report on the US job market, is that they raise the risk of a slowing economy. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario.



Some on Wall Street cautioned against overreacting to the weak data on US retail sales, even if it was broad-based. It could simply be a snap back after retail sales in earlier months were boosted by unusual factors such as big tax refunds, the World Cup and even an earlier Prime Day event at Amazon, according to Jennifer Timmerman, senior investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. US consumers nevertheless appear to be getting more discouraged about the economy. A preliminary survey by the University of Michigan suggested sentiment among them is weakening by more than economists expected. The survey said drops occurred across the political spectrum and showed up particularly among older, lower-income and other groups who can be hurt most by inflation. On Wall Street, Reddit jumped 12.6 per cent after learning its stock will join the S&P 500 index on Tuesday. Many professional investors and funds closely track the index, either mimicking it or at least measuring their performance against it. That can push many to buy a stock automatically when it enters the index. Applied Materials fell 5.1 per cent even though the company, whose technology helps make semiconductors, reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Gary Dickerson said global hunger for artificial-intelligence technology helped it deliver another record quarter.



But its stock had already more than doubled this year and built expectations very high, which helped pressure the stock on Friday. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last AI stocks in general have been swinging sharply on worries that their prices shot too high because of AI euphoria and that their strong growth in revenue may not be sustainable. All told, the S&P 500 fell 13.23 points to 7,785.76. Despite the loss, it nevertheless closed out a third straight winning week, its longest such streak since a nine-week run that ended in May. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107.58 to 53,732.41, and the Nasdaq composite sank 73.86 to 26,729.16.



In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher and followed the price of oil. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.69 per cent from 4.63 per cent late Thursday. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. London’s FTSE 100 slipped 0.2 per cent after Nigel Farage regained the seat in Parliament he quit a month ago, beating trash-can wearing comic candidate Count Binface in a special election. South Korea’s Kospi again had one of the world’s sharpest moves and jumped 2.4 per cent for its third straight gain of at least that much. Seoul has been at the centre of the world’s swings for AI stocks because its market is dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. World.title: In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare?
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPay In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare? Matt Wade and Craig Butt August 17, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The top 1 per cent of income earners in 83 Sydney suburbs take home over $1 million a year on average, while in a cluster of harbourside neighbourhoods, to make the 1 per cent bracket, you need to earn more than $3 million. Analysis of official personal income data by this masthead casts fresh light on how ultra-high pay packets are distributed across the city. In Bellevue Hill, about five kilometres east of Sydney’s central business district, the average income for the highest paid 1 per cent of taxpayers was $6.3 million in 2022-23. That was $1.2 million lower than the previous year but it was still the highest average for the 1 per cent in any city suburb. The top 1 per cent of Sydney earners takes home over $1 million a year. Nine



The adjacent neighbourhood of Rose Bay-Vaucluse-Watsons Bay had the city’s second-highest average earnings for the top 1 per cent at $6.12 million (down from $6.37 million the previous year). Third was Woollahra, where the top 1 per cent took home an average of $5.05 million (up from $4.99 million). There were eight Sydney neighbourhoods where the top 1 per cent had average earnings between $3 million and $5 million (all of them waterfront suburbs) and 72 where average earnings were between $1 million and $3 million. You can search how suburbs and localities across NSW compare here: While suburbs with the highest average incomes for the top 1 per cent were mostly in the eastern suburbs and on the north shore, several were located in the city’s north-west, including Dural-Kenthurst ($1.66 million) and Glenhaven ($1.58 million).



In two outer western Sydney neighbourhoods – Horsley Park-Kemps Creek and Mulgoa-Luddenham-Orchard Hills – the top 1 per cent took home just over $1 million a year. Demographer and social researcher Mark McCrindle said the high average earnings for the top 1 per cent in parts of western and north-western Sydney showed how patterns of income and wealth have shifted. “It tells a story of a changing Sydney,” he said. “Yes, we’ve got very high incomes in those harbourside suburbs which has been the case for 100 years, but we’ve got new locations with high incomes as well. The dynamics of wealth have spread geographically.” McCrindle said income distribution patterns across Sydney showed not all high-income earners wanted to live on the waterfront.



“Some choose to invest their money in a large property, perhaps in bushland, rather than in the harbour area. Places like Dural, Kenthurst and Glenhaven in Sydney’s north-west have really changed economically.” However, in some western suburbs, the earnings of the top 1 per cent was well below the citywide average. Lowest was Auburn North, about 20 kilometres west of the CBD, where the average income of the best paid 1 per cent was $200,656. Suburbs where the top 1 per cent have especially high incomes correlate closely with house prices. Bellevue Hill, which had Sydney’s best paid 1 per cent of earners, also had the city’s highest median house price of $10.4 million, according to Domain’s June quarter House Price Report. In neighbouring Vaucluse, the median house price was $9.5 million and in Rose Bay it was $6.5 million. In Bellevue Hill, the best paid 1 per cent earned an average of $6.3 million a year in 2022-23. It also has a median house price over $10 million. Renee Nowytarger The top 1 per cent of earners across the whole of Greater Sydney had an average income of $1,027,863 in 2022-23.



That was about 12 times more than the average annual personal income for all Greater Sydney taxpayers of $84,947 and 16 times the city’s median income (the middle value of all earners) of $62,180. Sydney was the only Australian capital where the average earnings for the top 1 per cent was a seven-figure total. Next highest was Perth, with average earnings of $928,762 a year for the top 1 per cent, followed by Melbourne with $792,491. The earnings figures show Sydney is Australia’s most unequal capital city for income: the top 1 per cent of earners received 12.1 per cent of the city’s income in 2022-23. That compares with 11.1 per cent in Perth, 10.2 per cent in Melbourne and 8.7 per cent in Brisbane. Nationally, the top 1 per cent earned 9.9 per cent of all personal income. Outside of Sydney there were some localities where the top 1 per cent had extremely high earnings. In the Upper Hunter town of Scone, the average income of the top 1 per cent of earners was just under $5 million, the fourth highest in NSW.



In Bangalow, near Byron Bay, the average income for the top 1 per cent was $1.9 million while in Robertson-Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands, that average was $1.87 million. The suburb with the highest 1 per cent average income of anywhere in Australia was Cottesloe in Perth, where you need to be bringing in $36 million a year on average to be in that suburb’s top 1 per cent. In many neighbourhoods, including Cottesloe, the average income among the top 1 per cent is skewed by a few earners with extremely high earners – the top 0.1 per cent – who drive up the average. The analysis used Australian Bureau of Statistics personal income data, which draws on Tax Office records for the 2022-23 financial year, the most recent available. It includes figures for “Statistical Area Level 2” (SA2) localities that are similar to suburbs.



The data covers only individual pre-tax income; it does not include assets owned by individuals such as housing and shares. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul
World.content:
Breaking WorldAsiaDonald Trump Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul Costas Pitas Updated August 17, 2026 — 8:42am ,first published 8:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump said he had instructed the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea in a social media post that also mentioned Seoul’s refusal to take part in actions against Iran. Trump said in a post on his Truth Social site on Monday morning (AEST) that, although it was too late to cancel the latest round of exercises entirely, he was “not happy” that the US had previously agreed to participate. Donald Trump and Kim Jong-un in 2020. The US president met the North Korean leader three times during his first term. Getty Images The US president also cited his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un. “These exercises are not only costly ... but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” he wrote.



Trump also pointed to South Korea’s stance on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran. “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’” Trump wrote. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military drills are scheduled to run from August 17 to 27. A South Korean army K1A2 tank fires during a drill as part of the annual the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercise in Cheorwon, South Korea, in 2023. AP/South Korea Defence Ministry The exercises involving 18,000 South Korean soldiers are designed to beef up readiness against North Korean threats.



North Korea on Friday threatened unspecified stern steps against the US and South Korea, describing their military drills as a “a rehearsal for an aggressive war” that are triggering greater instability in the region. The warning was typical of the harsh rhetoric that North Korea often deploys ahead of major US-South Korean military exercises. Members of US Special Operations Command Korea and South Korea’s Army Special Warfare Command during Ulchi Freedom Shield in Yangyang in 2023. AP Experts say North Korea has often used its rivals’ drills as a pretext to ramp up testing activities to expand its weapons arsenals and promote public support for leader Kim. US and South Korean forces were expected to practice joint operations in complex scenarios, including a live-fire exercise to test joint precision targeting and manoeuvre, a wet gap crossing, and distribution of prepositioned military equipment, according to the US military.



The US military has said the exercise “reinforces the role of the alliance as the linchpin for regional peace and security” and reaffirms “the ironclad commitment between the United States and the Republic of Korea to defend their homelands”. The joint training comes days after North Korea resumed ballistic missile testing activities that are banned by the UN. Photo: TruthSocial Earlier this month, South Korea, the U.S. and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from North Korea in what was the North’s first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June. The missile landed in the waters off North Korea’s east coast. North Korea has been pushing hard to enlarge its nuclear and missile arsenals since Kim’s high-stakes diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. Experts say Kim likely believes a bigger weapons arsenal would increase his chances for wresting more concessions from the US in future negotiations.



Trump met with the reclusive North Korean leader three times during his first term to discuss the country’s nuclear program, most recently in 2019. Since returning to office, Trump has expressed interest in continuing those discussions. Trump’s announcement came a day after he posted a photo of himself standing next to North Korea’s Kim, writing that the two leaders get along great “despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture”. This is not the first time that Trump has sought to end the exercises. During his first term he also issued a surprise announcement that called the war games “provocative”. “We will be stopping the war games, which will save us a tremendous amount of money, unless and until we see the future negotiation is not going along like it should,” Trump told reporters after his 2018 meeting with Kim in Singapore. World.content:
London: The BBC asked a US court for help in getting documents and testimony from members of President Donald Trump’s family in connection with his $US10 billion ($14 billion) defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster, a court document showed.

Lawyers for the BBC argued that Ivanka Trump, her husband Jared Kushner, and Donald Trump Jr have “personal knowledge” and likely have records relevant to elements of Trump’s claims against the broadcaster. The broadcaster has been unable to serve subpoenas because the three have Secret Service protection, the court filing says.

Donald Trump in New York on Friday. AP

The president filed the lawsuit in December, accusing the BBC of defamation and deceptive and unfair trade practices. The allegations centre on the way a 2024 documentary edited a speech Trump gave on January 6, 2021, before protesters attacked the Capitol in Washington.



The lawsuit accuses the BBC of “splicing together two entirely separate parts” of Trump’s speech to “intentionally misrepresent the meaning of what [he] said” and that the editing was “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 election.



The BBC apologised to Trump for the misleading edit, but said it had not defamed him.



The latest court filing said that Trump’s family members had knowledge relevant to Trump’s argument “that it would be materially false to imply that he incited violence”. The BBC asked the court to allow the subpoenas to be served by email and certified mail.



Trump’s legal team said “the BBC is seeking to harass [Donald Trump], his family, and supporters by abusing the deposition process”. A trial has been provisionally set for February.

World.title: Haddara crime family boss shot in Altona North
World.content:
Alleged one-time gangland boss Fadi Haddara has been ambushed and shot in the driveway of his Altona North home. Police believe Haddara, 48, was the victim of a targeted attack when he was shot in a parked car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue, near Millers Road, just before 8pm on Sunday. Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South Neighbours, who did not want to be identified over fears of retaliation, said they heard multiple gunshots around 8pm. Police and paramedics were quickly on scene. The neighbours said they heard yelling inside the home as detectives arrived.



Haddara was ambushed in his driveway on Sunday evening. Penny Stephens Despite his reputation, neighbours said Haddara was friendly, often waving to neighbours as he drove along the street. He is believed to be in a stable condition at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Haddara’s lawyer has been contacted for comment. Police were quickly on scene after the shooting. Nine



The road remained blocked off on Monday morning. Penny Stephens Half of Marigold Avenue remained completely blocked off on Monday morning. Police cars can be seen parked outside the home and along the street. The front lights at Haddara’s home were on, but police tape has blocked the driveway. Alleged gangland boss Fadi Haddara.



Haddara, the alleged patriarch of the Haddara crime family, once held a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne but had been squeezed out by new gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2024. Related Article Exclusive

Crime When the head of a crime family found trackers on his car, he knew the game was up The Age has previously reported that the Haddaras surrendered their stake in the illicit tobacco smuggling and distribution market following a relentless firebombing and shooting campaign waged by Hamad in 2023-2024, including Fadi finding multiple GPS trackers on his car. The attack on Fadi has been met with surprise in the underworld given the clan was largely sidelined following Hamad’s establishment of cartel-like control over the tobacco market. Attempts by some criminal players to take advantage of Hamad’s arrest in Iraq in January have met with acts of serious retribution by Hamad’s gang, known as The Commission or the 313.



Four businesses and a home owned or linked to the crime gang led by Haddara were attacked in March of this year alone, including the torching of the Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown and a drive-by shooting targeting a crowd of men standing outside an Altona North kebab shop in the heart of the gang’s territory. World.title: The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw Michael Gleeson Updated August 17, 2026 — 5:56am ,first published 6:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Carlton lost their coach in round nine and surely found their new one in the next 13 rounds.

Magpie Dan McStay continues a resurgence that few could have foreseen

Remember this: Hawks would not have won had they attempted to rush the ball through.

North’s win over the Dogs last week and the loss this week against Geelong shows the movement at Arden Street.

Quirky rule exposed Hawthorn would not have won had they attempted to rush the ball through for a behind after the siren. But they would have won had Collingwood punched it over the goal line. Weird, isn’t it? Collingwood’s Sam Swadling punches the post-siren kick from Dylan Moore into the field of play, ensuring Saturday night’s match at the MCG ended in a draw. @CollingwoodFC



Hawthorn’s Dylan Moore launches his shot at goal. Getty Images Under AFL rules, if Hawthorn – say Lloyd Meek for instance, who wound up to punch the ball and missed – knocked the ball through it would not have registered as a rushed behind to deliver a Hawthorn win. You can’t punch your own ball through for a score after the siren. It’s considered a secondary act of play to assist the score, and given play is technically dead after the siren, there can’t be a secondary play after the siren. Unless you are the other team. Under rule 16.5.2, had Collingwood punched the ball through, or it came off Collingwood hands and crossed the line, then a behind would have been registered and Hawthorn would have won. So, this won’t comfort Dylan Moore any, but he needed to clear the pack and get a score off his own boot. It does seem inconsistent that one team can create a score by touching the ball after the siren and not the other. Logically, any team touching the ball from the kick should mean it is a secondary act.



Incidentally, viewers had no idea what was happening on the goal line watching the lamentable Fox coverage, which managed at the most critical moment to crop out all of the play on the goal line. Draw’s a win for Fraser, his Blues and the AFL’s wildcard In a game with no winner there were two victors and a clear loser. Josh Fraser’s Carlton won. The AFL’s contentious wildcard round won. St Kilda lost. Josh Fraser was typically understated as the Blues locked away a wildcard berth with a draw against the Bulldogs. Getty Images Josh Fraser’s Carlton will play “finals”, or at least a quasi-final round. St Kilda will not.



Carlton lost the biggest name of the off-season to St Kilda as well as the son of a scion of the club, and are now certain to finish ahead of the Saints. Carlton lost their coach in round nine and surely found their new one in the next 13 rounds. View post on X Fraser should not have needed the draw, which affirms the Blues of a place in the pre-elimination final elimination final that is the wildcard round, to convince those who matter of his bona fides as a senior coach, but it can’t have hurt. Appropriately for the wildcard round concept, the final team to qualify is the very definition of a joker in the pack.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 No Joshing: The AFL’s second draw in 24 hours confirms Carlton’s stunning run to finals spot To take a rabble of a team and turn them around in season is a major achievement. For Carlton to have the wherewithal to know in the last minute that a draw was enough for them to make the wildcard round, and then to have the composure to just hold possession, betrayed a maturity not long seen at Princes Park. I’ve been a cynic of the whole wildcard round based on it rewarding the mediocre – 10th in a field of 18 making the finals has shades of ribbons and lollipops for everyone. But it is difficult to argue with the merit of it after this game. Does it mean the ninth and 10th sides are serious chances of going anywhere in September? Maybe not, but in a competition of small margins and a season in which one of those teams under their caretaker coach has been one of the best performed in the league over 13 rounds, anything is possible. It now feels implausible that the person who inherited the team that had won one game in the first nine matches could not then be appointed senior coach for next year. Josh Fraser has now won 10 and a half games from 13 matches.



The Bulldogs’ Matthew Kennedy and Carlton’s Patrick Cripps come to terms with Sunday’s draw. AFL Photos via Getty Images Put differently, consider an alternative world in which Fraser was not appointed senior coach. Firstly, who has the conversation with the players and explains the rationale? Who says, “I know we’ve just won 10 and a half games of 13 (it could be 11 in the unlikely event they beat Fremantle next week) and we made finals, but we’re still not sure he’s the man for us. We’d rather go with someone else, someone who has not coached at this level for three months and turned around an entire team and this club in a short space of time”? Pity also then the coach they do appoint instead of Fraser, especially if they then lose a few games on end next year. Those fans who were chanting “Fraaaser” after recent wins will only get louder. But the niggling memory of David Teague is sitting there for all Carlton fans and board members alike. It is an unsettling memory and completely unfair on Fraser who is plainly a very different person and coach.



Carlton’s victory in securing the top-10 place – as opposed to a win – was St Kilda’s loss. The Saints’ big cash splash recruiting splurge of last off-season results in them finishing no higher than 11th. Last year they finished 12th, the same place they finished in 2024. They look a different team, and they have played a better brand of football. But as their coach is wont to say, football gives you feedback every week, and in this results-based industry the result of this year is no finals. It is not to say their decisions were wrong, but it is a reminder that the storylines of summer are different to those of spring.



Two points each, two different views of a draw Craig McRae had a choice. In the moment of the draw, the Collingwood coach got to instantly choose – much like the English cricket team after losing another Ashes Test – whether to view the result really as a win or a loss. McRae channelled the English and chose to own victory. Hopefully for his sake the comparison ends there. McRae celebrated like the Magpies had won a final because they sort of had, but also because he knew that with the team they had out there they should not really have been able to beat a top-four team. Taking two points with that team against Hawthorn was as good as a win. Craig McRae pumped his fist after the Magpies came away with a draw. Getty Images



Hawks coach Sam Mitchell confessed to not knowing if a draw was good for his team or bad. In truth, ladder position movements were irrelevant to whether the draw was good for them or not. A draw against this Collingwood team was a loss, even putting aside the fact victory was in their hands until even after the siren had sounded. Hawthorn will still make the top four, but they are not playing like a top-four team. And that is the reason Mitchell should be under no illusions that this provided a signal about where his team is at. Loading In the six games since their loss to Melbourne, Hawthorn’s only impressive win came against resurgent Carlton. Outside of that, they have been a “victim” of a soft draw which had them touch up only the lowly Richmond, Essendon and North Melbourne in successive weeks. Their subsequent 67-point loss to Brisbane came off that run, showing their previous weeks flattered to deceive. They needed a corrective performance against Collingwood. They needed to make a statement, but the only comment they offered was, “yeah, nah, not sure”.



They were outplayed for much of what was a finals-like game of high pressure. They were certainly outplayed in the first half when they kicked only three goals. They then played very well in bursts but never with the sort of ruthlessness you would expect of a top-four side. Related Article AFL 2026 Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw That they were playing such a callow, albeit well-coached, opposition only accentuated the point. Hawthorn gave up 60 inside-50s to 47, they lost clearances 41 to 29, and were out-worked with 92 tackles to 55 and, in particular, out-muscled inside the arcs, where Collingwood laid 20 inside-50 tackles to Hawthorn’s three. Tom Barrass was lumbering and a liability when the ball hit the ground. He also gave away a 50m penalty and certain goal for being lippy. James Sicily looked more influential on a wing after being out-marked in defence and looking slow at ground level. As for Mitchell being unsure whether a draw was good or bad for the Hawks, it’s true that two points was better than none, but how his team played will have been little comfort to the coach.



McRae, on the other hand, knew he wanted to appropriate the narrative. This was as good as a win, is what he wanted to say. And given his team lost the ability to control the result with Dylan Moore’s final kick, the fact they did not lose was a victory of sorts. But McRae was speaking to an understanding of his team. He got away with Noah Howes in the back line, and even playing at length on Nick Watson. He had Liam Puncher doing OK on Jack Gunston. Beau McCreery played his best game for the club and Sam Swadling, like Ed Allan, demonstrated that the Pies can pick good players when they don’t trade away their draft picks. But most critically Dan McStay continued a resurgence that few could have foreseen. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was not as certain about how he felt after Saturday night’s draw against Collingwood. Getty Images He looked gone early in the year. He was the player who looked, as Woody Allen would say, like a cellist in a marching band. In the past two months he has played the best football of his career.



That is a turnaround that not only has in-season ramifications, but out-of-season consequences as the Magpies consider their trade options. Roos leaping forward In two weeks North Melbourne, with nothing to play for, have played like they are playing for something. Their win over the Dogs last week and loss this week against the Cats –which should have been a win – shows the movement at Arden Street. The Geelong loss sort of felt like a win, which is also the crappy netherworld of small mercies North still find themselves in to find succour from loss.



Losing Harry Sheezel to a head knock was a blow for North Melbourne in Saturday’s game against Geelong. AFL Photos Related Article AFL 2026 Swans secure two home finals, Gulden picks up 47 touches in Dons demolition At least North have shown something. Is it all a bit hollow once the season is dusted, or does it suggest a spirit that they are playing out the season and showing some pride and commitment to carrying momentum from one season into another? That will only answerable next year, but Nick Larkey was back to kicking straight and looking authoritative, and they found another player in Zac Banch, a crafty little forward. If Harry Sheezel had played out the game, it feels like North probably would have won. Maybe that’s unfair on Geelong, who found a way to win, as the better sides do. The Cats also lost players but none of them were as important as Sheezel, or playing as well as Sheezel was. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Surge in demand for Sydney’s metro trains leaves passengers waiting
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney Metro Surge in demand for Sydney’s metro trains leaves passengers waiting Matt O'Sullivan August 17, 2026 — 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Commuters catching trains on Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro rail line during the morning peak have surged over the past 12 months: two stations in the central city have easily exceeded forecasts made two years ago and some trains have been too packed for passengers to get on. On the eve of the two-year anniversary of the opening of the line’s city section, new government figures show a 14 per cent rise in passengers filing through ticket gates at Martin Place metro station during the morning peak in May and June, compared to the same months a year earlier. A commuter waits for the next train at Crows Nest station because he cannot get on a packed service. Peter Rae Martin Place station’s average patronage of 20,500 passengers on weekday mornings in May was almost a third higher than forecasts released in 2024, shortly before the section between Chatswood and Sydenham opened on August 19 of that year. Gadigal station, near Town Hall, is also easily beating forecasts. About 10,700 commuters passed through its gates in the morning peak between 6.30 and 10 in May, up 8 per cent on the prior period, and 43 per cent higher than predictions made in 2024.



Victoria Cross station in North Sydney had a rise of more than 10 per cent during morning peaks in May and June, while Central Station’s metro platforms were up about 9 per cent, as commuters switched from heavy rail services to metro trains. The number of commuters entering and exiting North Sydney station on a typical weekday has halved since the metro’s city-section opened two years ago and patronage for St Leonards station has fallen by a third. Both heavy rail stations are close to metro stations. The growth in patronage on metro trains comes two months before the M1 line’s final stage between Sydenham and Bankstown is expected to open. Confidential government documents have slated a target date of mid-October, but the start of passenger services will hinge on approval by the national rail regulator. Crows Nest resident Lucy Wang catches metro trains every weekday to travel to Martin Place for work because they are faster than double-decker services on the T1 North Shore heavy rail line.



Wang said it was always a case of squeezing into packed metro carriages or waiting for the next one if she could not get on during the morning peak. “I usually only wait for one, or squish [into a carriage],” she said. “I do wish it was less packed, but there’s really nothing you can do.” Crows Nest resident Lucy Wang, left, on a packed city-bound metro train during the morning peak. Peter Rae After driving to Crows Nest to drop her daughter at day care, Norwest resident Ashley Felsman is used to being unable to get on a city-bound metro train during the morning peak. “I’m always having to wait for the next one because I can’t get on,” she said. Trains run every four minutes in both directions on the M1 line during weekday peaks between about 7am and 10am, and from 3pm to 7pm. They operate every five minutes from 10am to 3pm, and every 10 minutes at other times. Over the coming years, the two options for boosting passenger capacity on the M1 line are to lengthen trains from six to eight carriages, or to increase the frequency to a service every three minutes, which would require the NSW government to buy more trains.



Sydney Metro customer and planning executive director Samantha Phillips said the agency was keeping a close eye on crowding on city-bound trains departing Crows Nest, which was the “pinch point” on the network in the morning peak. Passengers file through Gadigal station during the morning peak. Peter Rae Phillips said the most likely option, if capacity was boosted, would be to increase train frequency to every three minutes. “Frequency matters. That’s what people really value,” she said. “I want to make sure I’ve looked at all the different options before I’m saying to government or to the community we need to spend a lot more money on additional fleet. It is a big investment.” Phillips said increased housing along the rail corridor and commuters’ willingness to give up seats on double-decker trains for a faster journey standing in metro carriages were key drivers of the patronage growth.



Related Article Exclusive

Sydney Metro Secret chart that reveals target date for Sydney metro line’s opening “I was always really a bit sceptical around people preferring to give up their seat to choose the metro, but the evidence is speaking for itself. People are choosing those faster journeys,” she said of commuters switching from heavy rail to metro services at stations such as Chatswood and Epping. University of Technology transport researcher Mathew Hounsell said the metro line’s strong patronage growth demonstrated that modelling had underestimated passenger demand. “It is the same all over the world – when you build an automated metro that is reliable and fast, people use it,” he said. “Buses are great for moving people around a local area but it’s trains that build a city.” Hounsell said the government needed to improve feeder bus links to metro stations along the M1 line, especially in Sydney’s northwest. “Getting people to these stations now is the limiting factor in terms of [patronage] growth,” he said.



While Martin Place and Gadigal are easily beating expectations, Waterloo station continues to lag Sydney Metro’s patronage forecasts and Barangaroo’s figures were nearly flat year-on-year. Phillips said Waterloo and other stations that had had slower patronage growth reflected a lag in proposed development around them. World.title: Record number of fraudsters booted from NDIS as Labor negotiates path for cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDisability Record number of fraudsters booted from NDIS as Labor negotiates path for cuts Nick Newling August 17, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 100 criminals and “dodgy consultants” operating within the National Disability Insurance Scheme have been banned as Labor seeks to crack down on fraudsters amid ongoing negotiations over the future of the $56 billion scheme. In the three months following the Albanese government’s April move to empower the scheme’s policing body, 111 individuals and providers have been issued banning orders, including one supplier who is alleged to have fraudulently claimed around $4 million in NDIS funds. The fraud crackdown comes as the federal government attempts to cut $36.2 billion out of the scheme by removing up to 300,000 participants. Shutterstock A Sydney operator was banned in May after at least 70 NDIS participants told investigators from the scheme’s Quality and Standards Commission they were not aware of the firm and did not authorise claims on their behalf. The record uptick in bans represented 70 per cent of the 158 bans handed down in 2026, and constituted the highest number of bans issued in a single quarter.



“Working in the NDIS is a great privilege, and if you abuse that privilege, you will be kicked out of the scheme,” NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said. Related Article Disability Labor-led committee warns of human rights risks in NDIS reform “The new powers we’ve legislated have given the NDIS Commission the strong powers it needed to really take the fight to the shonks and grifters who thought they could take advantage of one of our society’s most important social programs.” The crackdown comes as the government attempts to cut $36.2 billion out of the system by removing up to 300,000 participants, returning the scheme to its foundational intention of only supporting people with permanent and significant impairment. Appearing on ABC TV’s Insiders on Sunday, McAllister said the government was confident of reaching an agreement on the legislation this week, and that attempts to curb fraud in the scheme were of “very strong” interest to both Labor and the Coalition.



“This scheme has to operate with integrity. When we see fraud, we very frequently see harm to people with disability, and I think there’s a shared view across ourselves and the Coalition,” McAllister said. The NDIS has suffered significant hits in public perception after years of reports of rorts within the scheme, and its ballooning bottom line. Health Minister Mark Butler, who announced changes to both youth participation in the scheme and its overall size in speeches over the past 12 months, is seeking to restrict eligibility to those who can prove permanent impairment from 2028. A Senate inquiry into Labor’s NDIS reforms released its final report green-lighting the laws on Friday despite weeks of testimony from disabled Australians, rights groups and legal services who said the changes could remove hundreds of thousands of people from the scheme within five years. “I remember what it was like when we didn’t have a scheme of this kind. It was really bad,” McAllister said. “We consider that changes to clarify who is eligible for the scheme and clarify what kinds of supports they should receive are absolutely essential if the community is to retain confidence in the scheme.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street slips after weak update on the US economy
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street slips after weak update on the US economy Stan Choe August 17, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market edged back from its all-time high following the latest report on the economy to come in surprisingly weak, this time about how much shoppers are spending at retailers. Such data could keep interest rates low, which is something Wall Street loves, but it also raises the risk of a slowing economy when inflation is still high. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent from its record set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.3 per cent. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 33 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The Australia dollar was trading at US70.79¢ at 5.16am AEST. US stocks gave up modest gains from early in the morning after oil prices swung higher. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1.7 per cent to $US88.52 as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again.



Also raising uncertainty was a report showing shoppers spent less at US retailers last month than the month before. That surprised economists, who were forecasting another month of growth. On the bright side for financial markets, such a pullback in spending could take pressure off inflation. Inflation remains much higher than anyone would like, but reports earlier this week suggested the pace of increases in prices is decelerating. Related Article Opinion

Big four Betting against the bank. ‘Widow-maker’ trades are making a comeback Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor If inflation keeps trending that way, it could encourage the Federal Reserve to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The downside of such data, including last week’s surprisingly weak report on the US job market, is that they raise the risk of a slowing economy. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario.



Some on Wall Street cautioned against overreacting to the weak data on US retail sales, even if it was broad-based. It could simply be a snap back after retail sales in earlier months were boosted by unusual factors such as big tax refunds, the World Cup and even an earlier Prime Day event at Amazon, according to Jennifer Timmerman, senior investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. US consumers nevertheless appear to be getting more discouraged about the economy. A preliminary survey by the University of Michigan suggested sentiment among them is weakening by more than economists expected. The survey said drops occurred across the political spectrum and showed up particularly among older, lower-income and other groups who can be hurt most by inflation. On Wall Street, Reddit jumped 12.6 per cent after learning its stock will join the S&P 500 index on Tuesday. Many professional investors and funds closely track the index, either mimicking it or at least measuring their performance against it. That can push many to buy a stock automatically when it enters the index. Applied Materials fell 5.1 per cent even though the company, whose technology helps make semiconductors, reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Gary Dickerson said global hunger for artificial-intelligence technology helped it deliver another record quarter.



But its stock had already more than doubled this year and built expectations very high, which helped pressure the stock on Friday. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last AI stocks in general have been swinging sharply on worries that their prices shot too high because of AI euphoria and that their strong growth in revenue may not be sustainable. All told, the S&P 500 fell 13.23 points to 7,785.76. Despite the loss, it nevertheless closed out a third straight winning week, its longest such streak since a nine-week run that ended in May. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107.58 to 53,732.41, and the Nasdaq composite sank 73.86 to 26,729.16.



In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher and followed the price of oil. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.69 per cent from 4.63 per cent late Thursday. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. London’s FTSE 100 slipped 0.2 per cent after Nigel Farage regained the seat in Parliament he quit a month ago, beating trash-can wearing comic candidate Count Binface in a special election. South Korea’s Kospi again had one of the world’s sharpest moves and jumped 2.4 per cent for its third straight gain of at least that much. Seoul has been at the centre of the world’s swings for AI stocks because its market is dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
