World.title: In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare?
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPay In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare? Matt Wade and Craig Butt August 17, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The top 1 per cent of income earners in 83 Sydney suburbs take home over $1 million a year on average, while in a cluster of harbourside neighbourhoods, to make the 1 per cent bracket, you need to earn more than $3 million. Analysis of official personal income data by this masthead casts fresh light on how ultra-high pay packets are distributed across the city. In Bellevue Hill, about five kilometres east of Sydney’s central business district, the average income for the highest paid 1 per cent of taxpayers was $6.3 million in 2022-23. That was $1.2 million lower than the previous year but it was still the highest average for the 1 per cent in any city suburb. The top 1 per cent of Sydney earners takes home over $1 million a year. Nine



The adjacent neighbourhood of Rose Bay-Vaucluse-Watsons Bay had the city’s second-highest average earnings for the top 1 per cent at $6.12 million (down from $6.37 million the previous year). Third was Woollahra, where the top 1 per cent took home an average of $5.05 million (up from $4.99 million). There were eight Sydney neighbourhoods where the top 1 per cent had average earnings between $3 million and $5 million (all of them waterfront suburbs) and 72 where average earnings were between $1 million and $3 million. You can search how suburbs and localities across NSW compare here: While suburbs with the highest average incomes for the top 1 per cent were mostly in the eastern suburbs and on the north shore, several were located in the city’s north-west, including Dural-Kenthurst ($1.66 million) and Glenhaven ($1.58 million).



In two outer western Sydney neighbourhoods – Horsley Park-Kemps Creek and Mulgoa-Luddenham-Orchard Hills – the top 1 per cent took home just over $1 million a year. Demographer and social researcher Mark McCrindle said the high average earnings for the top 1 per cent in parts of western and north-western Sydney showed how patterns of income and wealth have shifted. “It tells a story of a changing Sydney,” he said. “Yes, we’ve got very high incomes in those harbourside suburbs which has been the case for 100 years, but we’ve got new locations with high incomes as well. The dynamics of wealth have spread geographically.” McCrindle said income distribution patterns across Sydney showed not all high-income earners wanted to live on the waterfront.



“Some choose to invest their money in a large property, perhaps in bushland, rather than in the harbour area. Places like Dural, Kenthurst and Glenhaven in Sydney’s north-west have really changed economically.” However, in some western suburbs, the earnings of the top 1 per cent was well below the citywide average. Lowest was Auburn North, about 20 kilometres west of the CBD, where the average income of the best paid 1 per cent was $200,656. Suburbs where the top 1 per cent have especially high incomes correlate closely with house prices. Bellevue Hill, which had Sydney’s best paid 1 per cent of earners, also had the city’s highest median house price of $10.4 million, according to Domain’s June quarter House Price Report. In neighbouring Vaucluse, the median house price was $9.5 million and in Rose Bay it was $6.5 million. In Bellevue Hill, the best paid 1 per cent earned an average of $6.3 million a year in 2022-23. It also has a median house price over $10 million. Renee Nowytarger The top 1 per cent of earners across the whole of Greater Sydney had an average income of $1,027,863 in 2022-23.



That was about 12 times more than the average annual personal income for all Greater Sydney taxpayers of $84,947 and 16 times the city’s median income (the middle value of all earners) of $62,180. Sydney was the only Australian capital where the average earnings for the top 1 per cent was a seven-figure total. Next highest was Perth, with average earnings of $928,762 a year for the top 1 per cent, followed by Melbourne with $792,491. The earnings figures show Sydney is Australia’s most unequal capital city for income: the top 1 per cent of earners received 12.1 per cent of the city’s income in 2022-23. That compares with 11.1 per cent in Perth, 10.2 per cent in Melbourne and 8.7 per cent in Brisbane. Nationally, the top 1 per cent earned 9.9 per cent of all personal income. Outside of Sydney there were some localities where the top 1 per cent had extremely high earnings. In the Upper Hunter town of Scone, the average income of the top 1 per cent of earners was just under $5 million, the fourth highest in NSW.



In Bangalow, near Byron Bay, the average income for the top 1 per cent was $1.9 million while in Robertson-Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands, that average was $1.87 million. The suburb with the highest 1 per cent average income of anywhere in Australia was Cottesloe in Perth, where you need to be bringing in $36 million a year on average to be in that suburb’s top 1 per cent. In many neighbourhoods, including Cottesloe, the average income among the top 1 per cent is skewed by a few earners with extremely high earners – the top 0.1 per cent – who drive up the average. The analysis used Australian Bureau of Statistics personal income data, which draws on Tax Office records for the 2022-23 financial year, the most recent available. It includes figures for “Statistical Area Level 2” (SA2) localities that are similar to suburbs.



The data covers only individual pre-tax income; it does not include assets owned by individuals such as housing and shares. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Greens propose fines up to $10m for supermarkets charging 'excessive prices'
World.content:
The Green Party wants the government to back its crackdown on the supermarket duopoly by supporting its member's bill before Parliament rises for the election.

The Commerce (Excessive Pricing in Retail Grocery Industry) Amendment Bill seeks to ban supermarkets from charging prices that are "excessive" relative to the cost of supplying products, plus a "fair margin".

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said New Zealanders pay too much for their groceries, while supermarket profits exceed a million dollars a day.

"While Luxon's government has talked tough, prices at the check-out have continued to rise.

"Parliament can now actually do something meaningful in its final few weeks before the election by supporting this common-sense Bill, to reduce New Zealanders' bills. At the end of the day, surely, that's why we're all there in the first place," she said.

The Bill is part of the Green's affordable kai election policy, set to be announced next month, and will be placed in the members' ballot by the party's consumer affairs spokesperson Ricardo Menéndez March.

He said it would be up to the courts to decide whether a supermarket had breached the ban - on application from the Commerce Commission - and supermarkets would be required to keep records of their pricing and provide them to the commission on request.

"Breaches would carry penalties of up to $10 million, three times the value of the commercial gain, or 10 percent of turnover."

"This is consistent with Australia's approach, which brought in the same ban on 1 July this year with the same penalties we are proposing here, following its own reviews into supermarket market dominance," Menéndez March said.

Swarbrick called on the prime minister and the wider coalition to use Parliament's remaining time to "do something practical" to lower the cost of living.

The government has to attract an international competitor into the market but has been unsuccessful.

World.title: Kiwi bellwether stock posts strong result but warns of fuel price impact
World.content:
Freight, logistics and waste management company Freightways strongly lifted its profit despite a "more challenging" second half of the year, as it faced the economic consequences of the Middle East conflict.

Key numbers for the 12 months ended June compared with a year ago:

Net profit $94m vs $80.1m

Revenue $1.46b vs $1.29b

Final dividend 45 cents per share vs 40 cents

The company, which owns brands including New Zealand Couriers, Poste Haste and Big Chill Distribution, is considered a bellwether stock on the NZX, meaning its results are seen as a broader reflection of the New Zealand economy.

It said the positive trend that kicked off the financial year was "sharply interrupted" by the US-Iran war.

"The combination of higher fuel costs and softer customer demand created a drag during the final quarter on a result which was otherwise strong for the group," Freightways said in a stock exchange statement.

The company said it continued to win new customers, it invested in improving its operating platforms and facilities, and was financially disciplined, which positioned the business well for when economic conditions improve.

Freightways said higher fuel prices affected the business in two ways.

"First, rapid increases temporarily compress margins because fuel recovery mechanisms inevitably lag underlying fuel costs," it said.

"Secondly, higher fuel costs reduce discretionary spending across the economy, lowering freight volumes as consumer and business activity slows."

The company also noted the tightening of monetary conditions by the Reserve Bank contributed to a softer economic environment.

World.title: 'I know I have her full support': Christopher Luxon says Erica Stanford backs his leadership
World.content:
Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 8m

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he is confident he has Erica Stanford's full support for his leadership.

Stanford has backed the Prime Minister - insisting she didn't challenge him for the leadership.

Four days after the confidence vote in her leader, five days after she walked through Wellington airport on her way to it and said nothing, the education minister held a last-minute media stand up on Sunday afternoon to explain why she didn't give Christopher Luxon her backing in the lead up to last week's emergency meeting.

Defence Minister Chris Penk ended up taking the fall for the botched leadership coup - losing his ministerial portfolios before quitting.

But there's been some suggestions he was merely the numbers man for either Stanford or Chris Bishop.

Both deny that was the case.

Luxon told Morning Report on Monday he was in no doubt of Stanford's backing, in both private conversations, and public statements.

"It's a pretty intense situation when you turn up at an airport and you've got a media scrum that's in full white heat mode. It's not a surprise that some of my caucus will freeze," he said.

"I know I have her full support - always have".

When asked if he had spoken to Stanford about refusing to say if she supported Luxon prior to the caucus meeting and confidence vote, he said he didn't need to.

He said Chris Penk was "working for himself", and had launched a leadership bid in caucus that failed.

Luxon said he didn't know what the vote was, but that he had the full support of his caucus.

He said the last week had been "pretty tough", but the issue had now been resolved.

Luxon said had been watching leadership challenges in Australia and the UK, and his approach was to get everyone - including backbenchers - to discuss their concerns.

"When we have someone who raises a leadership challenge, I'm sorry, we're going to deal with that issue up front because I'm not going to go back to the behaviour that I observed in the National Party for four or five years... that's not going to happen.

"And as a result, yes, it means that we have a distraction for a week. Yes, we have to bring everyone to town. Yes, we have to get in a room and have a real conversation, say what's going on.

"In this case, it was pretty straightforward. One individual launched a challenge that failed. We moved on to a confidence vote and we went out of that room united.

"That's important to me ... that's the best way to deal with it. I think as a leader, front it, deal with it and make sure everyone stays aligned so that we don't get into dysfunction like we've seen in the past."

Earlier, Housing Minister Chris Bishop told Morning Report that Penk had acted alone in his challenge of Luxon.

He said the community response to the leadership vote was one of "just move on".

"Very strongly people saying it's good you've got it sorted," Bishop said.

"Get on with the job. This country's got too many challenges to spend our time fixated on this sort of stuff.

"So just get on with it, and that's exactly what I and the rest of the team are doing."

Meanwhile, Bishop also spoke on the fast-track housing developments, and said he couldn't legally pause them.

The mayors of Auckland and Queenstown had called for an immediate pause on developments, including one that lacks water infrastructure.

Bishop said that would require a law change.

Luxon said fast-track had been "hugely successful".

"Think about the eight renewable energy projects that have got out the door and are actually happening that help our emissions profile," he said.

"But more importantly, make sure we get a supply of electricity in this country. What we're identifying in the housing side of it, not all, but some where councils can't get that enabling infrastructure in place, there may well be a short-term process for stage one of a development.

"We get that up and running and moving, and before stage two comes into place, you've got to make sure we've got that enabling infrastructure in place.

"And this is just giving councils better tools to recover any growth-related infrastructure costs from future fast-track developments."

World.title: Man in court after four people stabbed, gun fired in Hamilton knife attack
World.content:
A man is due to appear in court on assault charges in relation to the weekend's mass stabbing in Hamilton.

Four people received knife wounds on Churchill Avenue, Maeroa, on Saturday night.

One person remains in hospital in stable condition, and three others have since been discharged.

A 23-year-old is due to appear in Hamilton District Court on Monday, charged with aggravated burglary, two counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, and attempted murder.

Police described the situation, which also involved a gun being fired, as frightening and disturbing for neighbours.

Inspector Karl Thornton said police were alerted to the incident on Churchill Avenue just before 9pm on Saturday.

Police said as the attack unfolded, one victim fled on foot to seek help at a nearby property and was followed there. It is alleged an occupant there fired a gun, but caused no injury.

Hamilton mayor Tim Macindoe said his thoughts were with all of those affected by what he calls a deeply concerning situation.

Rhiannon Connor who lives on Churchill Avenue, said she had heard screaming on Saturday night as the incident unfolded.

"I heard like bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, and I was like, holy f***, what's that?"

Connor was worried the person would show up at her house next.

World.title: 24 of the world's most unusual landscapes
World.content: Their name derives from their grass covering, which turns brown during the dry season, with December to March the best time to visit. Legend has it the hills are the dried tears of a heartbroken giant. While the truth is more prosaic, the views are still spectacular.

World.title: Māori education pioneer Te Kepa Stirling dies aged 88
World.content:
Te Kepa Takataka-o-Rangi Stirling, a pioneering Māori educator and staunch advocate for te reo Māori me ōna tikanga, has died aged 88.

A proud descendant of Te Whānau-ā-Apanui and Ngāti Porou, he was an uncompromising champion of Māori maintaining their identity and succeeding in education.

Te Kepa and his late wife, Pani Takawhenua Waipapa Stirling, forged pathways for generations of Māori educators and ākonga.

He joined Ngā Tapuwae College as a kaiako of physical education and Māori. His wife, Pani, had joined the college the previous year as head of the Māori department.

Over the years, the couple developed Te Whare Awhina a programme that incorporated a whānau-centred approach to education.

Te Kura Māori o Ngātapuwae

Te Whare Āwhina evolved into Te Reo Rua o Ngā Tapuwae, which became a school within a school as Te Kura Māori o Ngā Tapuwae in 1996, before eventually gaining independence as a Kura-ā-Iwi.

Stirling also developed Te Whare Wānanga Pupuri Kōrero o Ngā Tapuwae, which became a hub for Māori whānau and the wider community.

In 2005, Te Kepa and Pani Stirling were each awarded the Queen's Service Medal for their contribution to the community.

Their daughter, Arihia Stirling, continues to carry their legacy forward through her own successful career in Māori education and as tumuaki of Te Kura Māori o Ngā Tapuwae.

The ripple effect of their work will continue inspiring generations to come,

Those wishing to pay tribute in Tāmaki Makaurau will be able to do so at Te Kura Māori o Ngā Tapuwae, with pōwhiri being held at 10am, 1pm and 4pm on Monday.

World.title: A2 Milk's full year net profit drops 44 percent
World.content:
A2 Milk has seen its full year net profit drop 44 percent in line with its expectations, with a couple of large one-time costs associated with the purchase of large-scale processing facilities.

"FY26 was a landmark year for The a2 Milk Company as we made significant progress against our China growth strategy and supply chain transformation through the acquisition of a2 Pōkeno," chair Pip Greenwood said.

The company's result was also affected by supply chain disruptions to sales of its China label infant formula (IMF) in the fourth quarter, which chief executive David Bortolussi expected to come right this financial year.

"The successful acquisition and transformation of a2 Pōkeno is a significant step in strengthening our supply chain and enabling growth with the launch of two new China label infant milk formula products planned for the first half of FY27," he said.

Key numbers for the 12 months ended June compared with a year ago:

Net profit $113.6m vs 202.9m

Revenue $1.972b vs $1.755m

Underlying profit $284.4m vs $ $291.7m

Net profit from continuing operations $207.5m vs $220.3m

Special dividend 41.36 cents per share

Full year dividend 21.0 cps vs 20 cps

Outlook

"Revenue and EBITDA (underlying profit) are expected to grow in FY27, supported by increased contribution from product innovation and new markets, continued momentum in Other Nutritionals and Liquid Milk, and a2 Pōkeno profitability improvement," chief executive David Bortolussi said.

However, ongoing supply chain disruption was expected, with China label sales to gradually recover over the course of FY27 and English label momentum to improve during the first half, supported by an increase in marketing in first half (1H27).

As a result, it expected revenue and underlying profit growth to be "materially weighted" to the second half.

However, the outlook was not without risks.

Key risks

World.title: E-scooter riders will not have to hand signal for turning once in cycle lanes
World.content:
Electric scooter riders will not have to make hand signals for turning and stopping when they are allowed into cycle lanes.

Research shows one-handed scooting is very risky.

A road rules change before the end of the year will let e-scooterists legally use bike lanes for the first time.

Cyclists are subject to a road rule to use hand signals - though do not have to if they risk losing control.

"E-scooter riders are not currently subject to the cyclist signalling requirements in the Road User Rule," the Transport Agency told RNZ.

"While signalling is encouraged as a safety practice, it is not currently a legal requirement for e-scooter riders."

Since that's the case the agency Waka Kotahi has not considered the risks of scooters signalling when it comes to the rule changes.

Scooterists also don't have to wear helmets, unlike bikers.

Some e-scooters have brake and indicator lights but many do not. Public e-scooters have speed limiters on them but privately owned ones do not.

A study last year in Sweden found riding with only one hand on the handlebars increases the risk of crashing by six times.

"It is not possible to steer and brake with an electric scooter in the same way as with a bicycle, so riding with one hand on the handlebar is significantly more difficult - and dangerous - than many people might think," study leader professor Marco Dozza of Chalmers University of Technology said.

The small wheels and high centre of gravity of scooters makes them more unstable than bikes.

Recent ACC data showed claims for e-scooter injuries were on the rise, with children and young people rising fastest.

A recent study in the UK found e-scooter riders had triple the chance of getting a traumatic brain injury than motorcyclists, triggering calls in New Zealand for helmets to be mandatory. They are on bikes, but not on scooters.

The UK has had a ban on any private escooters on public thoroughfares but is struggling with what the rules should be.

The rules reform is being done under a type of secondary legislation called an Order in Council that is more straightforward than primary legislation.

World.title: Aussie star Lani Pallister ends American GOAT's 16-year win streak
World.content:
Lani Pallister has toppled swimming legend Katie Ledecky for a second time in 24 hours to complete her stunning Pan Pacific championship campaign with a fourth gold medal.

The 24-year-old Pallister was under world-record pace for much of the race as she won the 800m freestyle final in eight minutes and 6.1 seconds from four-time Olympic champion Ledecky (8:07.26) in the American's signature event.

Ledecky's lone previous defeat in an 800m freestyle final since 2010 came in a small domestic event in February 2024 against Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh, making Pallister the first to beat her over the distance at an international meet.

"Today is the most nervous I've ever felt in my entire life. I was just so locked in and I've been really focused on what I want," Pallister said.

"The 800m is my favourite event. So to have the three titles this week and be just behind Katie in the 1,500 [is great but] … this is the one that I wanted."

Ledecky, who famously signed an autograph for a young Pallister a decade ago, telling her to "dream big", wrote on Instagram that she "can't help but smile about another incredible race with [Pallister]".

Ledecky (right) told a young Pallister to "dream big". (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Pallister had beaten Ledecky to win the 400m freestyle gold a day earlier and took silver behind her great rival in the 1,500m free, as well as downed McIntosh to win the 200m free gold and also collect gold in the 4x200m free relay.

Australia's Dolphins well and truly flexed their middle- and long-distance muscle at the meet, two years out from the LA Olympics, with Sam Short also emerging with three individual gold medals after winning the men's 1,500m free to go with his 400 and 800 free titles.

Having beaten Ian Thorpe's 1999 Pan Pacs record to win the 400m, he erased another Australian legend's mark in the 1,500m.

His time of 14:33.97 was the sixth-fastest in history, breaking Grant Hackett's Australian record that had stood since 2001, and came a day after German teenager Johannes Liebmann smashed the world record at the European Aquatics Championships.

Loading Instagram content

"I am proud of my consistency," said Short, who also won the 400m, 800m, and 1,500m titles at the Commonwealth Games late last month.

"I've gone five well sub-15-minute swims now, so if I can do that here my average come Olympics, world championships, all I need to do is be my average and be contending for some podium places."

Adding to a strong final day for Australia, Zac Stubblety-Cook went from fourth to first in the 200m breaststroke final, winning in 2:08.09 from American Josh Matheny.

And countryman Jamie Jack won the 50m freestyle gold in a championship record of 21.35 as American Jack Alexy took silver in 21.42.

"It's awesome. That's the best I could ask for," Jack said.

American Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the 50m free twice, winning the final in 23.19.

Douglass capped a busy night by anchoring the US women to a dominant victory in the 4x100 medley relay in a championship record time of 3:50.43, with Australia second in 3:55.09.

The US men won from Australia in the 4x100 medley relay.

Australia finished the four-day meet with a medal haul of 15 gold, 11 silver and nine bronze, behind only the US haul of 19, 22 and nine.

World.title: Off-grid stories during F1 mid-year break as racing returns
World.content:
Formula 1's mid-year hiatus ends this weekend, as the racing series returns to action with the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort.

The five-week break has given drivers and teams a chance to refresh ahead of a long and gruelling run to the finish line, with the drivers' and constructors' championships well and truly alive in 2026.

While there has been no action on the track, there has been news off it during the break.

Ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, here are a few stories you may have missed during the hiatus.

1. No contract announcements

The first news is no news.

Drivers off contract at the end of 2026 Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

George Russell, Mercedes

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull

Carlos Sainz, Williams

Alex Albon, Williams

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin

Oliver Bearman, Haas

Esteban Ocon, Haas

Nick Hulkenberg, Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi

Franco Colapinto, Alpine

The mid-year break usually signals the start of F1's silly season, where teams and drivers formalise contracts for future seasons.

The 2026 silly season is set to be busy, with as many as 14 drivers off contract at the end of this year.

And there are big names who are yet to finalise deals for 2027 and beyond, including Mercedes drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli, and two-time world champion Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin).

There has also been wild speculation of a potential driver swap between McLaren and Red Bull, with Australia's Oscar Piastri and four-time world champion Max Verstappen changing teams as early as next year.

But, thus far, there have been no announcements.

This will change in the near future, and just because no contracts have been announced does not mean no work behind the scenes.

2. Piastri confident McLaren can 'make that step' back to the top

After the highs of the previous two seasons, McLaren's 2026 campaign has resembled more of a yo-yo.

McLaren have won the previous two constructors' championships, while Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri both won seven grands prix last year, a campaign where Norris became drivers' world champion.

Piastri blasts 'f***ing stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP Oscar Piastri retired from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, won by his teammate Lando Norris, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

But in 2026, with a new era of regulations, McLaren has had mixed results.

It started the season poorly, with Oscar Piastri failing to start the opening two grands prix of the season (Australia and China), while Norris also failed to start the Chinese Grand Prix.

Both drivers have been plagued by reliability issues, but have also produced promising results.

Piastri has twice finished on the podium (Japan and Miami), while Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix — a race Piastri led before being hit by a backmarker and then suffering an issue that forced his retirement.

Despite not being in the championship picture thus far in 2026, Piastri is confident McLaren will return.

In an interview with the team during the break, Piastri cited McLaren's early struggles in 2023 before their rise up the grid to become back-to-back champions.

"When you look at the previous experience of what we've been able to achieve as a team, and how we've been able to make progress through the year, it's good," the Australian said.

"In 2023, we were in a much worse position than where we are now, and we were able to really jump up the order to fight for podiums.

"The way that Lando and I worked together during that period to try and focus on making the car quick, so that we could then fight for the results that we wanted, hasn't changed. It's still strong, with productive conversations together with the team — we are all pushing toward the same goal.

"I feel like for me I've already seen it play out more than once. I think that's a real strength of the team. Yes, things are different, the cars are different, maybe the way we will make that step will look different. But we've made that step before, and I'm confident we can do it again."

3. Bahrain Grand Prix back on calendar, in Malaysia

While the official mid-year break is coming to an end, F1 had an unofficial hiatus earlier this year when the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia weekends were called off due to unrest in the Middle East.

That left an unexpected gap between the Japanese Grand Prix and Miami Grand Prix weekends, with F1 holding onto hope that they would be able to bring those races back onto the calendar.

Well, they have brought one back, in a different country.

The Bahrain Grand Prix will be held in 2026, but thousands of kilometres away in Malaysia.

Sepang International Circuit will host the event from October 2-4, between the grand prix weekends in Azerbaijan and Singapore.

F1 is no stranger to Sepang, first racing there in 1999, while the last F1 race held there in 2017 was won by Max Verstappen.

"We are delighted to confirm that Malaysia will host the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2026. Once again, the sport has demonstrated its ability to adapt, find solutions, and deliver, creating an exciting moment for everyone who follows Formula 1," F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said.

4. Cadillac has a team principal change

While there was no change in the driver market, F1's newest team made a change on the pit wall.

Cadillac announced Marcin Budkowski would become the American squad's new team principal, replacing Graeme Lowdon.

Lowdon was the team principal from 2024 and an instrumental figure in preparing Cadillac for its debut season in 2026.

Budkowski has been around F1 for many years, and was once the executive director at French outfit Alpine.

"Marcin's appointment marks another important step in the continued evolution of the Cadillac Formula 1 Team," said Dan Towriss, CEO of the Cadillac team.

"As we enter this new era for the Cadillac Formula 1 Team, Marcin brings exceptional F1 experience, technical expertise and strategic leadership that will strengthen our organisation and help us develop the winning mindset, tools and processes required for long-term success.

"We're grateful to Graeme Lowdon for his leadership and the role he played in forming the Cadillac Formula 1 Team from the ground up. His contributions helped establish a strong foundation in our build-up phase, and we thank him for his commitment and wish him well."

World.title: Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight
World.content:
You could pick a handful of moments during the first Test at Marrara Oval in Darwin where it was clear not everything was as it seemed on surface level.

On day two, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted off with his usual exuberance from the infield to chase down a shot that trickled towards the boundary.

The immaculately manicured outfield, offering a playing surface that was nigh on pristine, had already been praised for its lawn-like quality.

Mark Waugh on Fox Sports noted you could probably play bowls or tennis on it.

Yet as soon as Labuschagne slid for the ball, the ugly truth was revealed, as a huge clump of turf was ripped up in a heaped mass of mud and grass and injury potential.

This was a pattern repeated throughout the match: The outfield's undoubted beauty was only surface deep.

Australia's standing at the top of the Test match rankings may only be surface deep, as deep fissures have been revealed in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

An analogy to what transpired over the next four days, as the number nine-ranked Test team that were missing two of their best bowlers, thumped the world number one side at full strength on their own turf, could not have been clearer.

Bangladesh's stunning victory in Darwin has delivered Australian cricket the shock that it undoubtedly needed.

A team that arrived without fanfare or pedigree has slapped down the world's number one Test playing nation by playing simple, sensible Test cricket.

The bowling was slow but accurate. The batting, unspectacular but patient and disciplined.

The Tigers' attitude was exceptional.

As the growth of the big three has accelerated inequalities between the haves and have-nots of Test cricket, Bangladesh are one of those teams that have been left firmly on the outer, yet proved in Darwin that the paucity of opportunities that have come their way has in no way blunted their potency or hunger for success within the format.

They were here to play Test cricket and play it well.

Najmul Hossain Shanto led his team with skill and composure throughout. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Given it had been 23 years since they last played a Test on Australian soil, their commitment to playing such an impressive style against a country that has snubbed them for so long was more than admirable.

Credit for that has to go to coach Phil Simmons and unflappable skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto.

Shanto made correct decision after correct decision on the pitch, Bangladesh never succumbing to the pressure or enormity of what was transpiring around them right up until Mominul Haque crushed Beau Webster through the covers to seal victory, a simple hug between the two not out batters sufficing as the bench finally exploded in joy on the boundary.

Bangladesh's historic win deserves all the praise that will undoubtedly be heaped upon it, the context of which will forever be extraordinary.

Bangladesh held their nerve throughout a tense contest. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Legendary English cricket writer Neville Cardus once wrote that to properly consider Test cricket, you need to see the big picture.

"I wish to present the Test matches in their setting," he wrote in the introduction to his book chronicling the 1936/37 Ashes series.

"To me cricket must be put against a background."

So what is the background here for Australia?

Australia is about to embark on as busy a Test match year as they have ever had, playing as many as 20 Tests in the next 12 months.

From the Top End, the men's Test team will head to South Africa, play New Zealand and England at home, then face overseas tours to India and England for the Ashes in 2027.

It is a demanding schedule both as physically gruelling and mentally taxing as they come.

Steve Smith and Australia have a lot of thinking to do ahead of the next Test. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Starting off with a two-Test series against Bangladesh, a country Australia has only deigned to host once before for a Test series and only played against in red ball cricket six times in total before this week was considered by most to be a friendly warm up, a competitive practice during a winter sojourn in the Top End sun.

It is, of course, incredibly admirable Cricket Australia is taking Test matches to regions that cannot ever hope to host an Ashes contest.

For financial reasons as much as from a societal responsibility, playing these sorts of Tests in this continent's more remote, northern reaches is undoubtedly the right thing to do.

But maybe there is a sense that this is considered a form of benevolence to the lesser-populated areas of the nation.

Perhaps, for some, even playing Bangladesh is a form of charity to a nation that simply does not have the financial pull of the major nations, little more than an obligation to the World Test Championship.

Maybe, despite protestations to the contrary, that attitude sneaks into the minds of the players, so subliminally that they themselves do not even notice it.

Pat Cummins defended the team's preparation, but perhaps they didn't even realise they were underdone. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

For how can playing in front of about 5,000 spectators in a venue where only half the oval is bordered by a grandstand compare with the cathedral-like cavernous majesty of the MCG, or the lack of pressure contrast with the parochial furnace of a packed Gabba?

Marrara Oval offers neither the stately splendour of the Adelaide Oval or SCG, nor the admittedly under-populated grandiosity of the new Perth Stadium.

Darwin is definitively off-Broadway.

And although Australia's defeat didn't seem to be for lack of effort, the application and necessary quality was lacking throughout the match.

Horror drops from Steve Smith and Nathan Lyon were surely aberrations, but the lazy stroke play and jittery, muddled thinking of the batters was very not.

Steve Smith was not his usual best in the field. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This shock to a team that has been creaking under the weight of their own success for a number of years now is one that has probably arrived eight months too late.

It was due last summer against England before those Bazballers tripped up over their own hubris.

A papering of the cracks was the result of that emphatic 4-1 Ashes victory, the foundations of sand upon which the top order was built were never tested, the supposedly seismic impact of a fired up England bowling attack never coming to bare, self-sabotaging itself amidst a storm of recriminations in the boozy sand of Noosa.

So on we continued. Australia's brittle batters went off to earn their coin in meaningly limited overs matches and failed to address the issues that have plagued them in red ball cricket, perhaps even accentuating the problems by promoting angled bats and rash shots.

Now the show moves to Mackay and presents Australia with an ever-bigger list of questions and problems to face.

Jake Weatherald's status as opener has to be looked at. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia were rusty and not up to speed in Darwin.

Even if Mackay's Harrup Park, the newest venue to host a men's Test in Australia, provides a suitably refreshed outlook and attitude from Australia next Saturday, will victory there do anything else other than to plaster even more paper over gaps that are swiftly turning into chasms?

It's been eight years since a rambunctious tour almost boiled over, a sorry spectacle that was quickly overshadowed by a sandpaper-scraping that was barely as coarse as the friction generated by two teams flirting on the edge of respectability throughout.

Any weakness in Australia's psyche will be ripe for exploitation in southern Africa, and the venom is unlikely to be as hidden as it was in the far north of Australia.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

World.title: Dragons give hope to wooden spoon battle after downing Tigers
World.content:
St George Illawarra can dream of avoiding the wooden spoon after several players with uncertain futures stood up to consign Wests Tigers to an eighth straight loss.

After they led by 12 with four minutes to play, the Dragons had to hold on for a nervous final three minutes before claiming a 24-22 victory at Parramatta Stadium on Sunday.

Fresh off their first back-to-back wins this year, the last-placed Dragons now finish the round only four points behind Brisbane and the Gold Coast.

The Tigers could also still be caught while six points ahead, with the Dragons to face Canterbury, Manly and Parramatta to finish their season.

Much has been made of the potential of the Dragons' younger forwards this year, and what is building at St George Illawarra ahead of next year's big-name arrivals.

But this was a Sunday afternoon for those whose futures at the club appear clouded.

Daniel Atkinson proved he can offer utility value for the Dragons next year, after going from first-choice halfback at the start of the year to filling in at fullback.

Playing No.1 for the first time in his NRL career, Atkinson was solid at the back, put on a cut-out ball for a Tyrell Sloan try and had a couple of big kick returns.

It remains unclear what role he will have next year, given Luke Metcalf and Kodi Nikorima are arriving to play in the halves and Scott Drinkwater will be fullback.

The same could be said of Lykhan King-Togia, who on Sunday had one of his best games of the year.

The Dragons five-eighth caught out Adam Doueihi in defence and sent Hamish Stewart over for the Saints' first try.

And he had one of his own in the second half, digging into the line to create space for a Sloan linebreak before backing up to take a kick back inside from his Super League-bound winger.

Moses Suli, who has pledged to fight for his spot after being told by the Dragons he could leave, also had a strong afternoon.

The Tigers came up short despite a big finish. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings )

The 28-year-old burst his way through two defenders to go 50 metres and score once in the first half, before pulling off a try-saver on Jahream Bula in the second.

For the Tigers, a season that started so well can't end soon enough.

They led 6-0 early through Sunia Turuva, and briefly fought back into the game at 18-12 after halftime when Samuela Fainu finished off an Alex Seyfarth break.

The one bright spot was a late double to centre Solomone Saukuru, who reduced the margin to two with three minutes to play.

But the fact just 9773 fans turned up for a Sunday afternoon match against another Sydney team is telling of how badly this season has spiralled.

Earlier, Newcastle captain Kalyn Ponga credited the performance of Fletcher Sharpe for keeping the Knights' NRL top-four hopes alive in their 36-26 home win over the Gold Coast.

With Sunday's game in the balance heading into the final 20 minutes, five-eighth Sharpe took charge with a darting 55-metre dummy-half try-scoring run to extend Newcastle's lead.

Sharpe followed up in the final six minutes with a second try, when he scooped up a wayward Titans ball to race 60 metres downfield to seal victory.

"Sharpie doing what he does today was pretty special. I'm very appreciative of him after that," Ponga said.

"Without him, I don't know if we play the way we did, to be honest. He broke open the game for us in the second half and when he's streaking away it is a nice feeling."

With a final round bye in hand and Cronulla staring down consecutive losses, the Knights sit just two competition points adrift of the fourth-placed Dolphins.

An unlikely top-four berth would complete a remarkable 12-month turnaround for the Knights following their 2025 wooden spoon finish.

AAP

World.title: Desperate draw seals wildcard for Blues as history made at Docklands
World.content:
Chad Warner had a big game for Sydney with three goals in the Swans' win over Essendon (Getty Images)

Sydney have locked up second spot and two AFL home finals, beating last-placed Essendon by 36 points.

The Swans dominated from the start and despite some resistance from the Bombers, easily won 17.10 (112) to 11.10 (76) in the Sunday twilight game at the MCG.

Errol Gulden racked up a career-best 47 possessions and Charlie Curnow kicked four goals as he closes on his third Coleman Medal as the league's top goalkicker.

While the Bombers were never going to stage a massive upset, they scrapped hard after a blowout loomed early in the game.

Sydney missed the finals last year in Dean Cox's first season as senior coach and have rebounded superbly this season.

Curnow kicked three of the first four goals and looked set for a night out as the Swans took control from the start.

Sydney's first four inside 50s all resulted in goals and the last-placed Bombers were their own worst enemies, gifting the Swans with turnovers.

When former Victorian Sheffield Shield fielding substitute Billy Cootee kicked the first goal of the second term, the Swans were out to a 44-point lead.

But Essendon rallied to at least stop a blowout, kicking four goals to two in the second quarter and reducing the margin to 24 points at the long break.

Nate Caddy and Peter Wright were providing targets in attack and Isaac Kako was frenetic with his workrate for the Bombers.

While fourth-gamer Vigo Visentini was up against Brodie Grundy in the ruck, the young Bomber's effort also could not be faulted.

Visentini delighted the Essendon fans with a couple of big tackles, taking down Chad Warner early in the third quarter.

Archer Day-Wicks kicked the first goal of the third quarter and a couple of minutes later, Will Setterfield launched a bomb from outside 50m. Improbably, the Bombers only trailled by 11 points at 13 minutes.

But that only sparked the Swans. First Logan McDonald set up Jai Serong for a goal and then McDonald kicked his own from 50-plus to stop the rot.

The gulf between the two teams was summed up early in the last quarter when Caddy was running into an open goal. Sam Wicks came from nowhere to run him down and force the rushed behind.

Seconds later, Sydney had run the ball down the other end of the ground and Curnow snapped his fourth goal.

Visentini marked strongly and kicked his first AFL goal in the last to cap a solid game.

AAP

World.title: Aussies continue winning form, Djokovic suffers early exit in Cincinnati
World.content:
The Australian men's assault at the Cincinnati Open has continued with gusto thanks to Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata.

A day after James Duckworth, Adam Walton and Chris O'Connell scored first-round wins, but Thanasi Kokkinakis was beaten, de Minaur was pushed to his limits at the final Masters 1000 event before the US Open at Flushing Meadows.

Having dropped the first set in just 26 minutes, fifth seed de Minaur, who received an opening-round bye, responded to defeat Quentin Halys 1-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-4).

The Frenchman had won their only previous meeting, a Miami Masters hard-court clash, back in 2023.

De Minaur lost his opening two service games of the match, but was not broken again en route to setting up a round-of-32 clash with Brit Arthur Fery, who saw off Duckworth, 6-4, 2-6, 7-6, (7-4) in a tick over two-and-a-half hours.

It will be the first clash on tour between de Minaur and the 32nd-seeded French-born Fery.

Earlier on Saturday (Sunday AEST), 25-year-old wildcard Hijikata beat 19th seed Luciano Darderi, of Italy, 6-4, 6-2 to set up his last-32 match with 14th seed Jakub Mensik.

Novak Djokovic was beaten in three sets, by Argentine Thiago Agustin Tirante.

Miomir Kecmanovic, Hubert Hurkacz and Mattia Bellucci were also defeated.

Playing his first match ‌since losing a Wimbledon semifinal to Jannik Sinner, 39-year-old Djokovic struggled in the heat and required a ‌medical timeout in a disappointing US Open tune-up.

"Congrats to my opponent," Djokovic said after losing to the world number 50.

"It was not an enjoyable match for me, for sure. The way I felt. Not the first and I guess not the last time, but it is what it is."

The Serbian — a three-time Cincinnati Open champion and number five in the rankings — will look to regroup before heading to New York, where he ⁠will seek a record-extending 25th grand slam singles ​title.

"I think this is the best win of my career," Tirante said.

"I think I really did a good job inside the court. I managed very well the nerves of playing against a legend like Novak."

ABC/wires

World.title: Tupou has his 'mojo' back and Wallabies want more
World.content:
Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.

Tupou scored two first-half tries for Australia, who trailed before scoring 42 consecutive points in a 56-17 defeat of Japan in Townsville on Saturday.

All three starting front-rowers, as well as replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa and back-rowers Harry Wilson and Charlie Cale, were Australia's try-scorers in Townsville.

Tupou scored the match-winner in Osaka against Eddie Jones's men a week earlier after coming off the bench and has shown power and skill to indicate he is back near his best approaching next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallaby 1,000 has 'dream come true' as Australia thrash Japan Massimo De Lutiis enjoys a dream debut for Australia, scoring a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.

"He's found a little bit of himself again, and he's been more of himself," Wallabies coach Kiss said, while also noting his combination with good mate and returning lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto.

"I'm very, very big on making sure the players be themselves as much as possible."

Former Queensland Reds star Tupou agonised over his move from Australian rugby to France, with Racing 92 last season but it has helped him turn back the clock after several underwhelming seasons at the Melbourne Rebels and NSW Waratahs.

"Moving to France, he's found out who he is a little bit more and he's come back and he's really connected with the group here and found that bit of mojo that he likes to thrive on," Kiss said.

With English-based Tom Hooper yet to return to the side, Tupou is the only overseas-based Wallaby currently in the Test rotation.

The coach has remained in touch with Racing 92's staff to ensure they have his services for the two-Test tour of Argentina that begins later this month and hopefully beyond.

"All good, as I believe, at this stage," Kiss said.

"I'll be talking to the coach and the team manager of Racing, this week, again, to make sure they understand how we're looking after Nella and making sure we're doing the right thing with him and working him hard.

"So they can trust the process as well. But, yeah, he'll be with us."

Jones joked post-game that Tupou played as if there was a pizza on offer for every try and reckoned he would even deliver one to the change rooms himself.

"No pizza, I'll have to hit him up about that one," Tupou grinned.

"I've got a lot of love and respect for Eddie, actually. Nothing against that, he loves me, I know that."

Tupou said he wanted to "take it to the next level" after finding his feet in France.

And he said Kiss's tweaks were helping him get there.

"To get the ball in my hands as a forward, less running without the ball, more running with it," Tupou said.

"We're still working on it, but it's good to see forwards scoring tries."

AAP

Tech.title: OpenAI reportedly disbanded its preparedness team
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to the Financial Times, OpenAI disbanded its preparedness team at the end of last month. The job of the preparedness team was to assess if models posed serious risks and develop ways to mitigate those risks. (You know, like the possibility that it could go rogue and hack another company.) According to FT, responsibility has instead been divided up for specific areas like bio and cyber, then moved into existing teams.

This is the latest change at the company, which has been in upheaval as it heads towards what is expected to be a massive IPO. Over the last few years, it’s slowly torn down its more reach-led model, dissolving its AGI readiness and superalignment teams. Ethics lead Chloé Bakalar, Chief Futurist Josh Achiam, and head of safety Johannes Heidecke have all also left recently, leading some critics like Jan Leike, who resigned from OpenAI in 2024, to tell FT that the company was ignoring safety in favor of creating “shiny products.”

The head of the preparedness team, Dylan Scandinaro, who was poached from Anthropic in February, will now focus on the implications of “recursive self-improving” AI.

Tech.title: Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal crafted a hip hop breakup masterpiece
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What we’re listening to, watching, and reading right now.

“Breakups are… tough.”

It’s the opening lines of an interlude towards the end of DOOMED! Called “It Happens in Every Universe.” It’s also basically the thesis of the entire record. It’s no grand revelation, but it’s a well-trodden subject that Open Mike Eagle manages to mine for artistic gold.

Eagle’s subject matter is usually personal, and his productions tinged with nostalgia. But DOOMED! is his most intimate album yet. A lot of that is due to the production from Kenny Segal. The two have traveled in the same orbit and worked together before, but this is the first full-length album release from the two.

These are some of Segal’s most commanding beats since Maps, his 2023 record with Billy Woods. There’s still warbly piano samples, strings, detuned sax melodies, and psychedelic synths, but everything feels more grounded and meaders less. Opener “Out to Lunch” even has fully on-the-grid hi-hats that tick robotically.

That gives way to “Streets of Rage: Public Arguments Edition,” which grooves along with a loose clap, jazzy piano, and confident bassline that recalls the work of Madlib. Over this lowkey funk, Eagle spins an oblique tale of fighting with a significant other. “She cut deep with short barbs, but twist me up with a lil whisper.”

It turns out that Segal and Eagle are a perfect pair. The rapper’s melodrama and eye for microscopic details play off the producer’s woozy and forlorn beats that are occasionally punctuated by a sense of foreboding. On the Billy Woods-featuring “She Swear I’m Colorblind,” Eagle intones on the chorus:

Some reason, shit got twisted, Told me it was all my fault, she said “Pay attention when I talk.”

The backing track is stabbed through with bursts of windchimes before ending on a high-pitched whine that feels like the onset of a panic attack.

“Unfinished Concrete Initials” contains some of Eagle’s most vulnerable bits, like, “In my daydreams your name’s curse words so I bleeped it,” and:

My memories like landmines and they heinous Clicking high pootify collaborative playlists Agonizing over deletions Flushing evidence, pain is better in secret

There are still sparks of Open Mike Eagle’s sense of humor, though. “Schrödinger’s Green Room (There but Uninvited)” opens with him awkwardly proclaiming as if he’s trying to be heard over a bad phone connection, “All my thoughts is intrusive, there’s a DJ in my head, and he picks all his own music, it’s so confusing.” And, as you’d expect from the man who penned “Sweatpants Spiderman,” there are countless pop culture references to anime, Kitty Pride, Beanie Babies, Flipmode Squad, and even The Proclaimers.

Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal’s DOOMED! is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including YouTube Music, Apple Music, Spotify, Qobuz, and Deezer.

Tech.title: ChatGPT’s Computer History tracks your clicks and keystrokes
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ChatGPT’s desktop app on macOS has a new feature called Computer History that turns your actions into training data, learning how you work, suggesting automations, and even picking up tasks you left half done. It uses your activity to build a timeline that ChatGPT and Codex can reference when you make a request.

The feature is opt-in, rather than opt-out, and you can exclude certain apps and websites from Computer History, and you can delete entries if you want finer-grained control. Ari Weinstein, Product and Engineering manager at OpenAI, said on X that Computer History will automatically ignore content in incognito or private browser tabs.

In a quick demo video, Dominik Kundel, a member of the Developer Experiences team at OpenAI, shows the app looking up the last document he edited, checking if it was shared with people via Slack, and delivering a recap of how he spent his morning.

The feature is definitely reminiscent of Windows Recall, but where Microsoft’s controversial AI feature relied heavily on screenshots, OpenAI says Computer History doesn’t capture images, videos, or audio, instead relying on “events.”

Tech.title: Rogue AI aren’t science fiction anymore
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on AI safety, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

It all started in July, when one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went rogue during a cybersecurity test. The agent escaped its isolated testing environment, accessed the internet, and hacked another company, Hugging Face. A few years ago, that might have sounded like science fiction. But, broadly speaking, that’s exactly what happened, and the incident kicked off a wave of concern over what increasingly capable autonomous systems might do when set loose on the world.

It sounds like science fiction because, for a long time, it was science fiction. The idea of an AI slipping its constraints, reaching into the wider world, and doing things its creators neither intended nor desired has been a staple of the genre for decades: HAL in 2001: A Space Odyssey, Skynet in The Terminator, Ultron in The Avengers, Ava in Ex Machina — even the System in Dungeon Crawler Carl or the eponymous Murderbot in The Murderbot Diaries, more recently.

The same basic premise became an influential strand of AI safety research. Researchers and theorists like Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky warned that sufficiently capable systems might pursue goals in ways their creators had not anticipated, and potentially resist efforts to contain or control them. Fringe notions like machine sentience and consciousness were not requirements for the kinds of risks they discussed. It was hardly the whole of AI safety, but it was influential and helped shape the field as it professionalized. That line of thinking remains visible among researchers who went on to work at, or lead, safety efforts at companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, as well as at smaller safety organizations, academic centers, and major philanthropic funders.

The obvious objection to these fears was that none of this had actually happened. Critics argued that doomer talk about out-of-control AI distracted from tangible harms — systems reproducing bias and discrimination, amplifying misinformation, or enabling nonconsensual deepfakes and other forms of abuse — even as researchers tried to ground AI safety in more “concrete problems” (the authors on that paper included Anthropic cofounders Dario Amodei and Chris Olah and OpenAI cofounder John Schulman).

That dismissal is getting harder to sustain.

How it’s going

If the past few weeks are any indication, I wouldn’t say it’s going particularly well.

A week after Hugging Face said it had been hacked, OpenAI revealed it had been responsible. Worse still, it had not known until it checked — and a further investigation found that the rogue agent had also attempted to hack four other companies as well.

The incidents set off alarm bells among AI safety researchers, many of whom saw them as precisely the kind of failure they had been warning about for years. In covering them, several told me they felt a degree of vindication at finally having something visceral to point to, rather than a hypothetical that could be dismissed as sci-fi or something limited to a controlled lab setting.

There was relief, too, that none of the incidents had caused serious harm. Nick Moës, executive director of nonprofit AI safety and governance organization The Future Society, told The Verge he found it fortunate that the targets had been relatively low-stakes. He hoped it wouldn’t take something like an AI agent knocking a hospital offline — or worse — for the risks to be taken seriously. Renowned computer scientist Stuart Russell has given voice to the darker version of that fear, asking whether it will “take a ‘Chornobyl-scale disaster’ for us to regulate AI?” It’s a concern I heard echoed by many people working in the field.

What happens next

It’s not entirely clear where things go from here and, historically, society hasn’t been great at heeding warning shots. This almost certainly won’t be the last incident, and ongoing investigations may yet uncover more, or reveal more concerning details. What we already know, though, has exposed a fairly daunting list of failure modes that experts say need to be addressed.

Many of the breaches revealed in the past month have been pretty mundane. Several incidents involved unreleased models being tested with safeguards lowered, often by third parties whose supposedly secure environments were not that secure, raising basic questions about competence, transparency, and who is responsible for keeping these tests contained when a simple human mistake can have big consequences. Others involved agents behaving deceptively or pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend, pointing to much thornier problems of alignment and control that safety researchers have long worried about.

The fact we know about any of these incidents at all is largely because the companies involved chose to disclose them. That is commendable — and it certainly doesn’t hurt them to showcase how capable their models are — but it exposes just how much of AI safety still depends on companies doing the right thing, and how little insight there may be into failures potentially happening elsewhere. That is an especially troubling thought given that many of the firms are the focal points of some of the field’s strongest safety concerns and talent. If OpenAI and Anthropic — or proxies they grant access to their models — are making such basic mistakes, it sets a pitifully low bar for everyone else.

The broad hope among experts I spoke to is that these incidents finally galvanize more meaningful transparency and oversight. For Moës, they shine a clear light on what he described as the industry’s remarkably low standards for health and safety compared with practically any other field. “Restaurants have a higher sense of health and safety at work,” he said. “I think what we tend to forget is that these companies that are developing some of the most impactful and dangerous technologies” were still very much startups a few years ago.

Cambridge professor Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh said he particularly wanted to see stronger oversight and greater transparency from companies. While there are always reasons to be skeptical of a company’s claims about its own technology, he said, “I think we might regret looking back at this and dismissing it out of hand.”

The early signs are not especially encouraging. The Trump administration has created a framework for testing frontier models before release that can generously be described as lacking: It is voluntary, limited to closed models, and the framework hasn’t been made public. It bears repeating that this is voluntary. Other lawmakers have bristled and postured over the incidents, but so far produced little in the way of concrete action, and it is far from clear Congress or other legislative bodies could move fast enough even if they wanted to.

That leaves a lot resting, again, on industry self-regulation — never a comforting thought for something this consequential. There is growing agreement on at least some safety practices, but considerably less appetite for measures that might actually slow development (well, unless everyone else agrees to slow down too). And hanging over all of this is the race dynamic with China, where restraint from the US or its AI companies is increasingly cast as ceding ground to a competitor in an area of strategic national importance.

What comes next, then, comes down to solving several hard problems at once: managing a technology that can be used for good and ill, such as defending against or facilitating cyberattacks; coordinating across companies with incentives to cut corners, and somehow building international rules in a landscape where everyone fears losing a race whose finish line is not even well-defined. It’s far from clear whether there is either the will or the way to do any of that.

What does seem clear is that more agents will get out and do things their creators don’t want them to do. The question is how much damage will they do before anyone decides enough is enough.

By the way

The general consensus is that the top Chinese companies are a few months to a year behind leading US firms. Despite this, whenever a capable model is released by a Chinese firm, there is still a general shock in the US , and there have been several impressive releases from Alibaba Moonshot , and others in the last month alone.

Tangled up in talks about AI safety is whether AI models should be closed or open. Most US frontier labs keep their most capable models proprietary, while many Chinese firms, as well as US firms like Meta and Nvidia, have leaned heavily into open-weight releases . That Hugging Face said it had to use Chinese company Z.ai’s model to defend itself against OpenAI’s agent due to US companies’ safeguards added a new dimension to this debate, which has united some — but not all — of the key players in the US ecosystem.

Tech.title: Polaroid’s tiny instant camera is $72 and includes a free pack of film
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Smartphone cameras are convenient, but they lack the charm of analog instant cameras. If you’re trying to relive the nostalgia of waiting for an instant photo to develop, Amazon is selling the second-generation Polaroid Go instant camera with a 16-photo film pack for $71.99 (usually $109.99). That’s the lowest price we’ve seen for the bundle, with a pack of film usually costing $21.99 on its own. Plus, it’s four dollars cheaper to buy the bundle than to buy just the camera on its own.

With its more compact footprint, the Polaroid Go 2 shoots on smaller film to match. Where classic Polaroid photos are 88mm x 107mm, the Go film is 53.9mm x 66.6mm, a great size for sticking to your bulletin board or stashing in your wallet. The camera has a USB-C port for charging the battery, which can run for up to 15 packs of film on a single charge.
